chapters.n: The book opens by introducing Jeremiah, son of a priest named Hilkiah, from the priestly town of Anathoth a few miles northeast of Jerusalem. He was a contemporary of Lehi, who also prophesied in Jerusalem.

f.g: A Levitical town in Benjamin, about 3 miles (5 km) from Jerusalem.

chapters.n: God’s word first came to Jeremiah in the 13th year of good King Josiah—about 627/626 BC—shortly before Josiah’s great religious reform.
His ministry continued through the reigns of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah until Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC—about forty years of warning a people who mostly didn’t listen.

f.w: the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month

chapters.n: Jeremiah begins telling of his call in the first person.

God tells Jeremiah: before I formed you in the womb I knew you; before you were born I set you apart and appointed you a prophet to the nations. Latter-day Saints see here a witness of premortal life and foreordination.

f.w: Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee

f.g: Set apart, consecrated for holy service.
Appointed (Hebrew natan, “gave/set”).

chapters.n: Jeremiah protests: “I don’t know how to speak—I’m only a youth.” Like Moses and Enoch, he feels inadequate for his calling.

f.g: Hebrew na‘ar—a youth or young man, not necessarily a small child.

chapters.n: The Lord answers: don’t say you’re too young. You’ll go wherever I send you and say whatever I command. The calling depends on God, not on Jeremiah’s age.

f.w: Say not, I am a child

chapters.n: Don’t be afraid of people’s faces—I am with you to rescue you. God’s presence would be tested often in Jeremiah’s hard life.

f.w: Be not afraid of their faces
I am with thee to deliver thee

chapters.n: The Lord touches Jeremiah’s mouth and says, “I have put My words in your mouth”—a symbolic commissioning, like the coal on Isaiah’s lips.

f.w: I have put my words in thy mouth

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s job description: four negative verbs (uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow) and two positive ones (build, plant). Judgment comes first, but the goal is restoration. These six verbs recur throughout the book.

f.w: to root out, and to pull down

chapters.n: God shows Jeremiah a vision: “What do you see?” He sees a branch of an almond tree.

f.w: a rod of an almond tree
f.g: Hebrew shaqed. The almond is the first tree to blossom in late winter, as if “awake” early.

chapters.n: “You’ve seen well, for I am watching over My word to fulfill it.” A Hebrew wordplay: almond (shaqed) and watching (shoqed). God is wide awake and will carry out His word.

f.w: I will hasten my word to perform it
f.g: Better: “I am watching (shoqed) over My word”—a pun on almond (shaqed).

chapters.n: A second vision: a boiling pot tilted from the north, about to spill over.

f.g: A boiling cooking pot.

chapters.n: Disaster will pour out from the north on everyone in the land. Invaders from Mesopotamia came into Judah from the north along the trade routes, even though Babylon lies to the east.

f.w: Out of the north an evil shall break forth

chapters.n: God will summon northern kingdoms, whose rulers will set up their thrones at Jerusalem’s gates—as conquering kings did to sit in judgment. This happened when Babylon’s officers sat in the city gate (Jeremiah 39:3).

f.w: set every one his throne at the entering of the gates

chapters.n: God will pronounce judgment on Judah for abandoning Him, burning incense to other gods, and worshipping what their own hands made.

f.w: worshipped the works of their own hands

chapters.n: So get ready—tuck up your robe for action—and speak everything I command. Don’t be terrified of them, or I’ll terrify you in front of them.

f.g: Tuck your long robe into your belt so you can move freely—“get ready for action.”
Shatter or dismay you.

chapters.n: God makes Jeremiah a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls against kings, officials, priests, and people. The young man who felt weak will be made unbreakable.

f.w: a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls

f.g: Fortified.

chapters.n: They will fight him but won’t win, because the Lord is with him. Jeremiah was beaten, imprisoned, and thrown into a pit, yet he survived Jerusalem’s fall.

f.w: they shall not prevail against thee

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s first recorded sermon begins. It’s like a lawsuit from God against His unfaithful people.
God remembers Israel’s early devotion—like a young bride’s love—when she followed Him through the barren desert after the Exodus. The covenant is pictured as a marriage.

f.g: Your love as a bride (espousals = betrothal or wedding).

f.w: a land that was not sown
f.g: An unplanted land—the wilderness.

chapters.n: Israel was holy to the Lord, like the firstfruits of a harvest set apart for Him. Anyone who “ate” this sacred portion was guilty and would suffer.

f.g: The first and best of the harvest, which belonged to God and was forbidden to others.

chapters.n: Hear the Lord’s word, all Israel’s families.
What fault did your ancestors find in Me that they wandered so far, chasing worthless idols and becoming worthless themselves? We become like what we worship.

f.w: walked after vanity, and are become vain
f.g: Vanity = Hebrew hevel, “breath, vapor”—emptiness. Followed emptiness and became empty.

chapters.n: They never even asked, “Where is the Lord who brought us out of Egypt and guided us through that terrible desert?” They forgot their history.

f.g: Deep darkness—a land of danger.

chapters.n: God brought them into a fruitful land, but they polluted it and made His inheritance disgusting.

f.g: Literally “a land of Carmel”—garden land.

chapters.n: Every kind of leader failed: priests didn’t seek God, teachers of the law didn’t know Him, rulers rebelled, and prophets spoke for Baal.

f.g: Shepherds—here meaning rulers.
The Canaanite storm and fertility god.

chapters.n: So God will bring charges against them—and against their grandchildren.

f.g: Bring a legal case, contend in court.

chapters.n: Go west to the islands of Cyprus or east to the Arabian tribes of Kedar and look carefully: has anything like this ever happened?

f.g: Kittim—Cyprus and the western coastlands.
Desert tribes to the east (Isaiah 21:16).

chapters.n: No nation ever traded its gods—even though they aren’t real gods. Yet Israel traded its glorious God for worthless things.
Be appalled, O heavens! Shudder and be horrified! God calls creation to witness this betrayal.

A famous image: My people did two wrongs. They abandoned Me, the spring of living water, and dug cracked cisterns that can’t hold water. Why trade a fresh, flowing spring for stale water in a leaking tank?

f.g: Living water = fresh, flowing spring water.
Plastered pits dug in rock to store rainwater; if cracked, they leaked.

chapters.n: Is Israel a slave by birth? Why has he become plunder?

f.g: A slave born in his master’s household.

chapters.n: Lions (foreign armies) have roared over him, wasted his land, and burned his cities.
Even Egyptians from Memphis and Tahpanhes have shaved Israel’s head—humiliated it. King Josiah later died fighting Egypt.

f.g: Memphis, a major city of Egypt.
Tahpanhes, an Egyptian border fortress (Jeremiah 43:7).

f.w: broken the crown of thy head
f.g: Shaved or cracked your skull—a humiliation.

chapters.n: Haven’t you brought this on yourself by abandoning the Lord when He was leading you?
Why go to Egypt to drink from the Nile, or to Assyria to drink from the Euphrates? Judah kept looking to foreign powers for security instead of God.

f.g: A branch of the Nile.
The Euphrates.

chapters.n: Your own wickedness will punish you. Learn how bitter it is to abandon the Lord. Sin often carries its own consequences.

f.w: Thine own wickedness shall correct thee

f.g: Turnings away; apostasy.

chapters.n: God broke Israel’s yoke of slavery long ago, and they promised to serve Him—yet on every high hill and under every green tree they committed spiritual adultery with idols.

f.g: A prophetic metaphor for worshipping other gods—covenant unfaithfulness.

chapters.n: God planted Israel as a choice vine from pure stock. How did it become a wild, corrupt vine? Compare Isaiah’s song of the vineyard and Zenos’s allegory of the olive tree.

f.g: Rotten, corrupted.

chapters.n: No amount of washing with lye and soap will remove the stain of their guilt. Only God can cleanse sin.

f.g: Natron or lye, a mineral used as soap.

f.w: thine iniquity is marked before me

chapters.n: How can you claim you haven’t worshipped Baals? Look at what you did in the valley (likely the Valley of Hinnom). You’re like a restless young camel running in every direction.

f.g: Plural of Baal—local versions of the god.

f.w: see thy way in the valley

f.g: Young camel.

chapters.n: Like a wild donkey in heat sniffing the wind, she can’t be restrained; her pursuers don’t even have to try. Judah eagerly chases idols.

f.g: In her mating season.

chapters.n: Don’t run your feet bare and your throat dry chasing idols! But Judah says, “It’s no use—I love foreign gods and I’ll follow them.”
Like a thief caught in the act, Israel—kings, princes, priests, and prophets—will be ashamed.
They call a block of wood “my father” and a stone “my mother,” turning their backs on God—yet in trouble they cry, “Save us!” People often remember God only in crisis.

f.g: Block of wood—an idol or wooden pole.

f.w: in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us

chapters.n: Where are the gods you made? Let them save you! Judah has as many gods as it has cities.

f.w: according to the number of thy cities are thy gods

chapters.n: Why argue with Me? You have all rebelled.
God disciplined them, but they didn’t learn. They killed their own prophets like a ravaging lion.

f.w: your own sword hath devoured your prophets

chapters.n: Have I been a barren desert or a dark land to Israel? Why do they say, “We’re free; we won’t come to You anymore”?

f.g: We roam freely; we answer to no one.

chapters.n: Does a bride forget her jewelry or wedding sash? Yet My people have forgotten Me for countless days.

f.g: Her bridal sash or adornment.

chapters.n: You’re so skilled at chasing lovers that even the wicked can learn from you.

f.g: Shape your path cleverly.

chapters.n: Your clothing is stained with the blood of innocent poor people—not hidden away, but out in the open.

f.w: the blood of the souls of the poor innocents

f.g: The hems of your garments.

chapters.n: Yet you insist, “I’m innocent; surely His anger has passed.” God will judge precisely because you say you haven’t sinned. Denial blocks repentance.
Why do you keep changing course, running from one ally to another? Egypt will disappoint you just as Assyria did.

f.g: Wander restlessly.

chapters.n: You’ll leave Egypt with your hands on your head—a sign of grief and shame—because the Lord has rejected the ones you trusted.

f.g: A gesture of mourning or disgrace.

chapters.n: Under the law, a man who divorced his wife couldn’t remarry her after she married someone else. Judah has been unfaithful with many “lovers” (idols)—yet amazingly God still says, “Return to Me.” His mercy goes beyond what the law required.

f.w: If a man put away his wife

chapters.n: Look at the hilltop shrines—there’s no place you haven’t been unfaithful. You sat by the roadside waiting for lovers like a desert nomad waiting to ambush travelers.

f.g: Hilltop shrines where idols were worshipped.

f.w: as the Arabian in the wilderness
f.g: Like a desert raider lying in wait.

chapters.n: That’s why the rains were held back. Yet you have the brazen face of a prostitute and refuse to be ashamed.

f.w: there hath been no latter rain
f.g: The spring rains (March–April) that ripen crops.
A shameless, hardened face.

chapters.n: Haven’t you just been calling Me, “My Father, the companion of my youth”? Their words were affectionate, but their lives didn’t match.

f.g: The close companion or husband of my youth.

chapters.n: “Surely He won’t stay angry forever!” they say—while doing all the evil they can. Easy talk about God’s mercy without repentance.

f.w: Will he reserve his anger for ever?

chapters.n: A new message from Josiah’s reign. God asks Jeremiah if he has noticed what “faithless Israel”—the northern kingdom—did on every hill and under every tree.

f.g: Faithless or turning-away Israel—the northern kingdom, conquered by Assyria in 722 BC.

chapters.n: God waited for Israel to return, but she didn’t, and her treacherous sister Judah watched it all.
God gave northern Israel a “certificate of divorce”—exile by Assyria—yet Judah wasn’t afraid and did the same thing.
Treating unfaithfulness lightly, Israel polluted the land, committing “adultery” with stone and wooden idols.

f.g: Stone pillars and wooden poles used in idol worship.

chapters.n: Even after all this, Judah returned to God only in pretense, not with her whole heart. Josiah’s reforms changed outward worship, but many hearts stayed the same.

f.g: In pretense, falsely.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, faithless Israel looks more righteous than treacherous Judah, because Judah had Israel’s example and still didn’t learn.
Jeremiah is sent to call toward the north, where Israel’s exiles were scattered: “Return, faithless Israel. I won’t frown on you, for I am merciful and won’t stay angry forever.”
Just admit your sin—that you rebelled, gave your love to foreign gods, and didn’t obey. Acknowledging sin is the doorway to forgiveness.

Return, faithless children, for I am your husband. I will take you one from a city and two from a family and bring you to Zion. Latter-day Saints often apply this to the latter-day gathering—converts gathered a few at a time.

f.w: one of a city, and two of a family

chapters.n: God will give them shepherds after His own heart who will feed them with knowledge and understanding—faithful leaders, unlike the self-serving ones of Jeremiah’s day.

When the people multiply, they won’t even talk about the ark of the covenant anymore, or miss it or rebuild it. God’s presence will no longer be tied to one sacred box. The ark seems to have disappeared around the Babylonian conquest.
Instead, all of Jerusalem will be called the throne of the Lord, and all nations will gather there in His name, no longer following their stubborn, evil hearts.

f.w: the imagination of their evil heart
f.g: Stubbornness of heart—a favorite phrase of Jeremiah.

chapters.n: Judah and Israel—divided since Solomon’s death—will walk together again, returning from the north to the promised land. A prophecy of reunion among the tribes.

f.w: the house of Judah shall walk with the house of Israel
out of the land of the north

chapters.n: God says: I longed to treat you as My own children, giving you the loveliest inheritance on earth, and I hoped you would call Me “My Father” and never turn away.

f.w: Thou shalt call me, My father

chapters.n: But like a wife who betrays her husband, Israel has been unfaithful to God.
Weeping is heard on the hilltops—the very places of idolatry—as Israel cries, realizing they twisted their path and forgot the Lord.

f.g: Crying and pleading prayers.

chapters.n: God calls, “Return, and I will heal your faithlessness.” The people respond: “Here we come, for You are the Lord our God.” A model of repentance: God invites, and people answer.
The people confess: the noisy rites on the hills were a delusion. Salvation is truly found only in the Lord our God.

f.w: truly in the LORD our God is the salvation of Israel

chapters.n: “The shameful thing” (often a nickname for Baal) has devoured everything our ancestors worked for—even our sons and daughters, possibly referring to child sacrifice.

f.g: Hebrew boshet, a mocking substitute for the name Baal.

chapters.n: Let us lie down in our shame and be covered with disgrace, for we and our ancestors have sinned and not obeyed. Honest, complete confession.

f.w: we have sinned against the LORD our God

chapters.n: God answers the people’s confession: if you truly return and remove your detestable idols, you won’t have to wander into exile.

f.w: If thou wilt return, O Israel

f.g: Wander—be driven from the land.

chapters.n: If you swear “As the Lord lives” with truth, justice, and righteousness, then the nations will be blessed through Him—fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: the nations shall bless themselves in him

chapters.n: An agricultural image: plow up your hard, unused ground and don’t sow among thorns. Prepare your hearts before trying to grow anything good.

f.g: Plow hard, unplowed soil—make your hearts soft and ready.

chapters.n: Circumcise your hearts. Physical circumcision was the sign of the covenant; God wants inner commitment—hearts cut free from sin—or His anger will burn like unquenchable fire.

f.w: take away the foreskins of your heart

chapters.n: Sound the alarm! Blow the trumpet across the land and tell people to flee to the fortified cities.

f.g: Fortified, walled towns.

chapters.n: Raise a signal flag toward Zion; run for safety and don’t delay! God is bringing disaster from the north.

f.g: Raise a signal pole to direct refugees.

f.w: I will bring evil from the north

chapters.n: A lion has come out of its thicket—a destroyer of nations is on the move to devastate Judah. The lion represents Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar.

f.w: The lion is come up from his thicket

f.g: The destroyer of nations.

chapters.n: So put on sackcloth, mourn, and wail—the Lord’s fierce anger has not turned away.

f.g: Wear rough goat-hair cloth—a sign of mourning.

chapters.n: On that day the king and officials will lose courage, the priests will be horrified, and the prophets stunned. The leaders who promised safety will be paralyzed.

f.w: the heart of the king shall perish

chapters.n: Jeremiah cries out in anguish: Lord, You’ve let this people be deceived by promises of peace, but the sword is at their throat! The false prophets had promised peace, and God allowed the deception they wanted to hear.

f.w: surely thou hast greatly deceived this people
f.g: A lament: God permitted false prophets’ comforting lies.

chapters.n: A scorching wind from the desert heights is blowing toward the people—not the gentle breeze used to winnow grain, but a destructive blast.

f.w: not to fan, nor to cleanse
f.g: Not a winnowing breeze that separates chaff, but a hot, destructive wind (the sirocco).

chapters.n: This wind is too strong for winnowing; it comes at God’s command as He pronounces judgment.
Look! The enemy rises like storm clouds, chariots like a whirlwind, horses faster than eagles. “Woe to us—we are ruined!”

f.w: his horses are swifter than eagles

f.g: Plundered, devastated.

chapters.n: Jerusalem, wash the evil from your heart so you can be saved. How long will you harbor wicked thoughts? Even at the last moment, repentance is possible.

f.g: Wicked or worthless thoughts.

chapters.n: A messenger announces disaster from Dan in the far north and then from the hills of Ephraim, closer to Jerusalem. The news travels south as the invader approaches.

f.g: Israel’s northernmost city.
The hill country just north of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Announce to the nations: besiegers are coming from a distant land, shouting war cries against Judah’s cities.

f.g: Besiegers, those who surround a city.

chapters.n: Like guards around a field, they surround Jerusalem—because she rebelled against God.
Your own behavior brought this on you. This is the bitter fruit of your wickedness, and it pierces to your heart.

f.w: Thy way and thy doings have procured these things

chapters.n: Jeremiah cries out in physical pain: “My anguish, my anguish! My heart is pounding—I can’t keep quiet!” He hears the war trumpet in his soul. Jeremiah is often called the “weeping prophet.”

f.g: My insides, my deepest feelings—the seat of emotion in Hebrew thought.

chapters.n: Disaster after disaster—the whole land is ruined. Suddenly the tents are destroyed, the curtains torn down in a moment.

f.g: Homes—Jeremiah speaks for the whole people.

chapters.n: How long must I see the battle flag and hear the trumpet?
God explains: My people are foolish. They don’t know Me. They are clever at doing evil but have no idea how to do good.

f.g: Stupid, senseless.

f.w: they are wise to do evil

chapters.n: Jeremiah sees a vision of creation undone: the earth “without form and void” and the sky dark—the same words as Genesis 1:2. Sin is pictured as reversing creation.

f.g: Hebrew tohu va-bohu—the phrase used for the earth before creation.

chapters.n: Mountains quake and hills sway—the stable world shaken.

f.w: the mountains, and, lo, they trembled

chapters.n: No people anywhere, and even the birds have fled. Creation’s final works—humans and birds—are gone.
The fertile land has become desert and its cities lie in ruins before the Lord’s fierce anger. A garden turned back to wilderness.

f.g: Hebrew Carmel—the garden land.

chapters.n: Yet a glimmer of mercy: the whole land will be desolate, but God will not make a complete end. A remnant will survive.

f.w: yet will I not make a full end

chapters.n: The earth mourns and the heavens grow dark, because God has spoken and will not change His decision.

f.g: Will not change My mind or relent.

chapters.n: At the sound of horsemen and archers, every town empties; people hide in thickets and climb among rocks.
Jerusalem is pictured as a woman dressing in scarlet, gold jewelry, and eye makeup to win over her lovers (foreign allies). It’s useless—those lovers despise her and want her dead.

f.g: Enlarge your eyes with dark eye paint (kohl).

chapters.n: Jeremiah hears a cry like a woman in labor with her first child—Zion gasping, stretching out her hands: “Woe is me! I’m fainting before murderers.”

f.g: Stretching out hands in helpless pleading.

chapters.n: God challenges: search Jerusalem’s streets and squares—if you can find even one person who acts justly and seeks truth, I will forgive the city. It recalls Abraham bargaining for Sodom.

f.w: if ye can find a man

f.g: Public squares.

chapters.n: Even when they swear “As the Lord lives,” their oaths are lies. Religious words without honest hearts.
Jeremiah prays: Lord, You look for faithfulness. You struck them, but they felt nothing; You disciplined them, but they refused correction. They made their faces harder than rock.

f.w: they have made their faces harder than a rock
they have refused to receive correction

chapters.n: Jeremiah thought: maybe these are just poor, uneducated people who don’t know God’s ways.
So he went to the leaders, who surely knew God’s law—but they too had snapped the yoke and broken the bonds. Rich and poor alike had thrown off the covenant.

f.w: broken the yoke, and burst the bonds

chapters.n: So wild beasts will attack: a lion from the forest, a desert wolf, a leopard prowling near their towns—images of the invading armies.

f.g: Or “a wolf of the deserts.”

chapters.n: How can I forgive this? Your children abandoned Me and swore by false gods. When I fed them full, they committed adultery and flocked to prostitutes’ houses. Prosperity led to spiritual and moral decay.

f.w: when I had fed them to the full

chapters.n: They were like well-fed stallions, each neighing for his neighbor’s wife—an earthy image of lust out of control.

f.g: Lusty, well-fed stallions.

chapters.n: Shouldn’t I punish such things? Shouldn’t I avenge Myself on a nation like this?

f.g: Here means punish or call to account.

chapters.n: Enemies are told to go through her vineyard rows and destroy—but not completely. Strip away the branches, for they don’t belong to the Lord.

f.g: Probably “branches” of a vine—Israel pictured as a vineyard.

chapters.n: Both Israel and Judah have been utterly unfaithful.
They lied about the Lord, saying, “He won’t do anything; no disaster will come; we’ll never see war or famine.” Denying consequences is a classic form of unbelief.

f.g: “He won’t act” or “He doesn’t exist.”

f.w: neither shall evil come upon us

chapters.n: They say the prophets are just wind with no word from God—so let what they predict happen to them.

f.g: A pun: ruach means both wind and spirit.

chapters.n: Because they say this, God will make His words in Jeremiah’s mouth a fire and the people wood, and the fire will consume them.

f.w: I will make my words in thy mouth fire

chapters.n: God will bring a distant nation—mighty, ancient, speaking a language you don’t understand. This was Babylon.

f.w: a nation whose language thou knowest not

chapters.n: Their quivers are like open graves—every arrow brings death—and all their soldiers are warriors.

f.g: An open tomb, ready to swallow the dead.

chapters.n: They will devour everything—harvest, food, children, flocks, vines, fig trees—and break down the fortified cities you trusted.

f.w: they shall eat up thine harvest

f.g: Walled, fortified cities.

chapters.n: Yet again God promises: even then, I will not make a complete end of you.

f.w: I will not make a full end with you

chapters.n: When people ask why God did this, answer: as you abandoned Me and served foreign gods in your own land, so you’ll serve foreigners in a land not yours. The punishment matches the sin.

f.w: so shall ye serve strangers in a land that is not yours

chapters.n: Announce this to all of Jacob and Judah.
Listen, foolish people who have eyes but don’t see and ears but don’t hear. Spiritual blindness is willful.

f.w: which have eyes, and see not

chapters.n: Don’t you fear Me? I set the sand as a permanent boundary for the sea; waves pound and roar, but can’t cross it. Even the sea obeys God—but His people don’t.

f.w: placed the sand for the bound of the sea

chapters.n: But this people has a stubborn, rebellious heart; they have turned away and gone.

f.w: a revolting and a rebellious heart

chapters.n: They never say, “Let’s fear the Lord, who gives the autumn and spring rains and guarantees our harvest weeks.” They take blessings for granted.

f.g: The early (autumn) and late (spring) rains essential for crops in Israel.

f.w: the appointed weeks of the harvest
f.g: The seven weeks between Passover and Pentecost (Shavuot).

chapters.n: Your sins have turned these blessings away and kept good things from you.

f.w: your sins have withholden good things from you

chapters.n: Wicked men lurk among God’s people like hunters setting traps—but they catch people, not birds.
Like a cage stuffed with birds, their houses are full of things gained by fraud. That’s how they became powerful and rich.

f.w: As a cage is full of birds
f.g: A fowler’s basket packed with trapped birds.

chapters.n: They’re fat and sleek, and their evil has no limits. They don’t defend orphans or the poor in court—yet they prosper. God sees injustice toward the vulnerable as a grave sin.
God repeats His question from verse 9: shouldn’t I punish these things?

f.w: Shall I not visit for these things?

chapters.n: Something shocking and horrible has happened in the land.
Prophets lie, priests rule by their own authority—and My people love it that way! But what will you do when the end comes? People often prefer leaders who tell them what they want to hear.

f.w: my people love to have it so

f.g: Rule at their own direction, or hand in hand with the false prophets.

chapters.n: Jeremiah, from the tribe of Benjamin, warns his kin to flee Jerusalem. Blow the trumpet in Tekoa and light a fire signal at Beth-haccerem—towns south of the city—because disaster is coming from the north. There’s a pun: Tekoa sounds like the Hebrew “blow” (tiq‘u).

f.g: A town about 10 miles south of Jerusalem; home of the prophet Amos.
“House of the vineyard,” a hill town near Jerusalem used for signal fires.

f.w: evil appeareth out of the north

chapters.n: Zion is like a lovely, delicate woman—or, as some translate, a pleasant pasture—about to be overrun.

f.g: Lovely, attractive.

chapters.n: Enemy kings, pictured as shepherds, will camp around her with their “flocks” (armies), each grazing his section bare.

f.g: A metaphor for foreign rulers and their troops.

chapters.n: The enemy speaks: “Get ready for battle! Let’s attack at noon!” Then, frustrated: “Too bad, the day is ending and the shadows are long.”

f.g: Literally “sanctify war”—armies performed religious rites before battle.

chapters.n: “Then let’s attack by night and destroy her palaces!” The enemy is relentless.
God Himself commands: cut down trees and build a siege ramp against Jerusalem. This city must be punished; it is full of oppression. The Babylonians built such ramps.

f.g: Build a siege ramp.

f.w: she is wholly oppression in the midst of her

chapters.n: As a well keeps its water fresh, Jerusalem keeps her wickedness flowing. Violence and destruction echo in her streets; sickness and wounds are always before God.

f.w: As a fountain casteth out her waters
f.g: As a well keeps its water flowing fresh.

chapters.n: Take warning, Jerusalem, or I will turn away from you in disgust and make you an empty wasteland. God still pleads.

f.w: lest my soul depart from thee

chapters.n: The enemy will glean Israel’s remnant thoroughly, like a grape picker passing his hand over the branches again and again to get every cluster.

f.g: Thoroughly pick over—gleaning means gathering what’s left after harvest.

chapters.n: Jeremiah asks: who will even listen to my warning? Their ears are “uncircumcised”—closed. God’s word offends them; they take no pleasure in it.

f.g: Closed, unresponsive—as if covered.

f.w: the word of the LORD is unto them a reproach

chapters.n: Jeremiah is full of the Lord’s anger and tired of holding it in. It will be poured out on children in the street, young men, husbands and wives, and the very old—no one exempt.

f.w: I am weary with holding in
him that is full of days
f.g: The very old.

chapters.n: Their houses, fields, and wives will be given to others when God stretches out His hand against the land—the curses of the covenant fulfilled.

f.w: their houses shall be turned unto others

chapters.n: From least to greatest, everyone is greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. Corruption runs through the whole society.

f.w: every one is given to covetousness

chapters.n: They dress the people’s wound superficially, saying “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. A key verse: false comfort that ignores the real problem only lets the wound fester.

f.w: Peace, peace; when there is no peace

f.g: Lightly, superficially.

chapters.n: Were they ashamed of their disgusting acts? Not at all—they didn’t even know how to blush. So they will fall with everyone else.
Stand at the crossroads and look; ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it—you’ll find rest for your souls. But they said, “We won’t.” Jesus echoes the promise of rest.

f.w: ye shall find rest for your souls

chapters.n: God posted watchmen—prophets—saying, “Listen for the trumpet!” But they replied, “We won’t listen.”
So God calls the nations as witnesses to see what will happen to His people.
Listen, earth: God will bring disaster on this people—the fruit of their own schemes—because they rejected His words and law.
Why bring Me imported frankincense from Sheba and fragrant cane from far away? Your offerings aren’t acceptable. Expensive worship can’t cover disobedience.

f.g: Frankincense from southern Arabia—a luxury import.

f.w: your burnt offerings are not acceptable

chapters.n: So God will put obstacles before them; fathers and sons, neighbors and friends will stumble and perish together.
A people is coming from the north—a great nation stirred up from the ends of the earth.

f.g: The farthest parts of the earth.

chapters.n: Armed with bow and spear, cruel and merciless, roaring like the sea, riding horses in battle formation against Zion.

f.w: they are cruel, and have no mercy

chapters.n: The people respond: we’ve heard the reports, and our hands hang limp; anguish grips us like a woman in labor.

f.w: as of a woman in travail

chapters.n: Don’t go out into the fields or walk the roads—the enemy’s sword is there, and terror is everywhere.

f.g: Hebrew magor missaviv—“terror all around,” a phrase Jeremiah repeats.

chapters.n: Put on sackcloth and roll in ashes; mourn bitterly as for an only son, for the destroyer will suddenly come.

f.g: Roll in ashes—an extreme sign of grief.

chapters.n: God tells Jeremiah: I have made you an assayer and tester among My people, to examine and test their ways—like someone testing metal.

f.g: Better: “an assayer and a tester” of metals.
Test their conduct, as metal is tested.

chapters.n: They are all hardened rebels, spreading slander—as hard as bronze and iron, and all corrupt.
A refining image: the bellows blow fiercely and the lead is consumed by fire, but the refining fails—the impurities won’t separate. Despite all efforts, the wicked aren’t removed.

f.g: The bellows blow hard (to heat the furnace).
The refiner smelts for nothing—the dross remains.

chapters.n: They’ll be called “rejected silver,” because the Lord has rejected them. Silver that can’t be purified is thrown away.

f.g: Rejected, worthless silver.

chapters.n: This begins Jeremiah’s famous “Temple Sermon,” probably given early in Jehoiakim’s reign (about 609 BC). Jeremiah 26 tells how it nearly got him killed.

f.w: The word that came to Jeremiah

chapters.n: God sends Jeremiah to stand at the temple gate and speak to worshippers as they enter—the most public and provocative place possible.

f.w: Stand in the gate of the LORD's house

chapters.n: The message: change your ways and actions, and I will let you keep living in this land.

f.w: Amend your ways and your doings

f.g: Improve, make good.

chapters.n: Don’t trust the deceptive chant, “This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord!” People assumed that because God’s house stood in Jerusalem, the city could never fall—no matter how they lived.

f.g: Repeated three times as a kind of magic slogan for safety.

f.w: Trust ye not in lying words

chapters.n: If you truly change your ways and deal justly with one another…

f.g: Practice justice.

chapters.n: …if you don’t oppress foreigners, orphans, and widows, don’t shed innocent blood, and don’t chase other gods to your own harm…

f.w: the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow

chapters.n: …then I will let you live in this land forever. The promise is conditional on covenant faithfulness.
But you trust in lies that won’t help you.
You steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods—breaking most of the Ten Commandments…

f.w: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery

chapters.n: …and then come stand in My house and say, “We’re safe!”—only to go on doing these detestable things? Worship cannot be a license to sin.

f.g: We are safe—as if the temple were a hiding place.

chapters.n: Has My house become a hideout for robbers? Jesus quoted this when He drove the moneychangers out of the temple. Robbers return to their den to be safe between crimes.
Go look at Shiloh, where My tabernacle once stood, and see what I did to it. Shiloh had been Israel’s worship center, but it was destroyed, likely by the Philistines.

f.g: A town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli and Samuel.

chapters.n: God “rose up early” to speak to them—an idiom for persistent, eager effort—but they wouldn’t listen or answer.

f.g: A Jeremiah idiom: speaking again and again, with eagerness.

chapters.n: So God will do to this temple what He did to Shiloh. Babylon destroyed Solomon’s temple in 586 BC.

f.w: as I have done to Shiloh

chapters.n: He will cast them out of His sight just as He cast out Ephraim—the northern kingdom, exiled by Assyria in 722 BC.
A startling command: don’t pray for this people—I won’t listen. Their rebellion has reached a point where intercession can’t stop the judgment.

f.w: pray not thou for this people

chapters.n: Don’t you see what they’re doing everywhere in Judah and Jerusalem?
Whole families join in: children gather wood, fathers light fires, women knead dough for cakes to the “queen of heaven”—probably the goddess Ishtar/Astarte. Idolatry had become a family tradition.

f.g: Likely the Mesopotamian Ishtar or Canaanite Astarte, goddess of love and fertility.
Wine or other liquid poured out as an offering.

chapters.n: Are they really hurting Me? No—they’re hurting themselves, to their own shame.

f.w: the confusion of their own faces
f.g: Their own disgrace and shame.

chapters.n: God’s anger will pour out on people, animals, trees, and crops, burning without being put out.
Sarcastically God says: go ahead, add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves—they mean nothing to Me.

f.w: Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices
f.g: Burnt offerings were wholly burned for God; God says eat them too—they’re no longer holy to Him.

chapters.n: When God brought Israel out of Egypt, His first concern wasn’t sacrifices. Sacrifices weren’t the heart of the covenant.
What He commanded was: obey My voice, and I will be your God and you will be My people. Obedience is the core of covenant relationship.

f.w: Obey my voice, and I will be your God

chapters.n: But they didn’t listen; they followed their own stubborn hearts and went backward instead of forward.
Since the Exodus, God sent prophet after prophet, day after day.
Yet they didn’t listen; they stiffened their necks and did worse than their ancestors.

f.g: Were stubborn, like an ox refusing the yoke.

chapters.n: God tells Jeremiah plainly: you will speak, but they won’t listen; you will call, but they won’t answer. Faithful prophets aren’t measured by how many listen.

f.w: they will not hearken to thee

chapters.n: Say: this nation won’t obey God or accept correction. Truth has died; it has vanished from their lips.
Cut off your hair and throw it away—a sign of mourning—and wail on the bare hills, for the Lord has rejected this generation.

f.g: Shaving the head was a sign of deep mourning.

chapters.n: They even put their idols in God’s own temple, defiling it.

f.w: they have set their abominations in the house

chapters.n: Worst of all, they built shrines at Tophet in the Valley of Hinnom to burn their children—something God never commanded and never even thought of. God is horrified by it.

f.g: A place of child sacrifice in the Hinnom Valley, south of Jerusalem.

f.w: the valley of the son of Hinnom
f.g: Hebrew Ge-Hinnom—the origin of “Gehenna,” a New Testament word for hell.

f.w: neither came it into my heart

chapters.n: That valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter; so many will die that they’ll bury people there until there’s no room left.
Bodies will be left as food for birds and beasts, with no one to scare them away—one of the covenant curses.

f.w: meat for the fowls of the heaven

f.g: Frighten, scare away.

chapters.n: God will silence every sound of joy—celebration, gladness, and the voices of bride and groom at weddings. The land will be desolate. Later Jeremiah promises these sounds will return.

f.w: the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride

chapters.n: Continuing from chapter 7: invaders will dig up the bones of kings, officials, priests, prophets, and citizens from their tombs—an extreme dishonor in the ancient world.

f.w: they shall bring out the bones

chapters.n: Their bones will be spread out before the sun, moon, and stars they loved and worshipped—exposed to the very “gods” that couldn’t help them—and left like manure on the ground.

f.g: The sun, moon, and stars, worshipped as gods.

f.w: for dung upon the face of the earth

chapters.n: Survivors scattered in exile will wish they were dead rather than alive.

f.w: death shall be chosen rather than life

chapters.n: God asks common-sense questions: when people fall, don’t they get back up? When someone goes the wrong way, doesn’t he turn back?
So why does Jerusalem keep turning away endlessly? They cling to deceit and refuse to come back. A wordplay: “turn” and “return” (shuv) run through these verses.

f.g: Constant turning away—a play on the Hebrew shuv (turn/return).

chapters.n: God listened, but no one said what was right or repented—no one asked, “What have I done?” Everyone charges ahead like a horse plunging into battle.

f.w: as the horse rusheth into the battle

chapters.n: Even migrating birds—stork, dove, crane, swallow—know their seasons and return on time. But God’s people don’t know His ways. Nature obeys its Creator better than His people do.

f.w: the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times

f.g: The turtledove, a migratory bird—not the reptile.

chapters.n: How can you claim to be wise because you have the Lord’s law, when the scribes’ lying pens have twisted it? Having scripture isn’t the same as obeying it.

f.w: the pen of the scribes is in vain
f.g: Or “the lying pen of the scribes has made it a lie.”

chapters.n: The so-called wise will be shamed and trapped. They rejected God’s word—so what wisdom do they really have?

f.w: they have rejected the word of the LORD

chapters.n: So their wives and fields will go to others, because everyone, from least to greatest, is greedy, and prophets and priests deal falsely. (Verses 10–12 repeat 6:12–15.)

f.w: I give their wives unto others

chapters.n: Leaders dress the people’s deep wound lightly, saying “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace.

f.w: Peace, peace; when there is no peace

chapters.n: They aren’t ashamed of their detestable deeds and can’t even blush, so they’ll fall when God calls them to account.
God will strip them bare: no grapes on the vine, no figs on the tree, even the leaves withered. What He gave will be taken away. Jesus’s cursing of the barren fig tree echoes this.

f.w: nor figs on the fig tree

chapters.n: The people say: why are we sitting here? Let’s flee to the fortified cities and die there quietly, because God has given us poisoned water to drink for our sins.

f.g: Poisoned or bitter water.

chapters.n: We hoped for peace, but nothing good came; we hoped for healing, but terror came instead.

f.w: We looked for peace, but no good came

chapters.n: The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan in the far north; the whole land shakes at the neighing of the war stallions as they devour the land.

f.g: His powerful war horses.

chapters.n: God will send poisonous snakes that can’t be charmed—an image of an enemy no one can bargain with or bribe.

f.g: Venomous snakes, vipers.

chapters.n: Jeremiah speaks his grief: my sorrow is beyond healing, my heart is sick within me.

f.w: my heart is faint in me

chapters.n: Listen to the cry of my people from a faraway land: “Isn’t the Lord in Zion? Isn’t her King there?” God answers: why did they provoke Me with idols and foreign nothings?

f.w: Is not the LORD in Zion?

f.g: Foreign worthless idols.

chapters.n: A haunting line: “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.” The seasons for help have come and gone. Latter-day revelation uses this line as a warning against delaying repentance.

f.w: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved

chapters.n: Jeremiah is crushed because his people are crushed. He mourns in dark clothes, and horror grips him. A prophet who feels deeply the suffering of the people he warns.

f.g: I go about in mourning (dark clothes or a darkened face).
Horror, dismay.

chapters.n: “Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there?” Gilead, east of the Jordan, was famous for a healing resin. Healing is available, so why won’t the people be healed? Christians often see Christ as the true balm and physician.

f.g: A fragrant healing resin exported from Gilead.

chapters.n: Jeremiah wishes his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain of tears so he could weep day and night for his slain people. This verse is why he’s called “the weeping prophet.” (In Hebrew Bibles this is 8:23.)

f.w: Oh that my head were waters

chapters.n: In the same breath, he wishes he had a traveler’s shack in the desert so he could get away from them all—a band of unfaithful traitors. Love and frustration mix in his heart.

f.w: a lodging place of wayfaring men
f.g: A rough desert inn for travelers.
Unfaithful—both literally and in breaking covenant with God.

chapters.n: They bend their tongues like bows to shoot lies. They aren’t courageous for truth; they go from one evil to another and don’t know God.

f.w: they are not valiant for the truth

chapters.n: Be careful of your neighbor; don’t trust even your brother—every brother is a deceiver like Jacob, and every friend a slanderer. Trust has collapsed.

f.g: A wordplay on Jacob’s name: “every brother will Jacob-ize”—cheat and trip up.

chapters.n: They deceive their neighbors and never speak the truth. They’ve trained their tongues to lie and wear themselves out doing wrong.

f.w: taught their tongue to speak lies

chapters.n: You live surrounded by deceit, and through deceit they refuse to know Me.
So God will refine and test them like metal in a furnace—what else can He do for His people?

f.w: I will melt them, and try them

chapters.n: Their tongue is a deadly arrow. A man speaks friendly words to his neighbor while secretly setting an ambush.

f.w: one speaketh peaceably to his neighbour with his mouth

f.g: Lies in ambush.

chapters.n: God repeats: shouldn’t I punish this? Shouldn’t I avenge Myself on such a nation?
Jeremiah (or God) mourns for the mountains and pastures, scorched so no one passes through. No cattle lowing, birds and animals gone—an eerie silence.

f.g: Pastures of the open country.

chapters.n: Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins and a home for jackals; Judah’s towns will be empty.

f.g: A haunt of jackals (Hebrew tannim).
Piles of rubble.

chapters.n: Who is wise enough to understand this? Who has heard from God and can explain why the land is ruined like a desert?
The Lord answers: because they abandoned My law and didn’t obey My voice.
They followed their own stubborn hearts and the Baals their fathers taught them. False traditions passed from parents to children.
So God will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water—bitterness and suffering.

f.g: A very bitter plant, a symbol of sorrow and bitterness.

chapters.n: He will scatter them among nations they never knew and send the sword after them. The scattering of Israel was foretold by Moses.

f.w: I will scatter them also among the heathen

chapters.n: Call for the professional mourning women—the skilled ones—to come. Ancient funerals employed women trained in lament.

f.g: Professional mourners who led public weeping.
Skilled women (expert at lament).

chapters.n: Let them hurry and wail for us until our eyes run with tears.
A cry is heard from Zion: “How we are ruined! We are deeply ashamed, for we’ve left our land and our homes have been torn down.”
Women, hear God’s word: teach your daughters to wail and one another a funeral song. So many will die that more mourners will be needed.
Death has climbed in through the windows and entered the palaces, cutting down children in the streets and young men in the squares. Death is pictured as a thief or invader.

f.w: death is come up into our windows

chapters.n: Bodies will lie like dung in open fields, like stalks left behind a reaper that no one gathers.

f.g: Bundles of cut grain left behind by a reaper.

chapters.n: One of Jeremiah’s best-known teachings: the wise shouldn’t boast in their wisdom, the strong in their strength, or the rich in their riches.

f.w: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom

f.g: Boast, take pride.

chapters.n: Instead, let anyone who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows Me—that I am the Lord who shows steadfast love, justice, and righteousness, for these delight Me. Knowing God is life’s true treasure.

f.w: that he understandeth and knoweth me

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, steadfast covenant love.

chapters.n: The days are coming when God will punish everyone circumcised only in the flesh—outward sign without inward faithfulness.

f.g: Circumcised in body but uncircumcised in heart.

chapters.n: Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and desert tribes who clip the hair at their temples—they all practiced circumcision, but it means nothing. Judah, though circumcised, is “uncircumcised in heart.”

f.w: all that are in the utmost corners
f.g: Literally “those with clipped temples”—desert tribes who cut their hair at the sides.

chapters.n: Jeremiah calls Israel to hear what the Lord says about the nations’ idols.
Don’t copy the ways of the nations or be terrified by signs in the sky, as they are. Ancient peoples feared eclipses and comets as omens; God’s people needn’t fear them.

f.w: Learn not the way of the heathen

f.g: Eclipses, comets, and other sky events read as omens by astrologers.

chapters.n: Their customs are empty: someone cuts down a tree, and a craftsman shapes it with a chisel.

f.w: the customs of the people are vain

chapters.n: They decorate it with silver and gold and nail it down so it won’t fall over. Some readers have compared this to modern Christmas trees, but the passage is about idols.
Idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field: they can’t talk, must be carried because they can’t walk. Don’t fear them—they can’t harm you or help you.

f.g: Better: “like a scarecrow in a cucumber field.”

chapters.n: No one is like You, Lord. You are great, and Your name is mighty.

f.w: there is none like unto thee

chapters.n: Who wouldn’t fear You, King of the nations? Among all the world’s wise men and kingdoms, there is no one like You.

f.g: Belong; it is Your due.

chapters.n: Idolaters are senseless and foolish; their teaching is worthless, coming from a block of wood.

f.g: Stupid, like an animal.

f.w: the stock is a doctrine of vanities
f.g: Instruction from a piece of wood is nonsense.

chapters.n: Imported silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz, shaped by skilled craftsmen and dressed in royal blue and purple—it’s all just human handiwork.

f.g: A distant western port, perhaps in Spain.
An unknown gold-producing region, possibly Ophir.
Expensive dyes reserved for royalty and the wealthy.

chapters.n: But the Lord is the true God, the living God, the eternal King. The earth quakes at His anger, and nations can’t endure His wrath.
Unusually, this verse is written in Aramaic, the international language of the day—perhaps so Judah could repeat it to Babylonians: gods who didn’t make heaven and earth will vanish from the earth.

f.w: The gods that have not made the heavens and the earth
f.g: The only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah, likely a ready-made reply to foreigners.

chapters.n: God made the earth by His power, set the world in place by His wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by His understanding.

f.w: He hath made the earth by his power

f.g: Understanding, insight.

chapters.n: When He speaks, the skies roar with water; He lifts clouds from the ends of the earth, sends lightning with rain, and brings wind from His storehouses. The true God controls the weather that Baal was falsely credited with.

f.w: bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures

chapters.n: Every idol maker is senseless and shamed by his idol. His image is a fraud—there’s no breath in it.

f.w: there is no breath in them

f.g: A metalworker who casts idols.

chapters.n: They are worthless, objects of mockery; when judgment comes they will perish.

f.g: A work of mockery—laughable.

chapters.n: But Jacob’s portion—the Lord—is nothing like them. He formed all things, and Israel is the tribe He claimed as His inheritance. His name is the Lord of Hosts.

f.g: The tribe of his inheritance.

chapters.n: Jeremiah turns to the coming siege: pick up your bundle and get ready to leave, you who live under siege.

f.g: Pack your bundle for exile.

chapters.n: God says He will sling out the land’s inhabitants like stones from a sling and press them hard so they feel it.

f.w: I will sling out the inhabitants

chapters.n: Jerusalem (or Jeremiah) cries: my wound is incurable! But I said, “This is my sickness, and I must bear it.” Accepting consequences is the first step toward healing.

f.w: Truly this is a grief, and I must bear it

chapters.n: My tent is ruined, its ropes snapped; my children are gone, and no one is left to pitch my tent again. Zion is pictured as a mother whose home and children are lost.

f.w: my children are gone forth of me

chapters.n: The shepherds (rulers) are senseless and don’t seek the Lord, so they fail and their flocks scatter. Leadership failure leads to scattering.
Listen—news is coming, a great uproar from the north, to make Judah’s towns desolate, a haunt of jackals.

f.g: Report, rumor, news (an old word).

chapters.n: A humble prayer: Lord, I know a person’s path isn’t in his own control; no one can direct his own steps. We need God’s guidance.

f.w: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps

chapters.n: Correct me, Lord, but with fairness—not in anger, or You’d reduce me to nothing. A plea for loving discipline.
Pour out Your fury on the nations that don’t know You and don’t call on Your name, for they have devoured Jacob. Psalm 79:6-7 contains nearly the same words.

f.w: Pour out thy fury upon the heathen

chapters.n: A new message from the Lord to Jeremiah, this time about the covenant.

Hear the words of “this covenant” and tell them to Judah and Jerusalem. Many scholars think this refers to the covenant renewed under Josiah after the Book of the Law (likely Deuteronomy) was found in the temple.
Cursed is anyone who doesn’t obey the terms of this covenant. The covenant included blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience.

f.w: Cursed be the man that obeyeth not

chapters.n: God gave this covenant when He brought Israel out of Egypt—the “iron furnace” of slavery. The heart of it: obey My voice, and you will be My people and I will be your God.

f.g: A smelting furnace—an image of Egypt’s harsh bondage.

f.w: so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God

chapters.n: Obedience allowed God to keep His oath to give them a land flowing with milk and honey. Jeremiah answers, “Amen, Lord”—he agrees with God’s terms.

f.w: a land flowing with milk and honey

f.g: Hebrew amen—“truly, let it be so.”

chapters.n: God sends Jeremiah through Judah’s towns and Jerusalem’s streets: listen to the covenant and live by it.

f.w: Hear ye the words of this covenant, and do them

chapters.n: Ever since the Exodus God warned their ancestors persistently—rising early to warn them—“Obey My voice.”

f.g: Warning urgently and repeatedly.

chapters.n: But they didn’t obey; each followed his stubborn heart. So God brought on them all the covenant’s curses.

f.w: the imagination of their evil heart

chapters.n: God reveals a conspiracy in Judah and Jerusalem—a deliberate, organized turning away from Him.
They have gone back to their ancestors’ sins and other gods. Both Israel and Judah have broken the covenant. Josiah’s reforms were apparently being undone.
So God will bring a disaster they can’t escape, and though they cry to Him, He won’t listen.

f.w: though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken

chapters.n: Then they’ll run to the gods they burned incense to—but those gods won’t save them at all.

f.w: they shall not save them at all

chapters.n: Judah has as many gods as towns and as many Baal altars as Jerusalem has streets. Baal is called “that shameful thing.”

f.w: according to the number of thy cities were thy gods

f.g: Hebrew boshet, a scornful substitute for Baal’s name.

chapters.n: So again: don’t pray for this people—God won’t listen when they cry out in trouble.

f.w: pray not thou for this people

chapters.n: What right does My beloved have in My house when she has done so many vile deeds? Can sacred meat (sacrifices) take away your sin? You even celebrate when you do evil.

f.g: Sacrificial meat; the Hebrew may ask, “Can vows and holy meat remove your evil?”

chapters.n: The Lord once called Israel a flourishing olive tree, beautiful with good fruit. Now, with a roar like a storm, He sets it on fire and its branches break. Compare Zenos’s allegory of Israel as an olive tree.
The Lord who planted Israel has decreed disaster because of the evil they did, provoking Him by burning incense to Baal. They brought it on themselves.

f.w: which they have done against themselves

chapters.n: A new section: God reveals to Jeremiah a plot against his life.

Jeremiah was like a trusting lamb led to slaughter, not knowing they were plotting: “Let’s destroy the tree with its fruit and wipe his name from memory.” The language anticipates Isaiah 53 and Jesus’s rejection.

f.w: like a lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter
cut him off from the land of the living

chapters.n: Jeremiah appeals to God, who judges fairly and tests the deepest thoughts and heart: let me see You act against them, for I’ve committed my case to You.

f.w: triest the reins and the heart
f.g: Reins = kidneys, thought of as the seat of emotions; God examines inner feelings and thoughts.

chapters.n: The plotters were men from Anathoth—Jeremiah’s own hometown and probably relatives—who threatened, “Stop prophesying in the Lord’s name or we’ll kill you.”

f.w: Prophesy not in the name of the LORD

chapters.n: God promises to punish them: young men will die by the sword and their children by famine.

No remnant of the plotters will be left when their time of punishment comes. Interestingly, Ezra 2:23 records 128 men of Anathoth returning from exile—the town survived, though the conspirators didn’t.

f.g: The time of their punishment.

f.w: there shall be no remnant of them

chapters.n: Jeremiah begins honestly: “Lord, You are always right—but let me argue my case with You. Why do the wicked prosper? Why do traitors live at ease?” Faith can include hard questions asked respectfully.

f.w: Wherefore doth the way of the wicked prosper?

chapters.n: You planted them and they took root and bear fruit. You are always on their lips but far from their hearts—religious talk without real devotion.

f.w: thou art near in their mouth, and far from their reins

f.g: Kidneys—the inner self, emotions.

chapters.n: But You know me, Lord; You’ve tested my heart. Drag them off like sheep to slaughter and set them apart for judgment.
How long will the land suffer drought because of the people’s wickedness? Animals and birds are dying, because the people say, “God won’t see what happens to us.”

f.w: He shall not see our last end
f.g: Possibly “He (Jeremiah) won’t live to see our end”—mocking the prophet.

chapters.n: God answers with a challenge rather than an explanation: if racing against men on foot has worn you out, how will you compete with horses? If you stumble in safe country, what will you do in the Jordan’s thick jungle? Harder trials are coming—God is training Jeremiah’s endurance.

f.w: how canst thou contend with horses?

f.g: The dense thickets along the Jordan River, where lions lurked.

chapters.n: Even your own brothers and family have betrayed you and are shouting against you. Don’t trust them, even when they speak kindly.

f.w: thy brethren, and the house of thy father

chapters.n: Now God expresses His own grief: I have abandoned My house, left My inheritance, and handed the love of My life to her enemies. God feels the pain of the judgment He must send.

f.w: the dearly beloved of my soul

chapters.n: My people have turned on Me like a lion roaring in the forest, so I have turned away from her.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “I have rejected it” or “turned away from it.”

chapters.n: My inheritance is like a strangely colored bird attacked by other birds of prey. Call the wild animals to come and devour! Israel, once distinct, is now a target.

f.g: A bird of unusual color, mobbed by others; or a hyena’s lair.

chapters.n: Many shepherds (foreign rulers) have ruined God’s vineyard, trampled His field, and turned His lovely land into a wasteland.

f.w: Many pastors have destroyed my vineyard

chapters.n: The desolate land mourns to God, because no one cares—no one takes it to heart.

f.w: no man layeth it to heart

chapters.n: Destroyers swarm over the bare hills; the Lord’s sword devours from one end of the land to the other. No one has peace.
They planted wheat but harvested thorns; they worked themselves sick for nothing. They will be ashamed of their meager crops because of God’s anger.

f.w: They have sown wheat, but shall reap thorns

chapters.n: God now speaks about Judah’s “evil neighbors”—nations that plundered Israel’s land. He will uproot them too, and uproot Judah from among them.

f.g: Neighboring nations such as Edom, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines.

chapters.n: Then, surprisingly, God will have compassion on them as well and bring each nation back to its own land. His mercy extends beyond Israel.

f.w: I will return, and have compassion on them

chapters.n: If those nations will truly learn the ways of God’s people and swear “As the Lord lives,” as they once taught Israel to swear by Baal, they will be established among God’s people. Gentiles can be grafted in.

f.w: then shall they be built in the midst of my people

chapters.n: But any nation that won’t obey will be completely uprooted and destroyed.

f.w: I will utterly pluck up and destroy that nation

chapters.n: God gives Jeremiah an object lesson: buy a linen waistcloth, wear it, and don’t wash it. Prophets often acted out messages so people would remember them. Linen also recalls priestly garments.

f.g: A linen sash or loincloth worn close to the body.
Don’t wash or soak it—keep it as is.

chapters.n: Jeremiah obeys and puts it on.
A second message comes.

Take the waistcloth to the Euphrates and hide it in a crack in the rocks. The Euphrates was hundreds of miles away; some think the Hebrew Perath could refer to Parah, a spring near Anathoth, chosen to evoke the Euphrates—Babylon’s river.

f.g: Hebrew Perath; possibly the village of Parah (Joshua 18:23) a few miles from Anathoth, symbolizing Babylon.

chapters.n: Jeremiah does exactly as told.
Many days later God tells him to go back and dig it up.
He finds it rotted and ruined—good for nothing.

f.g: Ruined, spoiled.

chapters.n: The Lord explains the sign.
In the same way, God will ruin Judah’s pride—the great pride of Jerusalem. What was close to God, once separated and left near Babylon, decays.
This wicked people who refuse to listen, follow their stubborn hearts, and worship other gods will become like this useless cloth.
The key meaning: as a waistcloth clings close to a man’s body, God bound Israel and Judah close to Himself, to be His people, His renown, praise, and glory. But they wouldn’t listen.

f.w: so have I caused to cleave unto me
for a name, and for a praise, and for a glory

chapters.n: Another sign: “Every jar should be filled with wine.” The people respond, “Obviously!”—a common saying, perhaps from wine-sellers or drinkers.

f.g: A large clay jar for storing wine.

chapters.n: God explains: I will fill everyone—kings on David’s throne, priests, prophets, and citizens—with drunkenness, meaning confusion and helplessness under judgment.
He will smash them against each other like jars—fathers and sons together—without pity.

f.w: I will dash them one against another

chapters.n: Listen and pay attention; don’t be proud—the Lord has spoken.
Give glory to God now, before darkness falls and your feet stumble on dark mountains—before the light you hope for becomes deep gloom. There is still time.

f.w: Give glory to the LORD your God

f.g: Mountains at dusk, where travelers stumble.

chapters.n: If you won’t listen, I will weep in secret for your pride, my eyes overflowing, because the Lord’s flock is taken captive. The prophet’s tears show his love.

f.w: my soul shall weep in secret places

chapters.n: Tell the king and queen mother: come down from your thrones, because your glorious crowns have fallen. This likely refers to young King Jehoiachin and his mother Nehushta, taken to Babylon in 597 BC.

f.w: the king and to the queen
f.g: Probably Jehoiachin and the queen mother Nehushta.
Royal headdresses, crowns.

chapters.n: The towns of the Negev in the south will be shut up with no one to open them. All Judah will be taken captive.

f.g: Towns in the Negev desert region.

chapters.n: Look at the invaders from the north! Where is the beautiful flock entrusted to you? Leaders will answer for their people.

f.w: where is the flock that was given thee

chapters.n: What will you say when the very allies you cultivated become your masters? Pain will seize you like a woman in labor.

f.w: thou hast taught them to be captains
f.g: You trained them (foreign powers) to be your friends—now they’ll rule you.

chapters.n: If you ask, “Why is this happening to me?”—it’s because of your many sins that your skirts are lifted and you are violated—a picture of public humiliation.

f.g: Your robes stripped up—exposed in shame.

chapters.n: A famous proverb: can an Ethiopian change his skin, or a leopard its spots? Then neither can you do good who are used to doing evil. Habits of sin become nearly unbreakable without God. (It is a statement about deep-rooted habits, not about race.)

f.w: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
f.g: Ethiopian here = Cushite, from the Nile region south of Egypt.

chapters.n: So God will scatter them like chaff blown by the desert wind.
This is your lot, the share I’ve measured out for you, because you forgot Me and trusted in lies.
God will lift her skirts over her face so her shame is seen—exposure as punishment for unfaithfulness.
I’ve seen your adulteries, your lustful neighing, your shameless idolatry on the hills. Woe to you, Jerusalem! How long until you’re made clean? God still longs for her cleansing.

f.w: wilt thou not be made clean?

chapters.n: A message about a severe drought. Under the covenant, drought was one of the warnings that came with disobedience.

f.g: Drought; literally “the droughts.”

chapters.n: Judah mourns; her city gates (where people gathered) are lifeless; people sit in black mourning on the ground, and Jerusalem’s cry rises up.

f.w: they are black unto the ground
f.g: Mourning in dark clothes, sitting on the ground.

chapters.n: Even nobles send servants for water; they reach the cisterns and find nothing, and come back with empty jars, covering their heads in shame.

f.g: Their servants or lesser people.
A sign of grief and shame.

chapters.n: The ground is cracked because there’s no rain; farmers are dismayed and cover their heads.

f.g: Chapped—cracked and dried.

chapters.n: Even a doe gives birth in the field and abandons her newborn because there’s no grass—a heartbreaking image of desperation in nature.

f.g: A female deer.

chapters.n: Wild donkeys stand on bare hills panting for air like jackals; their eyes fail because there’s no vegetation.

f.g: Jackals.

chapters.n: Jeremiah prays for the people: though our sins testify against us, act for the sake of Your name. We have turned away many times; we have sinned against You.

f.w: do thou it for thy name's sake

chapters.n: O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of trouble, why are You like a stranger in the land, a traveler who stops for just one night?
Why are You like a confused man, a warrior who can’t save? Yet You are among us, Lord, and we bear Your name—don’t abandon us.

f.g: Dumbfounded, stunned.

f.w: we are called by thy name

chapters.n: God answers: these people love to wander and don’t hold back their feet, so He doesn’t accept them. He will remember their sins and punish them.

f.w: Thus have they loved to wander

chapters.n: Again: don’t pray for this people’s welfare.
Even when they fast and offer sacrifices, God won’t accept them; instead sword, famine, and plague will come. Ritual without repentance doesn’t move God.

f.w: When they fast, I will not hear their cry
by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence

chapters.n: Jeremiah protests: but Lord, the prophets keep telling them, “You won’t see sword or famine; God will give you lasting peace here.” He partly excuses the people as misled.

f.w: I will give you assured peace

chapters.n: God replies: those prophets speak lies in My name. I didn’t send them, command them, or speak to them. Their visions are false, their divination worthless—products of their own hearts.

f.w: The prophets prophesy lies in my name

f.g: Fortune-telling, forbidden in Israel (Deuteronomy 18:10).

chapters.n: Those prophets who promise no sword or famine will themselves die by sword and famine.

f.w: By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed

chapters.n: The people who believed them will lie unburied in Jerusalem’s streets with their families. Following false prophets doesn’t excuse anyone from consequences.

f.w: they shall have none to bury them

chapters.n: Jeremiah is told to say: let my eyes overflow with tears night and day, for my people—the virgin daughter—has suffered a terrible wound.

f.w: Let mine eyes run down with tears

chapters.n: In the fields lie those killed by the sword; in the city, people dying of hunger. Prophets and priests wander into a land they don’t know—exile.

f.w: go about into a land that they know not
f.g: Or “go about the land without understanding.”

chapters.n: The people pray: have You completely rejected Judah? Do You despise Zion? We hoped for peace and healing but found only terror.

f.w: we looked for peace, and there is no good

f.g: Loathed, detested.

chapters.n: We admit our wickedness and our ancestors’ sin; we have sinned against You.

f.w: We acknowledge, O LORD, our wickedness

chapters.n: For the sake of Your name, don’t reject us or dishonor Your glorious throne (the temple). Remember Your covenant—don’t break it.

f.g: Jerusalem or the temple, where God’s presence was enthroned.

f.w: break not thy covenant with us

chapters.n: Can any of the nations’ idols bring rain? Can the sky give showers on its own? Only You, Lord. So we will hope in You, the Maker of all things. A confession that only God controls life’s blessings.

f.w: Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain?

chapters.n: God answers the people’s prayer of chapter 14: even if Moses and Samuel—Israel’s greatest intercessors—stood pleading before Me, I wouldn’t change My mind. Send them away. Judgment is now certain.

f.w: Though Moses and Samuel stood before me

chapters.n: If they ask where to go, tell them: those destined for death, to death; sword, to sword; famine, to famine; captivity, to captivity. Each will meet the fate their choices led to.

f.w: such as are for the captivity, to the captivity

chapters.n: God will send four destroyers: the sword to kill, dogs to drag away, birds and beasts to devour.

f.g: Four kinds of destroyers.

chapters.n: They will become a horror to all kingdoms because of what King Manasseh did in Jerusalem. Manasseh, Hezekiah’s son, filled the city with idols and innocent blood during his long reign.

f.w: because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah

chapters.n: Who will pity you, Jerusalem? Who will mourn for you or even stop to ask how you are?

f.w: who shall go aside to ask how thou doest?
f.g: Who will turn aside to ask about your peace (shalom)?

chapters.n: You rejected Me and kept going backward. So I will stretch out My hand and destroy you; I’m tired of holding back. God had relented many times before.

f.g: I am tired of relenting (changing My mind about punishment).

chapters.n: God will winnow them with a winnowing fork at the city gates, robbing them of children, because they won’t turn from their ways.

f.w: I will fan them with a fan
f.g: Winnow them with a winnowing fork—scatter them like chaff.

chapters.n: Widows will be more than the sand of the sea. A destroyer will strike mothers of young men at noon—when no attack is expected.

f.g: An attack at midday, a time thought safe.

chapters.n: The mother of seven—a picture of complete blessing—faints and breathes her last; her sun sets while it’s still day. Even the most blessed will suffer loss.

f.g: Seven sons was a sign of perfect fortune (Ruth 4:15; 1 Samuel 2:5).

f.w: her sun is gone down while it was yet day

chapters.n: Jeremiah cries: “Woe is me, my mother, that you gave birth to me—a man everyone quarrels with! I’ve neither lent nor borrowed money (which often caused disputes), yet everyone curses me.” His calling has made him an outcast.

f.g: Lending at interest; here simply lending and borrowing, which commonly bred conflict.

chapters.n: The Lord replies: surely I will strengthen you for good; I will make your enemies plead with you in times of disaster. This came true when Zedekiah later sought Jeremiah’s counsel.

f.w: I will cause the enemy to entreat thee well

chapters.n: Can anyone break iron—iron from the north and bronze? A riddle: Babylon’s power from the north can’t be broken by Judah—or, Jeremiah’s God-given strength can’t be broken.

f.g: Bronze (Hebrew neḥoshet); steel was not yet in common use.

chapters.n: God tells Judah: your wealth and treasures will be plundered without payment because of all your sins.
You will serve your enemies in a land you don’t know, for God’s anger burns like fire. (Verses 13–14 repeat 17:3-4.)

f.w: a fire is kindled in mine anger

chapters.n: Jeremiah prays: Lord, You understand. Remember me and take care of me; avenge me on my persecutors. Don’t let Your patience with them cost me my life. I suffer insults for Your sake.

f.w: for thy sake I have suffered rebuke

chapters.n: A beautiful verse: when Your words came, I devoured them, and they became my joy and my heart’s delight, for I bear Your name. Perhaps an echo of the Book of the Law found in Josiah’s day. Scripture can be food for the soul.

f.w: Thy words were found, and I did eat them
I am called by thy name

chapters.n: I never sat with the partygoers or joined their fun. Because Your hand was on me, I sat alone, filled with Your indignation at sin. Faithfulness cost him friendships.

f.w: I sat not in the assembly of the mockers
I sat alone because of thy hand

chapters.n: Why is my pain endless and my wound incurable? Will You be to me like a deceptive brook that dries up when needed? An astonishingly honest prayer from a weary prophet.

f.g: A wadi or stream that dries up in summer—disappointing the thirsty.

chapters.n: God responds with a gentle rebuke: if you turn back to Me, I will restore you and you’ll stand before Me. If you speak what is precious, not what is worthless, you’ll be My mouthpiece. Let them turn to you—don’t turn to them.

f.g: Even the prophet is called to “return” (repent) from discouragement.

f.w: thou shalt be as my mouth
take forth the precious from the vile
f.g: Separate what is valuable from what is worthless, like refining metal.

chapters.n: God renews the promise from Jeremiah’s call: I will make you a fortified bronze wall. They will fight you but won’t win, for I am with you to save and rescue you.

f.w: I am with thee to save thee

chapters.n: I will rescue you from the hands of the wicked and redeem you from the grip of the ruthless.

f.g: The ruthless, tyrants.

chapters.n: Another word from the Lord, this time affecting Jeremiah’s personal life.
God tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this land. In a culture where marriage and children were expected and treasured, his single life became a living sign of the coming disaster.

f.w: Thou shalt not take thee a wife

chapters.n: Here’s why: consider the children born in this land and their parents…
…they will die terrible deaths—from disease, sword, and famine—unmourned and unburied, their bodies food for birds and beasts.

f.w: they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth

chapters.n: Don’t enter a house of mourning or comfort the bereaved, for God has withdrawn His peace, steadfast love, and mercy from this people. Jeremiah’s absence from funerals was itself a message.

f.w: I have taken away my peace from this people

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—covenant love and loyalty.

chapters.n: Great and small will die unburied and unmourned. No one will cut themselves or shave their heads for them—pagan mourning customs the law forbade but which people still practiced.

f.w: nor cut themselves, nor make themselves bald

chapters.n: No one will break bread to comfort mourners or offer the “cup of consolation” for a lost father or mother. Even the rituals of comfort will disappear.

f.g: Better: “break bread”—a funeral meal for mourners.
A cup of wine given to comfort mourners.

chapters.n: Nor should Jeremiah join any feast. He abstains from both mourning and celebrating.
In your own lifetime, God will silence all joy—the sounds of celebration and weddings.

f.w: the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride

chapters.n: When the people hear this, they’ll ask, “What have we done? What sin deserves all this?” They seem genuinely blind to their guilt.
Answer: your ancestors abandoned Me, followed other gods, and didn’t keep My law.

f.w: Because your fathers have forsaken me

chapters.n: And you’ve done worse than they did, each following his stubborn, evil heart and refusing to listen.

f.w: ye have done worse than your fathers

chapters.n: So God will throw you out into a land you never knew, and there you’ll serve other gods day and night—getting what you wanted, with no favor from Him.

f.w: there shall ye serve other gods day and night

chapters.n: Suddenly, hope breaks in: a day is coming when people will no longer swear “As the Lord lives, who brought Israel out of Egypt”…

f.w: that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: …but “As the Lord lives, who brought Israel back from the north and from every land where He scattered them.” The future gathering will outshine even the Exodus. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the latter-day gathering of Israel, including from the “north countries.”

f.w: from the land of the north
I will bring them again into their land

chapters.n: God will send many fishermen to catch them and then many hunters to search every mountain, hill, and cave. In context this may describe enemies hunting the guilty, but Latter-day Saints have often applied it to missionaries gathering scattered Israel.

f.w: I will send for many fishers

chapters.n: God’s eyes are on all their ways; nothing is hidden from Him, including their sins.

f.w: mine eyes are upon all their ways

chapters.n: First, though, He will repay their sin in full, because they polluted His land with the lifeless “corpses” of their idols.

f.g: In full, to the complete measure.

f.w: the carcases of their detestable and abominable things
f.g: Lifeless idols, pictured as corpses defiling the land.

chapters.n: Jeremiah responds with a prayer of faith: Lord, my strength, fortress, and refuge, nations will come from the ends of the earth and confess, “Our ancestors inherited nothing but lies and worthless idols.” A vision of the Gentiles turning to God.

f.w: O LORD, my strength, and my fortress

chapters.n: Can people make their own gods? Such things are not gods at all.
So this time God will teach them—show them His hand and power—and they will know that His name is the Lord (Jehovah).

f.w: they shall know that my name is The LORD

chapters.n: Judah’s sin is engraved with an iron tool and a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts and on the horns of their altars. God once wrote His law on stone; now sin is etched deep inside them.

f.g: An iron stylus for carving stone.
The raised corners of an altar, where sacrificial blood was smeared for atonement (Leviticus 4:7).
