chapters.n: Their children remember their pagan altars and Asherah poles by every green tree on the high hills. Idolatry has been passed to the next generation.

f.g: Asherah poles—wooden symbols of the goddess Asherah.

chapters.n: God’s mountain (Jerusalem) and all its treasures will be plundered because of sin at its high places throughout the land.

f.w: O my mountain in the field

chapters.n: Through your own fault you’ll lose the inheritance God gave you, and serve enemies in a strange land. You’ve lit a fire in God’s anger that will burn on.

f.g: Let go of—lose—your inheritance, as in the sabbatical year when land was released.

chapters.n: A famous contrast in wisdom style: cursed is the person who trusts in mere humans, relies on human strength, and turns his heart from the Lord. Nephi echoes this almost exactly.

f.w: Cursed be the man that trusteth in man

f.g: Relies on human power for strength.

chapters.n: Such a person is like a scrubby bush in the desert that never sees good come—living in parched, salty, empty land.

f.g: A stunted desert shrub, perhaps the juniper.
Barren salt flats where nothing grows, like near the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: But blessed is the person who trusts in the Lord, whose confidence is the Lord Himself.

f.w: Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD

chapters.n: He is like a tree planted by water, sending roots down to the stream. It doesn’t fear the heat; its leaves stay green and it keeps bearing fruit even in drought. Trust in God gives deep roots that hold in hard seasons.

f.w: as a tree planted by the waters
shall not be careful in the year of drought
f.g: Careful = anxious, worried.

chapters.n: The heart is more deceitful than anything and desperately sick—who can understand it? We can fool even ourselves, which is why we need God’s searching light.

f.w: The heart is deceitful above all things

f.g: Incurably sick or diseased.

chapters.n: God answers: I, the Lord, search the heart and test the inner self, to give each person what his actions and choices deserve.

f.w: I the LORD search the heart
according to the fruit of his doings

chapters.n: Like a partridge sitting on eggs she didn’t lay (an ancient belief), a person who gets rich dishonestly will lose it in midlife and end up a fool.

f.w: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not
f.g: Ancient folk belief held that the partridge hatched other birds’ eggs, whose chicks then left her.

f.w: he that getteth riches, and not by right

chapters.n: Jeremiah praises: a glorious throne, exalted from the beginning, is the place of our sanctuary—God’s presence in the temple.

O Lord, Hope of Israel, all who abandon You will be ashamed; those who turn away will be written in the dust—quickly erased—because they forsook the Lord, the fountain of living water. Some connect this with Jesus writing in the dust in John 8.

f.g: Names written in dust, soon blotted out—unlike names written in the book of life.

chapters.n: Heal me, Lord, and I will be healed; save me, and I will be saved, for You are the one I praise. True healing and salvation come only from God.

f.w: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed

chapters.n: People taunt Jeremiah: “Where is this word of the Lord you keep predicting? Let it happen!” Mockers often scoff when judgment seems delayed.

f.w: Where is the word of the LORD?

chapters.n: Jeremiah protests his sincerity: I didn’t run from being Your shepherd, and I never wanted the day of disaster. You know what I said was right before You.

f.w: neither have I desired the woeful day

chapters.n: Don’t become a terror to me; You are my refuge in the day of disaster.

f.w: thou art my hope in the day of evil

chapters.n: Let my persecutors be shamed, not me; let them be terrified, not me. Bring on them the day of disaster with double destruction. Honest prayers in scripture sometimes voice raw feelings that the gospel of Christ later invites us to transform into forgiveness.

f.w: Let them be confounded that persecute me

chapters.n: God sends Jeremiah to stand at the People’s Gate, used by the kings, and at all of Jerusalem’s gates—the busiest public places.

f.w: the gate of the children of the people
f.g: Probably a main city gate used by the public and the royal household.

chapters.n: Listen, kings of Judah and all who come through these gates.
Be careful: don’t carry loads or bring goods through Jerusalem’s gates on the Sabbath. Commerce on the Sabbath had become normal.

f.w: bear no burden on the sabbath day

chapters.n: Don’t carry loads out of your houses or do any work, but keep the Sabbath holy as God commanded your ancestors.

f.g: Make holy, set apart.

chapters.n: But their ancestors didn’t listen—they stiffened their necks and refused to be taught.
If you carefully obey and keep the Sabbath holy, doing no work on it...

f.w: if ye diligently hearken unto me

chapters.n: …then kings on David’s throne will keep riding through these gates with their officials and people, and this city will be inhabited forever. Small acts of obedience carry big blessings.

f.w: sitting upon the throne of David

chapters.n: People will come from all over—Judah’s towns, Benjamin, the western foothills, the hill country, and the Negev—bringing offerings, incense, and thanksgiving to the Lord’s house.

f.g: The Shephelah—the low foothills west of Judah.
The Negev desert region.
Thank offerings.

chapters.n: But if you won’t keep the Sabbath holy and keep hauling loads through the gates, God will set fire to the gates that will consume Jerusalem’s palaces and can’t be put out. Babylon burned the city in 586 BC.

f.w: then will I kindle a fire in the gates thereof

chapters.n: A new message begins. As often in Jeremiah, the Lord teaches not only with words but with an object lesson drawn from everyday life.
The Lord sends Jeremiah down to a potter’s workshop, promising to speak to him there. Ordinary work becomes a classroom for revelation.

f.g: Workshops were likely in the lower part of the city, near water and clay—perhaps by the Potsherd Gate (19:2).

chapters.n: Jeremiah obeys and watches a craftsman shaping clay on his wheel.

f.g: Wrought = worked, was making something.
Hebrew ’obnayim, literally “two stones”—a potter’s wheel of an upper and lower disk, turned by foot or hand.

chapters.n: The pot is flawed, but the potter doesn’t throw the clay away—he reshapes it into a new vessel. The point is hopeful: while clay is still soft, it can be remade.

f.g: Spoiled, ruined in the making.

chapters.n: Now the Lord explains what Jeremiah has just seen.
Israel is like clay in God’s hands. He has the right and power to reshape his people—but, as the next verses show, how he shapes them depends on how they respond.

f.w: as the clay is in the potter's hand

chapters.n: If God announces that a nation will be uprooted and torn down…

f.w: to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy

chapters.n: …and that nation repents, God will change course and not send the disaster. His warnings are invitations, not fixed fate.

f.g: In KJV usage, God “repenting” means relenting or changing a planned action; “evil” here means calamity, not sin.

chapters.n: Likewise, when God promises to build up and plant a nation…
…but it turns to evil and will not obey, he will withhold the blessing he promised. Covenant blessings depend on faithfulness—a principle of agency.
So the Lord tells Judah plainly: I am shaping disaster against you—but turn back now, every one of you, and make your lives good. The door is still open.

f.g: An old expression meaning “come now.”
Hebrew yotser—the same word as “potter.” God is “potting” a disaster, a deliberate wordplay.

chapters.n: The people’s answer is chilling: “It’s hopeless—we’ll do what we want.” They have given up on change and chosen their own stubborn hearts.

f.g: Stubbornness, the hardened will of the heart.

chapters.n: The Lord says even pagan nations have never seen anything like it: his own “virgin” people—meant to be pure and devoted—have done something horrible.

f.g: The nations, non-Israelite peoples.
A poetic name for the nation as God’s bride or daughter, stressing what she should have been.

chapters.n: Does snow ever leave Lebanon’s peaks, or do cold mountain streams dry up? Nature stays faithful to its course—but Israel has abandoned its true source.

f.g: Mount Hermon and the Lebanon range carry snow much of the year, feeding the Jordan and other streams.

chapters.n: They have forgotten God, burned incense to empty idols, and left the “ancient paths” for rough, unbuilt trails that make them stumble.

f.g: Emptiness—a common word for idols, which have no real power.
A road not built up or graded—an unmade, dangerous track.

chapters.n: The result will be a ruined land that passersby hiss and shake their heads at in shock.

f.g: Whistling or hissing in astonishment or scorn at a ruin.

chapters.n: God will scatter them like a scorching desert wind, and in their crisis he will turn his back to them, as they turned their backs on him.

f.g: The hot, dry sirocco from the desert that withers everything.

f.w: I will shew them the back, and not the face

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s enemies plot against him: “We’ll still have priests, wise men, and prophets without him—let’s attack him with words and ignore him.” They trusted religious institutions more than God’s living messenger.

f.g: Slander him, bring accusations against him.

chapters.n: Jeremiah turns to the Lord in prayer, asking him to listen to what his accusers are saying.
“Is good repaid with evil?” Jeremiah reminds God that he had once pleaded for these very people. Now they have dug a pit to trap him.

f.w: digged a pit for my soul
I stood before thee to speak good for them

chapters.n: In anguish, Jeremiah asks God to let the coming judgment fall on his persecutors. This is a raw, honest lament, like many Psalms—the Bible records his pain without endorsing every wish.

f.w: deliver up their children to the famine

chapters.n: He prays that cries of terror will be heard in their homes when raiders come, because they set traps for his feet.

f.g: A band of raiders or invading soldiers.

chapters.n: Jeremiah leaves justice with God, who knows their plots to kill him. Later revelation calls disciples to forgive, but this lament shows the real anguish of a persecuted prophet.
Another object lesson with pottery. This time Jeremiah buys a finished, fired clay jar and brings senior leaders of the people and priests as witnesses.

f.g: Hebrew baqbuq—a narrow-necked clay jug, named for the gurgling sound it makes when poured.
Elders, senior leaders.

chapters.n: He goes to the Valley of Hinnom just outside Jerusalem’s walls—the very place where the worst idolatry had been practiced.

f.w: the valley of the son of Hinnom
f.g: A ravine south and southwest of Jerusalem. Its Hebrew name, Ge-Hinnom, later became “Gehenna,” a New Testament word for hell.
Hebrew “Harsith gate,” likely the Potsherd Gate, where broken pottery was dumped.

chapters.n: Jeremiah addresses the kings and people of Jerusalem: disaster is coming so terrible that everyone who hears of it will have ringing ears.
The reasons: they abandoned the Lord, turned this place into a site of foreign worship, and filled it with the blood of innocent people.

f.g: Made it foreign—handed it over to strange gods.

chapters.n: Worst of all, they burned their own children as offerings to Baal. The Lord insists he never commanded such a thing—it never even entered his mind. Child sacrifice is the opposite of his nature.

f.w: to burn their sons with fire

f.g: Hilltop or raised shrines used for worship, often of false gods.

chapters.n: The valley will get a new name: no longer Tophet or Hinnom, but “Valley of Slaughter,” because the killing done there will be repaid there.

f.g: Probably “fire-place” or “hearth”—the altar area in Hinnom where children were burned.

chapters.n: God will empty out Judah’s plans and schemes. Its people will fall to enemies, and their unburied bodies will feed birds and beasts—the ultimate disgrace in the ancient world.

f.g: Hebrew baqqoti—a pun on baqbuq, the jar. As the jar is emptied and broken, so Judah’s counsel will be “poured out.”

f.w: meat for the fowls of the heaven

chapters.n: Jerusalem will become a ruin that passersby hiss at in shock.
The siege will become so desperate that people will even eat their own children—fulfilling the covenant curses of the law of Moses. Lamentations records that this horror really happened.

f.w: eat the flesh of their sons

f.g: Distress, being hemmed in by siege.

chapters.n: Then, in front of the witnesses, Jeremiah is to smash the jar.

The meaning: unlike soft clay that can be reshaped (chapter 18), a fired jar that is shattered can’t be repaired. Judah has hardened past the point of being remade before judgment comes. So many will die that Tophet will become a burial ground.
God will make the whole city like Tophet—an unclean place of death.
Even Jerusalem’s homes and royal palaces will be defiled, because on their flat rooftops people offered incense and drink offerings to the stars and other gods.

f.g: The sun, moon, and stars, worshipped as gods in Assyrian and Babylonian religion.
Wine or other liquid poured out as an act of worship.

chapters.n: Jeremiah returns from the valley and repeats the message publicly in the temple courtyard.
The summary: all the disasters announced will come, because the people “hardened their necks”—they stubbornly refused to listen.

f.g: An image of an ox stiffening its neck against the yoke—stubborn refusal.

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s temple sermon (19:14-15) reaches Pashur, a priest who was also the chief officer responsible for order in the temple.

f.g: A different man from the Pashur son of Malchiah in 21:1. Immer was a priestly family.
Chief overseer—something like head of temple security.

chapters.n: Pashur has Jeremiah beaten and locked overnight in the stocks at a temple gate, where he would be exposed to public shame.

f.g: A wooden frame that held the feet (and perhaps hands and neck) in a painful, cramped position.
An upper gate on the north side of the temple area, facing Benjamin’s territory.

chapters.n: Released the next morning, Jeremiah is not intimidated. He gives Pashur a new name: “Magor-missabib.”

f.g: Hebrew “terror on every side,” a phrase Jeremiah uses often.

chapters.n: Pashur’s new name will describe his life: he will be a terror to himself and his friends as he watches them fall. Babylon is now named outright as the instrument of judgment.

f.g: Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled about 605–562 BC.

chapters.n: All the city’s wealth—its produce, treasures, and royal riches—will be plundered and hauled to Babylon.

f.g: Plunder, loot.

f.w: all the treasures of the kings of Judah

chapters.n: Pashur himself will go into exile and die in Babylon, along with friends to whom he had preached false comfort. He was not just a priest but a false prophet.
Now Jeremiah pours out his heart. He feels God overpowered him into this calling and left him a laughingstock. His honesty with God is part of what makes him so relatable.

f.g: Hebrew pittitani—“you enticed/persuaded me.” Jeremiah feels he was talked into a calling he couldn’t foresee.
Mockery, ridicule.

chapters.n: Every time he speaks, his message is “Violence and destruction!”—and in return he gets only insults all day long.

f.g: Spoil here = destruction, ruin.

chapters.n: He tried to quit—but God’s word burned inside him like fire trapped in his bones. He was worn out trying to hold it in and couldn’t. A powerful picture of a testimony that won’t stay silent.

f.w: a burning fire shut up in my bones

f.g: Holding back, restraining.
Hold out, endure.

chapters.n: He hears whispering everywhere. Even his closest friends watch for him to slip, hoping to trap him and get revenge.

f.g: Hebrew magor missabib—the same phrase he used to rename Pashur, now turned against him by mockers.
Close friends, intimates.
Stumbling, a misstep.

chapters.n: Yet faith rises: the Lord is with him like a mighty warrior. His persecutors will stumble and be ashamed forever.

f.g: Terrible = awe-inspiring, formidable.

chapters.n: He commits his case to the Lord, who tests the righteous and sees into the deepest self.

f.g: Kidneys—in Hebrew thought, the seat of inner feelings and motives.

chapters.n: A sudden burst of praise: sing to the Lord, who rescues the poor from the wicked.

f.g: The needy and powerless—here Jeremiah counts himself among them.

chapters.n: Then just as suddenly he plunges into despair and curses the day he was born. These swings between praise and anguish show the real emotional cost of his mission.

f.w: Cursed be the day wherein I was born

chapters.n: He even curses the messenger who brought his father the happy news of his birth—a poetic way of wishing he had never existed.
May that messenger be like the cities God overthrew without pity (Sodom and Gomorrah), hearing alarms of war morning and noon.

f.w: the cities which the LORD overthrew

f.g: Did not relent or change his mind.

chapters.n: Because he wasn’t killed before birth—his mother’s womb could have been his grave. This is the language of deep grief, not a literal wish carried out.

Why was I born only to see trouble and sorrow and end my days in shame? The chapter ends unresolved, yet Jeremiah never stops serving. Even Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail would cry “O God, where art thou?”
Years have passed. Now Babylon’s army surrounds Jerusalem (about 588 BC), and King Zedekiah sends two officials to Jeremiah for a word from the Lord. Zedekiah was king when Lehi left Jerusalem.

f.g: Judah’s last king (about 597–586 BC), installed by Nebuchadnezzar.
Not the same Pashur as in chapter 20.

chapters.n: The king hopes for a miracle like the one in Hezekiah’s day, when the Lord drove the Assyrians away from Jerusalem overnight.

f.g: A spelling closer to the Babylonian Nabû-kudurri-uṣur; same king as Nebuchadnezzar.

f.w: according to all his wondrous works

chapters.n: Jeremiah gives the messengers a reply to carry back to the king.
The answer is the opposite of what Zedekiah hoped: the Lord will turn Judah’s weapons back on itself and drive the defenders inside the walls.

f.g: The people of southern Babylonia; the dynasty of Nebuchadnezzar was Chaldean, so the word often just means Babylonians.

chapters.n: Shockingly, God himself will fight against Jerusalem—using the same “outstretched hand” and “strong arm” language that once described him rescuing Israel from Egypt.

f.w: with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm

chapters.n: Disease will sweep through the crowded, besieged city, killing people and animals alike.

f.g: A deadly plague or epidemic.

chapters.n: Survivors of plague, sword, and famine—including Zedekiah himself—will fall into Nebuchadnezzar’s hands, and he will show no mercy. This was fulfilled when Jerusalem fell.

f.w: I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah

chapters.n: Now a message to the people: God sets before them two paths—life and death. The words echo Moses’ great choice, but here “life” means surrender.

f.w: the way of life, and the way of death

chapters.n: Those who stay in the city will die; those who go out and surrender to the Babylonians will survive, escaping with their lives as their only “prize.” This counsel later got Jeremiah accused of treason.

f.w: his life shall be unto him for a prey
f.g: An idiom: he will escape with his life as his only plunder.

chapters.n: God has set his face against the city. It will be handed to Babylon and burned.
A separate message for the royal family follows.
The kings in David’s line must do justice “in the morning”—promptly and consistently—and rescue the robbed from oppressors, or God’s anger will burn like an unquenchable fire.

f.g: Kings often held court early in the day; justice should be the first order of business.
The one who has been robbed.

chapters.n: God addresses Jerusalem as a proud “rock” on a plateau surrounded by valleys, whose people boast that no enemy can get in.

f.w: inhabitant of the valley, and rock of the plain
f.g: Jerusalem sits on ridges ringed by valleys—naturally defensible, which bred false confidence.

chapters.n: But God will repay them according to what their deeds deserve, setting a fire in their “forest”—possibly a poetic name for the cedar-paneled palace buildings.
Jeremiah is sent down from the temple to the royal palace, which stood just below it, to deliver a message straight to the king.

f.g: The palace lay slightly downhill, south of the temple.

chapters.n: The message is for the king on David’s throne, his officials, and everyone passing through the palace gates.

God’s requirement for a king is simple: do justice, rescue victims of robbery, and never mistreat foreigners, orphans, or widows or shed innocent blood. These were the most vulnerable people in ancient society.

f.w: the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow

chapters.n: If they obey, David’s dynasty will continue in glory, with kings riding in procession through these gates.

f.w: kings sitting upon the throne of David

chapters.n: If not, God swears by himself—there is no one higher to swear by—that the palace will become a ruin.
Though the royal house is as precious to God as the lush forests of Gilead and the heights of Lebanon, he will turn it into a wilderness.

f.g: A fertile, wooded region east of the Jordan, famous for balm and forests.
The summit of the Lebanon mountains, famous for its cedars—fitting, since the palace was built with cedar.

chapters.n: God will appoint “destroyers” who will cut down its fine cedars—the cedar beams and panels of the palace—and burn them.

f.g: Hebrew qiddashti—literally “consecrate,” set apart for a task.

chapters.n: Foreigners passing the ruins will ask each other why the Lord did this to such a great city.

f.w: Wherefore hath the LORD done thus unto this great city?

chapters.n: The answer: they broke their covenant with the Lord and worshipped other gods.
Don’t weep for the dead king (good Josiah, killed in battle in 609 BC); weep instead for the king being taken away, who will never come home.

f.g: King Josiah, killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho.

chapters.n: That exiled king is Shallum, Josiah’s son, better known by his throne name Jehoahaz. He reigned only three months before Pharaoh Necho deported him.

f.g: Throne name Jehoahaz.

chapters.n: He will die in Egypt as a captive and never see his homeland again.

f.w: he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive

chapters.n: Woe to the king who builds a palace through injustice, forcing people to work without paying them. The law required wages to be paid promptly.

f.w: useth his neighbour's service without wages

chapters.n: He boasts of a spacious palace with big upper rooms, wide windows, cedar paneling, and bright red paint—luxury built on others’ backs.

f.g: Paneled, lined (walls or ceiling).
A bright red pigment, a sign of luxury.

chapters.n: God asks: does having more cedar make you a real king? Your father Josiah lived well enough and did justice—and it went well for him.

f.g: Surround yourself with cedar; perhaps “compete in cedar” with other kings.
Josiah, the righteous reforming king.

chapters.n: Josiah defended the poor and needy. “Wasn’t this what it means to know me?” says the Lord. Knowing God is shown by caring for those in need.

f.w: was not this to know me?

chapters.n: But this king’s eyes and heart are fixed only on greed, bloodshed, oppression, and violence.
The king is now named: Jehoiakim, Josiah’s son. No one will mourn him with the usual funeral cries of “Alas, my brother!” or “Alas, lord!”

f.g: Reigned about 609–598 BC; originally named Eliakim, renamed by Pharaoh Necho.
A traditional cry of lament at a funeral.

chapters.n: He will get “the burial of a donkey”—dragged out and dumped outside Jerusalem’s gates, an image of utter dishonor.
Now Jerusalem is addressed as a woman: go up to the high places of Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim and wail, because all your allies are crushed.

f.g: A highland region east of the Sea of Galilee.
Hebrew ‘Abarim—the mountain range east of the Dead Sea where Moses viewed the promised land.
Judah’s foreign allies, such as Egypt, on whom she relied instead of God.

chapters.n: God warned you while times were good, but you refused to listen—as you have from your youth.
The wind will sweep away your shepherds (leaders), and your allies will go into captivity. Then you will feel the shame of your sin.

f.w: The wind shall eat up all thy pastors
f.g: Pastors = shepherds, i.e., rulers; a pun—the wind will “shepherd” the shepherds.

chapters.n: Jerusalem, nesting in cedar palaces as if safe in Lebanon’s trees, will groan like a woman in labor when disaster strikes.

f.g: Probably better “how you will groan.”

chapters.n: Now the young king Coniah (Jehoiachin). Even if he were God’s own signet ring—the most precious and personal sign of authority—God would pull him off.

f.g: Short form of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin; reigned three months in 597 BC.
A seal ring used to sign documents with a ruler’s authority.

chapters.n: He will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, the very person he dreads.
Coniah and his mother, the queen mother Nehushta, will be carried off to a foreign land and die there. This happened in 597 BC.
They will long to return but never will.
A sad question: is Coniah just a broken, worthless pot that no one wants? Why are he and his children thrown away into an unknown land?

f.w: a vessel wherein is no pleasure

chapters.n: A solemn triple call to the land itself to hear the Lord’s word.

f.g: Or “land, land, land”—the repetition adds weight and urgency.

chapters.n: Record him as “childless”—not literally (he had sons), but none of his descendants would reign on David’s throne. The royal line would continue in another way; the New Testament traces Jesus through Jechonias.
Woe to the “shepherds”—Judah’s kings and leaders—who were supposed to protect God’s flock but instead ruined and scattered it.

f.g: Shepherds—a common ancient image for kings and rulers.

chapters.n: Because the leaders neglected and drove away God’s people, God will “visit” on them the evil they have done—a wordplay: they didn’t “visit” (care for) the flock, so he will “visit” (punish) them.

f.g: Hebrew paqad—to attend to, care for; also to punish or call to account. The verse uses it both ways.

chapters.n: Then a promise of hope: God himself will gather the surviving remnant from every land where he scattered them, bring them home, and make them flourish again. Latter-day Saints see this gathering continuing in our day.

f.w: I will gather the remnant of my flock

chapters.n: He will appoint faithful shepherds who truly feed the flock, so that no one will be afraid or lost.

f.w: I will set up shepherds over them

chapters.n: A great messianic promise: God will raise up from David’s family a righteous “Branch”—a true King who will reign wisely and bring justice to the earth. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, see Jesus Christ as this King.

f.g: Hebrew tsemach, “sprout”—a title for the coming Messiah from David’s line.

chapters.n: Under him, Judah and Israel will be safe, and his name will be “The LORD Our Righteousness.” Notably, the reigning king was Zedekiah, whose name means “The LORD is my righteousness”—the coming King will truly be what Zedekiah only claimed.

f.g: Hebrew YHWH tsidqenu. Latter-day Saints understand Jehovah as the premortal Jesus Christ, whose righteousness is offered to us.

chapters.n: A day is coming when people will no longer swear by the God who brought Israel out of Egypt—the Exodus will be overshadowed by a greater one.

f.w: The LORD liveth, which brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt

chapters.n: Instead they will praise the God who gathered scattered Israel from the north and from every land back to their own inheritance. Latter-day Saints connect this to the latter-day gathering of Israel, whose keys were restored to Joseph Smith.
Jeremiah shifts to the false prophets. His heart is broken and his whole body trembles—he feels staggered like a drunk man because of the holy words of the Lord compared to what these men are saying.
The land is full of unfaithfulness. Because of curses and broken oaths, the land “mourns”—drought dries up the pastures. People run toward evil and use their strength wrongly.

f.g: Or “the curse”—the covenant curse brought on by unfaithfulness.
Pasturelands of the open country.

chapters.n: Both prophets and priests are corrupt; God has found their wickedness even inside his temple.

f.g: Godless, treating holy things as common.

f.w: in my house have I found their wickedness

chapters.n: Their path will become like a slippery trail in the dark; they will be pushed and will fall when their day of reckoning comes.

f.g: The time of their punishment.

chapters.n: In the old northern kingdom (Samaria), prophets openly spoke by Baal and led Israel astray—foolish and obvious.
But Jerusalem’s prophets are worse: they live immorally and dishonestly, encourage evildoers, and keep anyone from repenting. To God, they are like Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.w: strengthen also the hands of evildoers

chapters.n: So God will give them bitterness to eat and poison to drink, because the corruption spreading through the land started with them.

f.g: A very bitter plant, symbol of suffering.
A bitter, poisonous herb.

chapters.n: Don’t listen to them. They fill you with empty hopes and speak visions from their own imaginations, not from the mouth of the Lord.

f.g: They fill you with false hopes.

f.w: a vision of their own heart

chapters.n: They keep promising peace to people who despise God and assure the stubborn that nothing bad will happen. It’s the message people want to hear.
Who among them has actually stood in the Lord’s council and heard his word? True prophets are admitted to God’s council and learn his will there.

f.w: stood in the counsel of the LORD
f.g: Hebrew sod—a council or intimate circle; the heavenly assembly.

chapters.n: A storm of God’s anger is already unleashed—a whirlwind that will crash down on the heads of the wicked.
God’s anger won’t turn back until his purpose is fully carried out. “In the latter days” you will understand it clearly—looking back, his dealings will make sense.

f.w: in the latter days ye shall consider it perfectly

chapters.n: God didn’t send these prophets, yet they ran with messages; he didn’t speak to them, yet they prophesied. Authority to speak for God comes from his call, not self-appointment.

f.w: I have not sent these prophets

chapters.n: If they had truly stood in God’s council, their message would have called people to repent. A sign of true prophecy: it turns people away from sin, not toward comfort in it.
“Am I only a God nearby, and not a God far away?” God is not a local deity who can be ignored or managed; he is everywhere and sees everything.
No one can hide from him. He fills heaven and earth.

f.w: Do not I fill heaven and earth?

chapters.n: God has heard the false prophets claiming, “I had a dream! I had a dream!” as their proof of revelation.
How long will they keep this up? Their “revelations” come from their own self-deception.
Their dreams make people forget God’s name, just as earlier generations forgot him for Baal.
Let a dreamer tell his dream as a dream, but let the one with God’s word speak it faithfully. What does straw have to do with grain? Human ideas and divine revelation are not the same.

f.g: The light husks separated from grain at threshing—worthless.

chapters.n: God’s true word is like fire and like a hammer that shatters rock—it has real power to burn away and break hardness, unlike empty talk.
God is against prophets who borrow and recycle each other’s messages and pass them off as revelation.
He is against those who simply wag their tongues and say, “He says…” as if quoting God.

f.g: Hebrew ne’um—the formal phrase “declares [the LORD],” used by real prophets.

chapters.n: God is against those who spread false dreams and lead his people astray with lies and recklessness. He never sent them, and they bring no benefit to anyone.

f.g: Recklessness, empty boasting.

chapters.n: A wordplay follows. People mockingly ask, “What’s the burden (oracle) of the Lord now?” Jeremiah answers: “You are the burden—and the Lord will cast you off!”

f.g: Hebrew massa’—both “oracle” and “load.” The people used it sarcastically about Jeremiah’s heavy messages.

chapters.n: Anyone who keeps using the phrase “the burden of the Lord” in mockery will be punished along with his household.
Instead, people should sincerely ask one another, “What has the Lord answered? What has the Lord said?”
Stop using “the burden of the Lord,” because each person’s own words have become a burden—they have twisted the words of the living God.
When speaking to a prophet, ask respectfully, “What has the Lord answered you?”
Because they insisted on using the mocking phrase even after God told them to stop…
…God will lift them up like a burden and cast them away, along with the city he gave their ancestors, out of his presence.

f.g: A play on words: some manuscripts read “lift you up” (nasa’), echoing massa’, “burden.”

chapters.n: Their disgrace will be lasting, a shame never forgotten. Yet elsewhere Jeremiah promises a future restoration for those who return to God.

After the first major deportation in 597 BC, when King Jeconiah and Judah’s leaders and skilled workers were taken to Babylon, the Lord shows Jeremiah a vision of two baskets of figs set before the temple.

f.g: Also called Jehoiachin or Coniah.
Craftsmen and metalworkers—taken so Judah couldn’t rebuild weapons or fortifications.
Perhaps like baskets of firstfruits brought as offerings to the temple.

chapters.n: One basket held excellent early-ripe figs; the other held rotten figs too bad to eat.

f.g: Early figs, ripening in June, were considered a delicacy.
Bad, worthless (from “naught”), not “mischievous.”

chapters.n: God asks Jeremiah what he sees, drawing him into the lesson, and Jeremiah describes the contrast.
The Lord then explains the vision.
Surprisingly, the good figs are the exiles in Babylon. People in Jerusalem assumed the exiles were the cursed ones, but God says he sent them away for their own good.
God will watch over the exiles with favor and bring them home. He will build and plant them—echoing the words of Jeremiah’s call.

f.w: I will build them, and not pull them down

chapters.n: God will give them a heart to know him. They will be his covenant people because they will return to him wholeheartedly. Inner change is what God is really after.

f.w: they shall be my people, and I will be their God

chapters.n: The rotten figs are King Zedekiah, his officials, those who remained in Jerusalem, and those who fled to Egypt. They thought they were the favored ones.

f.w: them that dwell in the land of Egypt

chapters.n: They will be scattered among the nations as an example of disaster—a byword, a taunt, and a curse wherever they go.
Sword, famine, and disease will strike them until they are gone from the land God had given their ancestors.

f.w: the sword, the famine, and the pestilence

chapters.n: This message is dated precisely: the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, which was Nebuchadnezzar’s first year as king—605 BC, the year Babylon crushed Egypt at Carchemish and became the dominant world power.

f.g: Nebuchadnezzar became king in 605 BC after his father Nabopolassar died.

chapters.n: Jeremiah speaks this message to everyone in Judah and Jerusalem.
For 23 years—since Josiah’s 13th year (627/626 BC)—Jeremiah has delivered God’s word again and again, but the people have not listened.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for persistent, eager effort—doing something urgently and repeatedly.

chapters.n: And it wasn’t only Jeremiah—God had sent prophet after prophet, eagerly and persistently, but they refused to listen.
Their message was always the same: turn back from your evil ways, and you can stay in the land God gave your ancestors forever.

f.w: Turn ye again now every one from his evil way

chapters.n: Don’t chase other gods or anger God with idols you make—then he will not harm you.

f.g: Idols, which people made themselves.

chapters.n: But they would not listen, and by making idols they brought harm on themselves. Sin ultimately hurts the sinner.
Because they have not obeyed, the Lord pronounces sentence.
God will summon the peoples of the north, led by Nebuchadnezzar—whom he calls “my servant”—to devastate Judah and neighboring nations. God can use even a pagan king to accomplish his purposes.
All the ordinary sounds of happy life will disappear: laughter, wedding songs, the grinding of grain at the millstone each morning, and lamplight in homes at night.

f.w: the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride

f.g: Grinding grain was a daily household chore; silence meant no one was left.

chapters.n: The land will lie desolate, and these nations will serve Babylon for seventy years—a full lifetime. This prophecy became famous and was later studied by Daniel.

f.g: Often reckoned from about 605 BC to the fall of Babylon (539 BC) and the return (538 BC), or from the temple’s destruction (586) to its rebuilding (516).

chapters.n: After seventy years, God will punish Babylon itself for its sins and make it a permanent ruin. The instrument of judgment is also accountable.

f.w: I will punish the king of Babylon

chapters.n: Everything written in this book against the nations will come upon Babylon. This verse shows Jeremiah’s prophecies were being collected in written form.

f.w: all that is written in this book

chapters.n: Babylon, which enslaved others, will in turn be enslaved by many nations and great kings—repaid for its own deeds.

f.g: Make slaves of them.

chapters.n: Now a vivid image: God hands Jeremiah a wine cup full of his wrath and tells him to make every nation drink from it. To “drink the cup” means to experience God’s judgment.

f.w: the wine cup of this fury

chapters.n: Like drunken men, they will stagger and go mad because of the war God sends among them.

f.g: Stagger, reel.

chapters.n: Jeremiah takes the cup and “serves” it to the nations—probably in vision or by delivering God’s messages to them, as in chapters 46–51. Christ later spoke of drinking a bitter cup for us.
First in line is Jerusalem itself, with its kings and officials. Judgment begins at God’s own house.

f.g: Probably an editor’s note added after Jerusalem’s fall, confirming fulfillment.

f.w: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah

chapters.n: Next is Egypt—Pharaoh, his officials, and all his people.
Then mixed foreign populations, the land of Uz, and the Philistine cities along the coast.

f.g: Mixed foreign groups, perhaps mercenaries or foreigners living in Egypt.
Job’s homeland, probably in or near Edom.
Gaza.
Ashdod had been ruined by a long Egyptian siege, leaving only a remnant.

chapters.n: Then Judah’s neighbors east of the Jordan and Dead Sea: Edom, Moab, and Ammon.

f.w: Edom, and Moab, and the children of Ammon

chapters.n: Then the Phoenician sea-trading cities of Tyre and Sidon and their colonies across the Mediterranean.

f.g: Tyre.
Sidon.

f.w: the isles which are beyond the sea
f.g: Coastlands and islands of the Mediterranean—Phoenician colonies.

chapters.n: Then Arabian desert tribes: Dedan, Tema, Buz, and those who clip the hair at their temples.

f.g: Oasis trading centers in northern Arabia.

f.w: all that are in the utmost corners
f.g: Probably “those who clip the corners of their hair,” a desert custom.

chapters.n: All the kings of Arabia and the mixed desert peoples.
Further east: Zimri (location uncertain), Elam (in today’s southwest Iran), and the Medes (northwestern Iran).

f.g: The Medes later joined Persia in conquering Babylon.

chapters.n: Finally every kingdom near and far—and last of all, the king of “Sheshach” will drink. Sheshach is a coded name for Babylon. The oppressor drinks last.

f.g: A Hebrew cipher (atbash, swapping letters from the alphabet’s start and end) for Babel, Babylon.

chapters.n: God’s message to the nations: drink, get drunk, vomit, fall, and don’t get up—because of the war he is sending.

f.g: Vomit.

chapters.n: If any nation refuses the cup, Jeremiah must tell them: you will drink it anyway. No one can avoid God’s judgment.
If God is bringing disaster first on the city that bears his own name, how could other nations expect to escape? He is calling a sword against the whole earth.

f.w: the city which is called by my name

chapters.n: The Lord will roar like a lion from heaven and shout like workers treading grapes in a winepress—an image of crushing judgment over the whole earth.

f.w: The LORD shall roar from on high
as they that tread the grapes

chapters.n: The noise reaches the ends of the earth, for God is bringing a lawsuit against the nations. He will judge all humanity and give the wicked to the sword.

f.g: A legal case or lawsuit.

f.w: he will plead with all flesh

chapters.n: Disaster will spread from nation to nation like a great storm rising from the far corners of the earth.

f.g: Borders, farthest regions.

chapters.n: Those killed by the Lord’s judgment will be everywhere, unburied and unmourned, lying like refuse on the ground.
Wail, you shepherds and leaders of the flock! Roll in the ashes of mourning, for your time of slaughter has come; you will fall and shatter like a fine vase.

f.g: The leaders, the lead sheep or rams.
A precious, delicate jar.

chapters.n: There will be no escape for the leaders.
Their cries and howls will be heard, because the Lord is destroying their pasture—the lands they ruled.
Peaceful meadows and homes will be laid waste by the Lord’s fierce anger.

f.g: Peaceful pastures or folds.

chapters.n: Like a lion that leaves its den to hunt, the Lord has come out; the land is desolate because of the oppressor’s sword and God’s burning anger.

f.g: Hiding place, lair.
Some ancient versions read “the sword of the oppressor”—Babylon’s army.

chapters.n: This happened early in King Jehoiakim’s reign (about 609/608 BC). It is likely the same occasion as the “temple sermon” of chapter 7, here told from the angle of what happened to Jeremiah afterward.

f.w: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim

chapters.n: God sends Jeremiah to the temple courtyard, where crowds from all Judah gathered for worship, and commands him not to leave out a single word.
God’s hope is that people might listen and turn back, so he can withdraw the disaster. Even severe warnings come from a God who wants to forgive.

f.w: that I may repent me of the evil

chapters.n: The warning: if you won’t listen and live by the law I gave you…
…and won’t heed the prophets I have sent again and again…

…then I will make this temple like Shiloh and turn Jerusalem into a byword for a curse. Shiloh had held the tabernacle centuries earlier but was destroyed—proof that a holy place is no guarantee of safety.

f.g: Where the ark and tabernacle stood in the days of Eli and Samuel; it was later ruined, probably by the Philistines.

chapters.n: Priests, prophets, and the whole crowd hear Jeremiah’s words in the temple.
As soon as he finishes, they seize him: “You must die!” Predicting the temple’s fall seemed like blasphemy to them.
“How dare you say in the Lord’s name that this temple will be like Shiloh and the city empty?” A mob gathers around him.
Royal officials hear the uproar and come up from the palace to the temple, sitting at the New Gate as a court to judge the case.

f.g: Royal officials, high-ranking administrators.

f.w: sat down in the entry of the new gate
f.g: City and temple gates were where legal cases were heard.

chapters.n: The priests and prophets present their accusation: he deserves death for prophesying against the city.

f.w: This man is worthy to die

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s defense is simple: the Lord sent me to say every word you heard.
Even on trial, he keeps calling them to repent: change your ways, obey God, and he will withdraw the disaster.

f.w: amend your ways and your doings

chapters.n: “I’m in your hands—do what you think right.” He doesn’t resist or flee.

f.g: Fitting, proper.

chapters.n: But be sure of this: if you kill me, you bring innocent blood on yourselves and the city, because the Lord truly sent me.
The officials and the people are persuaded: he spoke in the Lord’s name and doesn’t deserve death. The crowd’s mood has turned.
Some respected elders stand up and remind the assembly of a precedent from history.

About a century earlier, the prophet Micah from Moresheth had predicted that Zion would be plowed like a field and the temple hill become overgrown. Jeremiah 26:18 is the only place in the Bible where one prophet’s book is quoted by name in another.

f.g: From Moresheth-gath in the lowlands of Judah.

f.w: Zion shall be plowed like a field

f.g: Heaps of rubble, ruins.

chapters.n: Did King Hezekiah kill Micah? No—he feared God and prayed, and the disaster was held back. If we kill Jeremiah, we bring great harm on ourselves.

f.g: Bring about.

chapters.n: But the record also tells of another prophet, Urijah, who preached the same message as Jeremiah—and fared very differently.

f.g: A town about 8 miles west of Jerusalem, where the ark once stayed.

chapters.n: King Jehoiakim tried to kill Urijah, who fled in fear to Egypt.
Jehoiakim sent a team led by Elnathan to bring him back. Egypt was then Judah’s overlord, so extradition was possible.

f.g: A high official; later he urged the king not to burn Jeremiah’s scroll.

chapters.n: They brought Urijah back, and the king executed him and dumped his body in the common burial ground—a dishonorable grave. This shows how real the danger to Jeremiah was.

f.w: the graves of the common people
f.g: A public burial ground in the Kidron Valley, without honor.

chapters.n: Jeremiah survived because Ahikam son of Shaphan protected him. Shaphan’s family served in Josiah’s reforms and repeatedly helped Jeremiah.

f.g: Father of Gedaliah, the later governor of Judah.

chapters.n: The KJV says “Jehoiakim,” but the chapter itself is about Zedekiah (verses 3 and 12), and 28:1 dates it to Zedekiah’s fourth year, about 594/593 BC. Most scholars think “Jehoiakim” here is an early copying slip.

f.g: A few Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read “Zedekiah.”

chapters.n: God tells Jeremiah to make a yoke—wooden bars tied with leather straps, like those on oxen—and wear it on his neck as a walking sermon about submitting to Babylon.

f.g: The straps and crossbars of an ox yoke.

chapters.n: Envoys from five neighboring kingdoms had come to Jerusalem, probably to plot a joint revolt against Babylon with Zedekiah. Jeremiah sends God’s message back with them.

f.w: the king of Edom, and to the king of Moab, and to the king of the Ammonites
f.g: Small kingdoms east and south of Judah, all under Babylon’s control.

chapters.n: They are to deliver this message to their own kings from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel—who claims authority over all nations, not just Israel.
God made the earth, people, and animals by his great power, and he gives it to whomever he chooses. He is Lord of history.

f.g: Right, fitting.

chapters.n: For now, God has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant”—even the wild animals will serve him. Babylon’s power is something God has permitted for a purpose.
Nations will serve him, his son, and grandson until Babylon’s own time is up; then it too will be conquered. Babylon fell to Persia in 539 BC.

f.w: his son, and his son's son
f.g: Nebuchadnezzar’s son Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk) reigned after him; Babylon fell under Nabonidus and his son Belshazzar.

chapters.n: Any nation that refuses Babylon’s yoke will be punished with war, famine, and disease until destroyed.
So don’t listen to your prophets, fortune-tellers, dream interpreters, mediums, or sorcerers who say you won’t have to serve Babylon. The surrounding nations relied on such practices.

f.g: People who claimed to read omens and predict the future.
Probably fortune-tellers who read signs in clouds or omens.

chapters.n: Their lies will only get you exiled from your land and destroyed—exactly the opposite of what they promise.
But nations that accept Babylon’s yoke will remain on their land, farming and living there.
Jeremiah delivers the same message to King Zedekiah: submit to Babylon and live.
“Why should you and your people die?” Jeremiah pleads. Death is unnecessary when life is offered.
Don’t listen to prophets who promise freedom from Babylon—they’re lying.
God did not send them; they lie in his name, leading to destruction for both them and those who listen.
Jeremiah tells the priests and people: ignore prophets who say the temple treasures taken in 597 BC will soon be returned.

f.w: the vessels of the LORD's house
f.g: Sacred gold and bronze objects from the temple.

chapters.n: Don’t listen—serve Babylon and live. Why should this city be destroyed?
A challenge: if they are true prophets, let them pray that the treasures still left in Jerusalem won’t also be taken. True prophets also interceded for the people.
God speaks about the great bronze items still in the temple: the pillars, the “sea,” the stands, and other vessels.

f.g: The two huge bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, at the temple entrance.
A giant bronze water basin resting on twelve bronze oxen.
Movable bronze stands for washing basins.

chapters.n: These were left behind when Nebuchadnezzar took King Jeconiah and the nobles to Babylon in 597 BC.
God repeats solemnly: here is what will happen to the vessels left in the temple and palace.
They too will go to Babylon and stay there until God decides to bring them back. This was fulfilled: they were taken in 586 BC, and many vessels were returned under Cyrus.

f.w: They shall be carried to Babylon
then will I bring them up, and restore them to this place

chapters.n: In Zedekiah’s fourth year (about 594/593 BC), the prophet Hananiah confronts Jeremiah publicly in the temple, before the priests and people. This is a showdown between two men both claiming to speak for God.

f.g: His name means “the LORD has been gracious”—ironic, since his message offered cheap grace.
A priestly town about 6 miles northwest of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Hananiah uses all the right prophetic language: “Thus says the Lord… I have broken Babylon’s yoke.” False messages can sound exactly like true ones.
Within two years, he claims, the temple treasures taken to Babylon will be returned.
And King Jeconiah and all the exiles will come home too. This openly contradicts Jeremiah’s seventy years.
Jeremiah responds publicly in the same setting.
“Amen! May the Lord do it!” Jeremiah genuinely wishes Hananiah were right—he takes no pleasure in disaster. But wishing doesn’t make it so.

f.g: So be it, may it be true.

chapters.n: “But listen to what I have to say to you and to everyone here.”
The prophets of old usually warned of war, disaster, and disease—calling people to repentance. A message of judgment fits the pattern of true prophecy.

f.w: The prophets that have been before me

chapters.n: A prophet who promises peace will be proven true only if it actually happens. This echoes the test in Deuteronomy for knowing a true prophet.

f.w: when the word of the prophet shall come to pass

chapters.n: Hananiah grabs the wooden yoke off Jeremiah’s neck and breaks it—a dramatic counter-symbol.
He announces that God will break Babylon’s yoke from all nations within two years. Jeremiah quietly walks away—he does not answer without a word from God.

f.w: the prophet Jeremiah went his way

chapters.n: Some time later, God gives Jeremiah a response to Hananiah.
“You broke a wooden yoke, but you have only made an iron one in its place.” Rejecting God’s lighter correction leads to a heavier burden.
God has placed an iron yoke on all these nations to serve Nebuchadnezzar—even the wild animals are in his power. The outcome is fixed.

f.w: I have given him the beasts of the field also

chapters.n: Jeremiah tells Hananiah directly: the Lord did not send you, and you have made the people trust a lie.

f.w: thou makest this people to trust in a lie

chapters.n: Because Hananiah taught rebellion against the Lord, he will die that very year. Under the law of Moses, a false prophet who led people astray deserved death.

f.w: I will cast thee from off the face of the earth
f.g: A pun: God “sent” (shalach) him not, but will “send/cast” (meshalleche) him off the earth.

f.w: thou hast taught rebellion against the LORD

chapters.n: Hananiah died two months later. His own two-year prophecy failed, while Jeremiah’s short-term prophecy came true—the very test Jeremiah had named.

f.g: Two months after the confrontation in the fifth month (verse 1).

chapters.n: Jeremiah writes a letter from Jerusalem to the Jews already deported to Babylon in 597 BC—the surviving elders, priests, prophets, and people. It is one of the earliest pastoral letters in scripture.

f.g: The elders who were still alive—some had evidently died.

chapters.n: A note sets the timing: after King Jeconiah, the queen mother, palace officials, leaders, and skilled craftsmen had been taken away.

f.g: The queen mother, Nehushta, an influential position in Judah.
Court officials; the Hebrew word can mean high officers generally.

chapters.n: The letter travels with two officials Zedekiah sent on a diplomatic mission to Babylon. Elasah was a son of Shaphan, the family that supported Jeremiah.

f.g: Possibly a son of the high priest Hilkiah who found the book of the law under Josiah.

chapters.n: God addresses the exiles—and notes that he himself sent them to Babylon. Their exile isn’t an accident; it’s part of his purpose.
Surprising advice: settle in. Build houses, plant gardens, and enjoy their produce. Exile won’t be short.
Marry, have children, arrange marriages for them, and grow in number. Don’t let your people dwindle away.
Seek the welfare of Babylon—your enemy’s city—and pray for it, because your peace is tied to its peace. A remarkable call to be good citizens even in a foreign land.

f.g: Hebrew shalom—welfare, wholeness, prosperity, not just absence of war.

f.w: pray unto the LORD for it

chapters.n: Don’t let the prophets and fortune-tellers among you in Babylon deceive you, or listen to the dreams you encourage them to have.

f.w: your dreams which ye cause to be dreamed
f.g: Dreams people seek out because they want to hear a certain answer.

chapters.n: They speak falsely in my name; I did not send them.
After seventy years for Babylon are complete, God will come to them and keep his good promise to bring them home. Daniel later read this very prophecy and prayed.
One of the most beloved verses in the Bible: God knows his plans for them—plans for peace, not disaster, to give them a future and a hope. Even in exile, he has not forgotten them.

f.g: Literally “a future and a hope”—a hopeful outcome.

chapters.n: Then you will call on me and pray, and I will listen. Exile will become a place of renewed prayer.
You will seek me and find me when you search for me with all your heart. Wholehearted seeking is the key to finding God.

f.w: when ye shall search for me with all your heart

chapters.n: God will let himself be found, end their captivity, and gather them from all nations back home. Latter-day Saints also see in such promises the broader gathering of Israel.

f.g: Or “restore your fortunes.”

f.w: I will gather you from all the nations

chapters.n: Some exiles boasted that God had given them prophets right there in Babylon—who were promising a quick return.
But God has a message about the king on David’s throne (Zedekiah) and the people still in Jerusalem…
…they will face sword, famine, and disease, and become like the rotten figs of chapter 24. Jerusalem is not the safe place the exiles imagined.

f.g: Rotten, disgusting figs.

chapters.n: God will pursue them with disaster and scatter them as an example of a curse and shame among the nations.

f.w: to be removed to all the kingdoms of the earth

chapters.n: Because they ignored God’s words sent by his prophets again and again—and you exiles didn’t listen either.

f.w: rising up early and sending them

chapters.n: So listen now, all you exiles God sent from Jerusalem to Babylon.
God names two false prophets among the exiles, Ahab and Zedekiah (not the king), who lie in his name. Nebuchadnezzar will execute them in front of everyone—likely for stirring up revolt.

f.g: A prophet, not King Zedekiah.

chapters.n: Their fate will become a curse formula: “May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and Ahab, whom Babylon’s king roasted in the fire.” Burning was a known Babylonian punishment.

f.g: Hebrew qalam, “roasted,” is a pun on qelalah, “curse.”

chapters.n: Their crimes: outrageous immorality, adultery with neighbors’ wives, and false prophecy. God says, “I know—and I am a witness.”

f.g: Hebrew nebalah—disgraceful folly, shameful acts.

f.w: I know, and am a witness

chapters.n: Next, a message for another false prophet in Babylon, Shemaiah the Nehelamite.

f.g: Of Nehelam—an unknown place or family name; possibly a wordplay on “dreamer.”

chapters.n: Shemaiah had written letters in his own name—not God’s—to Jerusalem’s priest Zephaniah and the other priests.
His letter reminded Zephaniah that as the temple’s overseer, he was supposed to lock up any “madman” who claimed to be a prophet in the stocks.

f.g: Probably a reference to the respected high priest of earlier times, or a recent officeholder.
Raving—prophets were sometimes mocked as crazy.

chapters.n: “So why haven’t you disciplined Jeremiah of Anathoth, who acts like a prophet?”
“He even wrote to us in Babylon telling us the captivity will be long and we should build homes and plant gardens!” He quotes Jeremiah’s letter as evidence against him.
Zephaniah read Shemaiah’s letter aloud to Jeremiah. Apparently he didn’t act against Jeremiah, showing some respect for him.
Then God gives Jeremiah a response.
Jeremiah must send word to all the exiles: Shemaiah prophesied without being sent and made people trust a lie.

f.w: he caused you to trust in a lie

chapters.n: God will punish Shemaiah and his descendants: none of them will live to see the good God will do for his people, because he preached rebellion against the Lord.

f.w: he hath taught rebellion against the LORD

chapters.n: Chapters 30–33 are often called the “Book of Consolation”—a cluster of hope-filled prophecies amid Jeremiah’s darker messages.
God tells Jeremiah to write these words down in a book, so the promise will be preserved for people who need it later.
The theme: the day is coming when God will bring both Israel (the northern tribes) and Judah home from captivity to possess their land again.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity
f.g: Or “restore the fortunes”—a key phrase repeated through these chapters.

chapters.n: These are the Lord’s words about Israel and Judah.
The scene opens with cries of terror and panic—no peace anywhere.
Strong men are clutching their sides and turning pale, as if they were women in labor. A vivid picture of helpless anguish.

f.g: Labor pains in childbirth.
Waist, lower back.

chapters.n: That day will be unlike any other—“the time of Jacob’s trouble.” Yet he will be saved out of it. Latter-day Saints often apply this phrase also to troubles preceding the Second Coming.

f.w: he shall be saved out of it

chapters.n: In that day God will break the oppressor’s yoke off Israel’s neck and snap its chains; foreigners will no longer enslave them.

f.w: I will break his yoke from off thy neck

chapters.n: Instead, they will serve the Lord their God and “David their king”—not the long-dead David but a future king from his line. Christians see this as the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Son of David.
Don’t be afraid, Jacob my servant. God will rescue you and your children from distant lands; you will return and live in quiet peace with no one to terrify you.

f.w: fear thou not, O my servant Jacob

chapters.n: God will completely destroy the nations where Israel was scattered, but never completely destroy Israel. He will discipline them fairly—not leave them unpunished, but not crush them.

f.w: I will correct thee in measure
f.g: Discipline with justice and restraint.

f.w: will I not make a full end of thee

chapters.n: God describes Israel’s condition honestly: the wound is incurable and severe. Human remedies can’t fix the damage sin has done.
No one will defend you or bind up your wound; there is no medicine that can heal you.
All your “lovers”—the foreign allies Judah relied on—have abandoned you. God wounded you like an enemy because your sins were so many.

f.g: Political allies like Egypt.

chapters.n: Why cry about your pain? You brought it on yourself through your many sins. Accepting responsibility is the first step toward healing.
But now the reversal: all who devoured Israel will be devoured; all oppressors will go into captivity; plunderers will be plundered.

f.w: they that spoil thee shall be a spoil

chapters.n: The “incurable” wound will be healed by God himself. Because the nations called Zion an outcast that nobody cares about, God will care for her. What no human can heal, God can.

f.w: I will restore health unto thee

chapters.n: God will restore Jacob’s homes; the city will be rebuilt on its own ruin-mound, and the palace will stand where it should.

f.g: Hebrew tel—the mound formed by layers of earlier ruins, on which ancient cities were rebuilt.

chapters.n: Songs of thanksgiving and celebration will be heard again. God will make them many and honored instead of few and despised.

f.w: the voice of them that make merry

chapters.n: Their children will flourish as in former days; their community will be firmly established before God, and oppressors will be punished.

Their ruler will be one of their own, not a foreigner. God will bring him near, and he will approach God—something only a person God invites dares to do. This hints at a priest-king, fulfilled for Christians in Christ.

f.g: Literally “pledged his heart”—risked his life.

chapters.n: The covenant is renewed: you will be my people, and I will be your God.

f.w: ye shall be my people, and I will be your God

chapters.n: A reminder: the Lord’s storm of judgment is already moving and will crash on the heads of the wicked.
God’s anger will not turn back until his purposes are complete. “In the latter days” you will understand it—the full meaning will be clear in time.

f.w: in the latter days ye shall consider it

chapters.n: Continuing the promises of chapter 30: in that coming day, God will be the God of all Israel’s families—north and south reunited—and they will be his people.
God recalls the Exodus: the people who survived the sword found grace in the wilderness when he led Israel toward rest. What he did once, he will do again.
“I have loved you with an everlasting love; that’s why I have drawn you to me with unfailing kindness.” God’s love, not Israel’s merit, is the root of restoration.

f.w: I have loved thee with an everlasting love

f.g: Hebrew chesed—loyal, covenant love that keeps faith.

chapters.n: God will rebuild “virgin Israel.” She will again pick up her tambourines and join the joyful dances.

f.g: Small hand drums or tambourines.

chapters.n: Vineyards will be planted again on Samaria’s hills, and the planters will enjoy the fruit themselves. Under the law, a new vineyard’s fruit had to wait several years before ordinary use—here peace lasts long enough to enjoy it.

f.g: Use the fruit freely after the waiting period.

chapters.n: Watchmen in the northern hills of Ephraim will call, “Come, let’s go up to Zion to the Lord!” The old split between north and south will be healed in worship.

f.w: let us go up to Zion

f.g: The central hill country of the former northern kingdom.

chapters.n: Sing and shout for Jacob among the nations! Proclaim, praise, and pray, “Lord, save your people, the remnant of Israel.”

f.g: Israel—the foremost of nations in God’s plan.

chapters.n: God will bring them from the north and from the ends of the earth—including the blind, the lame, and pregnant women. No one is too weak to be included in the gathering.

f.w: I will bring them from the north country

chapters.n: They will come weeping and praying, and God will lead them beside streams on a smooth road. He is a father to Israel, and Ephraim is his firstborn. Latter-day Saints note Ephraim’s special role in the latter-day gathering.
Announce it to the nations and distant coastlands: the God who scattered Israel will gather and protect them as a shepherd guards his flock.

f.w: as a shepherd doth his flock

chapters.n: The Lord has redeemed and ransomed Jacob from a stronger power—language of buying back a family member from slavery. Latter-day Saints see in this the redemption Jesus Christ offers.

f.g: Hebrew padah and ga’al—to ransom, to buy back as a near kinsman.

chapters.n: They will sing on Zion’s heights and stream toward God’s goodness—grain, wine, oil, and flocks. Their lives will be like a well-watered garden, with no more sorrow.

f.g: Stream like a river—or be radiant with joy.

chapters.n: Young women will dance, and young and old men will celebrate together. God will turn their mourning into joy and comfort them.

f.w: I will turn their mourning into joy

chapters.n: Priests will have abundant offerings to share, and God’s people will be fully satisfied with his goodness.

f.g: Richness, abundance—the best portions of offerings.

chapters.n: A haunting image: Rachel, mother of Joseph and Benjamin, weeps in Ramah for her lost children. Ramah was likely where exiles were gathered before being marched to Babylon. Matthew applies this verse to Herod’s slaughter of the children of Bethlehem.

f.g: A town about 5 miles north of Jerusalem, near Rachel’s tomb tradition.

chapters.n: God answers Rachel tenderly: stop weeping; your labor will be rewarded, and your children will come back from the enemy’s land.
There is hope for your future: your children will return home.

f.w: there is hope in thine end

chapters.n: God has heard Ephraim (the northern tribes) mourning: “You disciplined me like an untrained calf. Turn me back, and I will return—you are my God.” Repentance begins by asking God for help to change.

f.g: An untrained young ox that resists the yoke.

f.w: turn thou me, and I shall be turned

chapters.n: Ephraim continues: after I turned back, I repented; once I understood, I struck my thigh in grief and felt the shame of my youthful sins.

f.g: A gesture of grief and remorse.

chapters.n: God’s tender response: “Isn’t Ephraim my dear son, my delight? Even when I speak against him, I still remember him. My heart yearns for him—I will surely have mercy.” One of the most moving pictures of God as a loving Father.

f.w: my bowels are troubled for him
f.g: Bowels = the inner self, seat of deep emotion—“my heart aches for him.”

chapters.n: Set up road markers and signposts! Remember the road you took into exile, and come back along it, virgin Israel, to your cities.

f.g: Road markers, signposts.
Piles of stones as guideposts.

chapters.n: How long will you wander, unfaithful daughter? God has created something new on earth: “a woman shall encompass a man.” The meaning is debated—perhaps a reversal in which faithful Israel (the woman) now embraces or seeks the Lord, or protects her own.

f.w: A woman shall compass a man
f.g: Compass = surround, encircle. A cryptic proverb; scholars propose many explanations.
Turning away, unfaithful.

chapters.n: When God restores Judah, people will again bless Jerusalem: “The Lord bless you, home of righteousness, holy mountain.”
Farmers and shepherds will live together peacefully in Judah’s towns.

f.g: Farmers.

chapters.n: God will refresh the weary and fill every sorrowful soul.

f.w: I have satiated the weary soul

chapters.n: Jeremiah wakes up—this message may have come in a dream or vision—and for once his sleep was sweet. After so many grim messages, this one brought peace.
Days are coming when God will “sow” Israel and Judah with people and animals—repopulating the empty land.
Just as God watched over them to uproot and tear down, now he will watch over them to build and plant—the words of Jeremiah’s original call, now turned fully to hope.
People will stop quoting the proverb, “The parents ate sour grapes, but the children’s teeth are set on edge”—blaming their troubles on their ancestors.

f.w: The fathers have eaten a sour grape

f.g: Made raw and sensitive, as by sour fruit.

chapters.n: Instead each person will be accountable for his own sin. This is a principle Latter-day Saints affirm: we are punished for our own sins, not for Adam’s or our parents’.

f.w: every one shall die for his own iniquity

chapters.n: One of the great prophecies of scripture: God will make a “new covenant” with Israel and Judah. The phrase “new covenant” (new testament) gave the New Testament its name.
It won’t be like the Sinai covenant made when God led them out of Egypt by the hand, which they broke even though he was like a husband to them.

f.w: I was an husband unto them
f.g: Some ancient versions read “I disregarded them” (quoted that way in Hebrews 8:9).

chapters.n: In the new covenant, God will write his law on their hearts, not just on stone tablets. Obedience will come from inside—a changed nature. This is the “mighty change of heart” the Book of Mormon describes.

f.g: Innermost being.

chapters.n: Everyone, from least to greatest, will personally know the Lord, and he will forgive sins and remember them no more. Personal revelation and complete forgiveness through Christ are at the heart of this promise.

f.w: I will remember their sin no more

chapters.n: The God who makes this promise is the one who set the sun, moon, and stars in their places and controls the roaring sea.

f.g: Fixed laws, set order.

f.w: which divideth the sea when the waves thereof roar

chapters.n: Only if those laws of nature fail would Israel ever stop being a nation before God. His covenant is as reliable as the sunrise.
If anyone could measure the heavens or explore the earth’s foundations, only then would God reject all of Israel’s descendants. In other words—never.

f.w: I will also cast off all the seed of Israel

chapters.n: Jerusalem will be rebuilt for the Lord, from the Tower of Hananel in the north to the Corner Gate in the west.
The surveyor’s line will extend further to the hill of Gareb and around to Goath—places whose exact locations are now unknown, probably on the west and southwest.

Even the Valley of Hinnom—full of corpses and ashes of sacrifices—and the fields down to the Kidron will become holy to the Lord, never to be destroyed again. The most defiled place will be made holy.

f.w: the whole valley of the dead bodies

f.g: The valley east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives.

chapters.n: This message came in Zedekiah’s tenth year (about 588/587 BC), Nebuchadnezzar’s eighteenth—roughly a year before Jerusalem fell.
Babylon’s army was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah was confined in the guard courtyard of the royal palace—under arrest, but able to receive visitors.

f.g: The courtyard of the guard—an open area of detention, not a dungeon.

chapters.n: Zedekiah had locked him up because Jeremiah kept prophesying that God would hand the city over to Babylon.

f.w: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon

chapters.n: …and that Zedekiah himself would not escape but would be captured and meet Nebuchadnezzar face to face.

f.w: his eyes shall behold his eyes

chapters.n: …and be taken to Babylon until God dealt with him; fighting the Babylonians would be useless.

f.w: he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon

chapters.n: Jeremiah now tells what the Lord said to him.
God warned him that his cousin Hanameel would come and ask him to buy family land in Anathoth, because Jeremiah had the right to “redeem” it—to keep the property in the family.

f.g: Under the law, a near relative had the right and duty to buy land a family member had to sell, so it stayed in the family.
Jeremiah’s hometown, now in enemy-occupied territory.

chapters.n: Just as God said, his cousin came to the prison courtyard and asked him to buy the field. Then Jeremiah knew for certain it was the Lord’s doing. Sometimes confirmation comes as events unfold.

f.w: Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD

chapters.n: Jeremiah bought the field for seventeen shekels of silver, weighing out the money—coins weren’t yet common, so silver was measured by weight.

f.g: A shekel weighed roughly 11.5 grams (about 0.4 oz)—so roughly 7 ounces of silver.

chapters.n: He did it properly and legally: signed the deed, sealed it, called witnesses, and weighed the silver on scales.

f.g: Signed the deed (wrote it out and signed).
Scales.

chapters.n: He took both copies of the deed: one sealed for legal safekeeping, and one left open for easy reference—a standard practice in the ancient Near East.

f.g: The official copy, rolled up and sealed with clay; it could only be opened in a dispute.

chapters.n: He handed the deeds to Baruch, his scribe, in front of his cousin, the witnesses, and the Jews in the courtyard. This is Baruch’s first appearance in the book.

f.g: Jeremiah’s faithful scribe and companion.

chapters.n: Jeremiah gave Baruch instructions in front of everyone.

f.g: Commanded, instructed.

chapters.n: Put both deeds in a clay jar so they will last a long time. The Dead Sea Scrolls were preserved for about two thousand years in clay jars like this.

f.g: A clay jar—a common way to store documents safely for many years.

chapters.n: The point of the whole act: houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought and sold in this land. Buying land in a war zone was a bold act of faith in God’s promise of return.

f.w: Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again

chapters.n: After handing over the deed, Jeremiah prays.
“Ah, Lord God! You made heaven and earth by your great power—nothing is too hard for you.” He grounds his faith in God’s creative power.

f.w: there is nothing too hard for thee

chapters.n: God shows loyal love to thousands, yet the effects of parents’ sins fall on their children. He is great, mighty, the Lord of hosts.

f.w: into the bosom of their children
f.g: Into their laps—the consequences pass to them.

chapters.n: God is wise in planning and powerful in doing, seeing every person’s ways and rewarding each by their actions.

f.w: according to the fruit of his doings

chapters.n: He performed signs and wonders in Egypt and continues to do so in Israel and among all peoples, making his name known.
He brought Israel out of Egypt with miracles, a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror.

f.w: with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm

chapters.n: He gave them this land, as promised to their ancestors—“a land flowing with milk and honey.”

f.w: a land flowing with milk and honey

chapters.n: They entered and took it, but they didn’t obey or live by God’s law, so all this disaster came on them.
Look—the siege ramps have reached the city walls. Sword, famine, and disease are handing the city to the Babylonians. Everything God said is happening.

f.g: Siege ramps—earth mounds built against city walls so attackers could reach the top.

chapters.n: Yet God told me to buy a field with witnesses—while the city is falling! Jeremiah obeyed, but honestly asks how this makes sense.
God answers Jeremiah.
“I am the Lord, the God of all humanity. Is anything too hard for me?” God turns Jeremiah’s own words of faith into his answer.

f.w: is there any thing too hard for me?

chapters.n: Yes, the city will be handed to Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar will take it.
The Babylonians will burn the city, including the houses where incense and drink offerings were offered on rooftops to Baal and other gods.
From the beginning, Israel and Judah have done evil and provoked God with the idols they made.
Jerusalem has been a source of provocation since it was built, so God will remove it from his sight.

f.w: from the day that they built it

chapters.n: Every level of society shared the guilt: kings, officials, priests, prophets, and ordinary people.
They turned their backs on God instead of their faces. Though he taught them early and often, they wouldn’t accept correction.

f.w: turned unto me the back, and not the face

chapters.n: They even set up detestable idols in the temple itself, defiling God’s house.

f.g: Detestable things—idols and the objects of false worship.

chapters.n: They built shrines to Baal in the Valley of Hinnom to sacrifice their children to Molech—something God never commanded or even imagined.

f.g: A god associated with child sacrifice.
A euphemism for burning children as sacrifices.

chapters.n: But now God speaks about the city you say is doomed to the sword, famine, and disease…
…he will gather its people from every land where he scattered them and bring them back to live in safety.

f.w: I will gather them out of all countries

chapters.n: They will be his people, and he will be their God.
God will give them one heart and one way of life—unity and steadfast reverence—for their good and their children’s.
He will make an everlasting covenant with them, never stop doing them good, and place reverence in their hearts so they won’t turn away.
God will rejoice in doing them good and plant them in the land with all his heart and soul—the only place in scripture where God says he acts “with my whole heart and with my whole soul.”
Just as surely as he brought disaster, he will bring all the good he has promised.
Fields will again be bought in this land that people now call a desolate wasteland given to the Babylonians.

People will buy fields, sign and seal deeds, and call witnesses throughout Benjamin, Jerusalem, Judah, the hills, the lowlands, and the Negev—because God will restore their fortunes. Jeremiah’s purchase was a small down payment on that promise.

f.g: The Negev, the dry southern region.
The Shephelah, the foothills toward the coast.

chapters.n: While still confined in the guard courtyard, Jeremiah receives a second message continuing the promises of chapter 32.
The message comes from the Lord who made, shaped, and established the earth—and who will establish his promises too.
“Call to me and I will answer, and show you great and hidden things you do not know.” A beloved invitation to prayer and revelation.

f.w: Call unto me, and I will answer thee

f.g: Hebrew betsurot—fortified, inaccessible things; secrets only God can unlock.

chapters.n: God speaks about Jerusalem’s houses and royal buildings, torn down to strengthen the walls against siege ramps and swords.

f.g: Houses were demolished to get materials to reinforce walls against siege ramps.

chapters.n: The defenders fight on, but only fill those houses with corpses, because God has hidden his face from the city’s wickedness.
Yet God will heal the city and its people and reveal to them abundant peace and truth.

f.w: I will bring it health and cure

f.g: Shalom and ’emet—wholeness and faithfulness.

chapters.n: He will bring back the captives of both Judah and Israel and rebuild them as at the beginning.
He will cleanse them from all their sins and forgive every rebellion. Restoration of land comes with forgiveness of heart.

f.w: I will cleanse them from all their iniquity

chapters.n: Jerusalem will bring God joy, praise, and honor before all nations, who will tremble in awe at the good he does for her.

f.g: Provide, bring about.
