chapters.n: Again in this place—now called a wasteland without people or animals—there will be sound…

…the sounds of joy, weddings, and worshippers bringing thank offerings and singing, “Praise the Lord, for he is good; his mercy endures forever.” The very sounds silenced in 7:34 and 25:10 will return.

f.w: the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride
for his mercy endureth for ever

f.g: A thank offering.

chapters.n: Shepherds will again rest their flocks in pastures throughout this now-empty land.
In every region of Judah, flocks will again pass under the hand of the one counting them—an image of peaceful, ordered life. Christians also see the Good Shepherd who knows each sheep.

f.g: Telleth = counts. Shepherds counted sheep as they passed under the rod.

chapters.n: The days are coming when God will fulfill the good promise he made to Israel and Judah.
He will make a righteous “Branch” sprout from David’s line, who will do justice and righteousness in the land—repeating the messianic promise of 23:5.
Judah will be saved and Jerusalem safe. This time the name “The LORD our righteousness” is given to the city itself—the people take on the character of their King.
David will never lack a descendant to sit on Israel’s throne. Christians understand this to be fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the eternal King from David’s line.

f.w: David shall never want a man

f.g: Lack.

chapters.n: Nor will the Levite priests ever lack someone to offer sacrifices before God. Latter-day Saints see a latter-day fulfillment in the restoration of the Aaronic Priesthood and the prophecy of an offering by the sons of Levi.

f.g: Grain offerings (in KJV, “meat” means food).

chapters.n: Another word from the Lord comes to Jeremiah.
If you could break God’s “covenant” with day and night so that they didn’t come on schedule…

f.w: my covenant of the day, and my covenant of the night

chapters.n: …only then could his covenant with David and with the Levitical priests be broken.
Just as stars and sand can’t be counted, God will multiply David’s descendants and the Levites who serve him—echoing his promise to Abraham.

f.w: As the host of heaven cannot be numbered

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again to Jeremiah.
Have you heard people saying God has rejected the two families he chose (Israel and Judah, or the royal and priestly lines)? They treat God’s people with contempt, as if no longer a nation.
God replies: only if I had not established day and night and the laws of heaven and earth…

f.g: Fixed laws.

chapters.n: …would I reject Jacob’s descendants and David’s line. But I will restore them and have mercy on them. God’s covenant faithfulness is as certain as the sunrise.

f.w: I will cause their captivity to return

chapters.n: This message comes as Nebuchadnezzar’s huge army—drawn from all the peoples of his empire—attacks Jerusalem and the towns of Judah, about 588 BC.

f.w: all the kingdoms of the earth of his dominion
f.g: Babylon’s vassal states supplied troops for its campaigns.

chapters.n: Jeremiah must tell King Zedekiah plainly: the city will fall to Babylon and be burned.

f.w: he shall burn it with fire

chapters.n: Zedekiah won’t escape; he will meet Nebuchadnezzar face to face and be taken to Babylon.

f.w: thine eyes shall behold the eyes of the king of Babylon

chapters.n: But there is a word of mercy: Zedekiah will not be killed by the sword.

He will die in peace and be mourned with the customary honors—burning spices as for earlier kings and the lament “Alas, lord!” This mercy seems to have depended on his choices; his later blinding shows how much his refusals cost him.

f.g: Burning spices or incense to honor a king at his funeral—not cremation.

chapters.n: Jeremiah delivered all of this to Zedekiah in Jerusalem.

At that moment, only two fortified cities besides Jerusalem were still holding out: Lachish and Azekah. An ancient letter found at Lachish (one of the “Lachish Letters”) mentions watching for Lachish’s signals because Azekah’s could no longer be seen—a striking glimpse of these very days.

f.g: A major fortress city about 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem.
A fortified town about 11 miles north of Lachish.
Fortified cities.

chapters.n: Another message: earlier during the siege, Zedekiah had made a covenant with the people of Jerusalem to proclaim freedom.
They agreed that every Israelite slave, man or woman, would be freed, and no one would keep a fellow Jew in bondage.

f.g: A Hebrew woman.
That is, namely.

chapters.n: The leaders and people who entered the covenant obeyed and released their slaves. (Perhaps partly from conscience, and partly practical—fewer mouths to feed during a siege, and more men to fight.)
But afterward they changed their minds and forced the freed people back into slavery. This probably happened when the Babylonian army briefly withdrew to face Egypt (verse 21; 37:5).
So the Lord gives Jeremiah a message about this betrayal.
God reminds them: when he freed their ancestors from slavery in Egypt, he made a covenant with them—a people rescued from slavery must not enslave each other.

f.g: The house of slavery—Egypt.

chapters.n: The law said a Hebrew who sold himself into servitude (usually because of debt) must be freed after six years of service. But their ancestors ignored it.

f.w: At the end of seven years

chapters.n: You had recently done what was right—proclaiming freedom and making a solemn covenant in the temple itself.

f.w: in the house which is called by my name

chapters.n: But then you turned around and dishonored my name by taking back the people you had freed. Breaking a covenant made in God’s name profanes his name.

f.g: To go wherever they wished—fully free.

chapters.n: Biting irony: since you wouldn’t grant liberty, God will grant you “liberty”—freedom to the sword, disease, and famine—and scatter you among the nations.

f.w: I proclaim a liberty for you

chapters.n: They had made the covenant with an ancient ritual: cutting a calf in two and walking between the halves, meaning “may I be cut in pieces like this if I break my word.” Now God will hold them to it.

f.g: In Hebrew, to “make” a covenant is literally to “cut” a covenant.
Two.

chapters.n: All who walked between the pieces—officials, court officers, priests, and people—are accountable.
They will be handed to their enemies, and their bodies left for birds and wild animals—the very fate of the slain calf.

f.w: their dead bodies shall be for meat unto the fowls of the heaven

chapters.n: Zedekiah and his officials will be given to the Babylonian army—which has temporarily pulled back from the city.

f.w: which are gone up from you

chapters.n: God will order the Babylonians to return; they will capture and burn the city and leave Judah’s towns empty. Their temporary relief was not salvation.

f.w: cause them to return to this city

chapters.n: This story steps back in time to King Jehoiakim’s reign—probably near its end (about 599–598 BC), when Babylonian forces raided Judah (see verse 11).
God tells Jeremiah to bring the Rechabite clan into a temple room and offer them wine. It is a test—not to tempt them, but to put their faithfulness on display.

f.g: A clan descended from Rechab, related to the Kenites, who lived a nomadic life out of loyalty to their ancestor.
Side rooms built around the temple courts, used for storage, meetings, and priests.

chapters.n: Jeremiah gathers the whole clan, led by Jaazaniah. (This Jeremiah is a different man from the prophet.)
He brings them into a room belonging to the followers of Hanan, “a man of God,” located near rooms of high officials and above the room of a temple doorkeeper—a very public, official setting.

f.g: A title for a prophet.
A senior temple official; there were three.

chapters.n: He sets out bowls full of wine and cups, and invites them: “Drink.”
They refuse: their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them never to drink wine—them or their descendants forever.

f.g: A zealous supporter of King Jehu against Baal worship, about 250 years earlier.

chapters.n: He also told them never to build houses, plant crops, or own vineyards, but to live in tents all their lives, so they would live long as sojourners in the land. Perhaps he wanted to keep them free from the corrupting comforts of settled Canaanite life.

f.g: Resident foreigners, sojourners without land.

chapters.n: They have obeyed every part of his command—no wine for anyone in the family, men or women.
No houses, vineyards, fields, or seed.
They have lived in tents and done everything Jonadab commanded.
Only one exception: when Nebuchadnezzar invaded, they took refuge inside Jerusalem from the Babylonian and Aramean (Syrian) raiders. Even this was a practical necessity, not disloyalty.

f.g: Arameans, sent as raiders along with Babylonian troops.

chapters.n: Then the Lord gives Jeremiah the lesson.
Go tell Judah and Jerusalem: won’t you learn something from this and listen to my words?

f.g: Accept correction, learn the lesson.

chapters.n: The contrast is sharp: the Rechabites faithfully keep a mere human ancestor’s command for 250 years, but Judah ignores the living God, who has spoken to them over and over.
God sent prophet after prophet saying, “Turn from evil, stop serving other gods, and you will live in the land”—but they wouldn’t listen.
The Rechabites obeyed their father; God’s people have not obeyed him.

f.w: have performed the commandment of their father

chapters.n: So God will bring on Judah every disaster he warned of—because he spoke and they didn’t listen; he called and they didn’t answer.

f.w: I have called unto them, but they have not answered

chapters.n: Jeremiah then turns to the Rechabites with a blessing for their faithfulness.

Jonadab will never lack a descendant to “stand before” the Lord—serve him. Faithfulness to righteous family traditions brings enduring blessings, a principle Latter-day Saints value in keeping covenants across generations.

f.g: An idiom for serving God, used of priests and prophets.
Lack.

chapters.n: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year (605 BC)—the year Babylon rose to power—God gives Jeremiah a new assignment. This chapter shows how part of the book of Jeremiah came to be written.
Write on a scroll every message God has given you about Israel, Judah, and the nations, from Josiah’s day until now—about 23 years of prophecy.

f.g: A scroll, probably of papyrus or leather, rolled up rather than bound.

chapters.n: The purpose is hopeful: perhaps when Judah hears it all together, they will turn back and God can forgive them. Even judgment is written in hope of repentance.

f.w: that I may forgive their iniquity

chapters.n: Jeremiah dictates and his scribe Baruch writes everything down.

f.g: A clay seal impression reading “Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe” has been published, though its authenticity is debated.

chapters.n: Jeremiah tells Baruch he is barred from the temple—“shut up” likely means restricted or banned, not imprisoned.

f.g: Restricted, prevented—probably after his earlier temple sermons angered officials.

chapters.n: So Baruch must go read the scroll aloud in the temple on a fast day, when crowds from all Judah gather.

f.g: A special fast called in times of crisis.

chapters.n: Perhaps they will plead with God and turn from evil, because his announced anger is great.

f.g: Literally “let their plea fall before the LORD”—humble prayer.

chapters.n: Baruch did all that Jeremiah asked, reading the Lord’s words in the temple.
The reading took place in Jehoiakim’s fifth year, ninth month (December 604 BC), during a public fast—perhaps called after Babylon sacked the Philistine city of Ashkelon that winter.

f.g: Kislev, roughly November–December—winter in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Baruch read the scroll from the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan, in the upper courtyard by the New Gate, so all the people could hear. A clay seal impression bearing the name “Gemaryahu son of Shaphan” has been found in Jerusalem.

f.g: Brother of Ahikam, Jeremiah’s protector.

chapters.n: Gemariah’s son Michaiah listened to the whole reading.
He hurried to the palace, to the royal secretary’s office, where the king’s top officials were meeting.

f.g: The royal secretary—a cabinet-level official.

chapters.n: Michaiah reported everything he had heard.
The officials sent Jehudi to bring Baruch and the scroll. (Jehudi’s ancestry is traced back three generations, unusual in the Bible.)
They asked Baruch to sit and read it to them, and he did.
Hearing it, they turned to one another in fear and said, “We must tell the king.” They took the message seriously.
They asked Baruch how he had written it—had it really come from Jeremiah’s own mouth? They wanted to confirm its source before reporting it.
Baruch explained: Jeremiah dictated every word, and he wrote it in ink on the scroll.

f.g: Ink was made from soot (carbon) mixed with gum and water.

chapters.n: Knowing the king’s temper, the officials urged Baruch and Jeremiah to hide where no one could find them.

f.w: Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah

chapters.n: They left the scroll in Elishama’s office and went to tell the king what it said.
The king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and Jehudi read it aloud to the king with all his officials standing around.
It was winter, and the king sat in his winter apartment beside a fire burning in a brazier.

f.g: Rooms of the palace designed for winter use, with heating.
A brazier—a portable firepot.

chapters.n: Every time Jehudi read three or four columns, the king cut them off with a scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire—until the whole scroll was burned. A calculated, contemptuous act of rejecting God’s word.

f.g: Columns of text on the scroll.
A scribe’s knife, used to trim reed pens and cut scrolls.

chapters.n: Neither the king nor his servants showed fear or tore their clothes in grief. Contrast his father Josiah, who tore his clothes when he heard the book of the law read.
Three officials—Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah—begged the king not to burn the scroll, but he refused to listen.
The king ordered the arrest of Baruch and Jeremiah, but the Lord hid them. God protected his servants.

f.g: Or “the king’s son”—a royal prince.

chapters.n: After the scroll was burned, God spoke to Jeremiah again.
Get another scroll and write everything that was on the first one. God’s word can be burned, but it cannot be destroyed.
Tell Jehoiakim: you burned the scroll because it said Babylon would come and empty the land of people and animals.
So Jehoiakim will have no lasting heir on David’s throne (his son reigned only three months), and his body will be thrown out, exposed to the day’s heat and the night’s frost.

f.w: He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David
his dead body shall be cast out

chapters.n: God will punish him, his family, and his officials, and bring on Jerusalem and Judah every warned disaster, because they would not listen.
Jeremiah takes another scroll and Baruch writes it all again—with many similar messages added. Opposition didn’t silence the word; it produced more of it.

f.w: there were added besides unto them many like words

chapters.n: Jumping ahead about 18 years: Zedekiah, another son of Josiah, had been placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar in place of Coniah (Jehoiachin) in 597 BC.

f.g: Originally named Mattaniah; Nebuchadnezzar renamed him.

chapters.n: But Zedekiah, his officials, and the people ignored the Lord’s words through Jeremiah. That is the key to the tragedy that follows.

f.w: did hearken unto the words of the LORD

chapters.n: Still, Zedekiah sent messengers asking Jeremiah to pray for them. He wanted God’s help without obeying God’s word. (A clay seal bearing the name of Jehucal son of Shelemiah has been found in Jerusalem.)

f.w: Pray now unto the LORD our God for us

chapters.n: At this point Jeremiah was still free to move about; he hadn’t yet been imprisoned.
Pharaoh’s army (under Hophra) had marched out of Egypt, and the Babylonians lifted the siege to deal with them. Jerusalem breathed a sigh of relief.

f.g: Pharaoh Hophra (Apries), who reigned about 589–570 BC.

chapters.n: Then the Lord spoke to Jeremiah.
Tell the king: Pharaoh’s army that came to help you will go back home to Egypt.
And the Babylonians will return, attack, capture, and burn the city.
Don’t fool yourselves into thinking the Babylonians are gone for good. They are not.
Even if you defeated their entire army and only wounded men were left in their tents, those wounded men would get up and burn this city. The outcome is decided by God, not by military odds.
During that break in the siege, when the Babylonians withdrew because of Pharaoh’s army…
…Jeremiah set out for his home territory of Benjamin to take care of a property matter among family—probably connected with an inheritance share.

f.w: to separate himself thence in the midst of the people
f.g: Probably “to receive a share (of property) there among his people.”

chapters.n: At the Benjamin Gate, a guard officer named Irijah arrested him: “You’re deserting to the Babylonians!” Given Jeremiah’s message, the accusation seemed plausible.

f.g: An officer of the guard.

f.w: Thou fallest away to the Chaldeans
f.g: You’re defecting to the enemy.

chapters.n: Jeremiah denied it: “That’s a lie!” But Irijah wouldn’t listen and brought him to the officials.
The officials were furious, beat him, and imprisoned him in the house of Jonathan the royal secretary, which had been turned into a jail.

f.g: Angry.

chapters.n: Jeremiah was put in an underground cistern-like dungeon with vaulted cells, and stayed there a long time.

f.g: Vaulted cells or cellars.
Literally “house of the pit”—an underground cell or cistern.

chapters.n: Eventually Zedekiah secretly had him brought to the palace and asked, “Is there any word from the Lord?” “There is,” Jeremiah answered: “You will be handed over to the king of Babylon.” Even after suffering, Jeremiah won’t soften God’s message.

f.w: Is there any word from the LORD?

chapters.n: Jeremiah asks the king what crime he has committed against anyone to deserve prison.
“Where are your prophets now—the ones who promised Babylon would never attack?” Events had already exposed them.
He pleads humbly not to be sent back to Jonathan’s house, or he will die there. Jeremiah is bold with God’s message but humble about his own needs.

f.w: let my supplication, I pray thee, be accepted before thee
f.g: Literally “let my plea fall before you.”

chapters.n: Zedekiah moves him to the guard courtyard and orders a daily loaf of bread for him from the Bakers’ Street, as long as bread lasts in the city. God provides for his prophet even during famine.

f.g: Ancient cities grouped trades on particular streets.

f.w: until all the bread in the city were spent

chapters.n: Four powerful officials heard what Jeremiah was telling the people. Two of them—Jucal (Jehucal) and Pashur son of Malchiah—had earlier been sent by the king to consult him.
His message: whoever stays in the city will die by sword, famine, or disease; whoever surrenders to the Babylonians will escape with his life.

f.w: he shall have his life for a prey

chapters.n: And the city will certainly be captured by Babylon’s army.

The officials demand Jeremiah’s execution, charging that he is demoralizing the soldiers and people—“he doesn’t want their good, but their harm.” Ironically, Jeremiah was the one truly seeking their welfare.

f.g: An idiom for discouraging, undermining morale.
Hebrew shalom—peace, well-being.

chapters.n: Weak Zedekiah gives in: “He’s in your hands—the king can’t oppose you.” His spinelessness echoes Pilate’s washing of his hands.
They lower Jeremiah by ropes into a cistern in the guard courtyard. It has no water, only mud, and he sinks into it—left to die slowly without technically shedding his blood.

f.g: A cistern—a pit for storing rainwater, here nearly dry with deep mud at the bottom.
Deep mud.

chapters.n: Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian (Cushite) court official, hears of it. The king was sitting at the Benjamin Gate, probably hearing cases.

f.g: His name means “servant of the king.”
Hebrew Cushi—from Cush, the region south of Egypt (modern Sudan).
Court officials; the term often meant a high officer.

chapters.n: Ebed-melech leaves the palace and goes straight to the king.

He boldly tells the king that these men have done evil to the prophet, who will starve in the cistern now that bread has run out. A foreigner shows more courage and righteousness than Judah’s own leaders.

f.w: there is no more bread in the city

chapters.n: The king reverses himself and orders Ebed-melech to take thirty men and pull Jeremiah out before he dies.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “three men”; thirty would provide protection against the officials.

chapters.n: Ebed-melech gets worn-out clothes and rags from a storeroom under the palace treasury and lowers them by ropes to Jeremiah.

f.g: Worn-out, discarded pieces of cloth.

chapters.n: He tells Jeremiah to pad his armpits with the rags under the ropes so they won’t cut him as he’s pulled out of the thick mud. A small, thoughtful detail of compassion.

f.g: Armpits.

chapters.n: They hoist Jeremiah up, and he stays in the guard courtyard.
Zedekiah secretly brings Jeremiah to a private entrance of the temple and says, “I want to ask you something—hide nothing from me.”

f.g: An entrance to the temple, perhaps a private royal passage; its exact location is unknown.

chapters.n: Jeremiah answers frankly: if I tell you, won’t you kill me? And if I advise you, you won’t listen anyway.
Zedekiah swears secretly, by the Lord who gave us life, not to kill him or hand him to those who want him dead.

f.g: Who gave us life.

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s counsel: surrender to Babylon’s officers, and you, your family, and the city will survive and not be burned. Even now, a door of mercy is open.
If you refuse, the city will be burned and you will not escape.
Zedekiah admits his real fear: being handed over to Jews who had already defected and being mocked by them. Fear of people kept him from obeying God.

f.w: I am afraid of the Jews

chapters.n: Jeremiah assures him they won’t hand him over and pleads: please obey the Lord’s voice—it will go well for you, and you will live.
But if you refuse, here is what the Lord has shown me.

The women of the palace will be led out to Babylon’s officers, singing a taunt: “Your trusted friends misled you; now your feet are stuck in the mud and they’ve abandoned you.” Zedekiah would end up in the mire he let Jeremiah sink into.

f.w: thy feet are sunk in the mire

f.g: Misled, deceived you.

chapters.n: Your wives and children will be handed to the Babylonians, you will be captured, and you will be responsible for the city’s burning.

f.w: they shall bring out all thy wives and thy children

chapters.n: Zedekiah’s only response is to ask for secrecy: tell no one about this conversation, and you won’t die.
If the officials learn we talked and press you to reveal what was said, promising not to kill you…
…tell them you were pleading not to be sent back to Jonathan’s house to die. (That was a true request he had made earlier, so he isn’t inventing a lie.)
The officials did come, and Jeremiah answered as the king instructed. They dropped the matter because no one had overheard the real conversation.
Jeremiah stayed in the guard courtyard until the day Jerusalem was captured.

f.w: until the day that Jerusalem was taken

chapters.n: The siege began in Zedekiah’s ninth year, tenth month (January 588 BC by many reckonings). Jews still commemorate this day with a fast.

f.g: Tevet. The Fast of the Tenth of Tevet remembers the start of the siege.

chapters.n: About a year and a half later, in Zedekiah’s eleventh year, fourth month, ninth day (July 586 BC by most reckonings), the Babylonians broke through the wall.

f.g: A breach was made in the wall.

chapters.n: Babylon’s senior officials enter and sit in the Middle Gate—taking control of the city. Some names are titles: Rab-saris (“chief official”) and Rab-mag (a high court office). Nergal-sharezer may be Neriglissar, who later became king of Babylon.

f.g: A title: chief of the court officials.
A title for a high Babylonian official.
Babylonian Nergal-sharra-usur; probably Neriglissar, king 560–556 BC.

chapters.n: Seeing them, Zedekiah and his soldiers fled at night through the royal garden by a gate between the two walls, heading east toward the Jordan Valley.

f.g: Hebrew Arabah—the Jordan rift valley.

f.w: the gate betwixt the two walls
f.g: Probably near the southern tip of the city, by the Pool of Siloam.

chapters.n: The Babylonians caught him in the plains near Jericho and brought him north to Nebuchadnezzar’s headquarters at Riblah in Syria for sentencing.

f.w: Riblah in the land of Hamath
f.g: A town on the Orontes River in Syria, used as a Babylonian military base.

chapters.n: At Riblah, Nebuchadnezzar killed Zedekiah’s sons in front of him, along with Judah’s nobles. The Book of Mormon reveals that one son, Mulek, escaped and was led to the Americas.
Then he blinded Zedekiah and bound him in bronze chains to take him to Babylon. This reconciles two prophecies: he would see Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 32:4) yet not see Babylon (Ezekiel 12:13).
The Babylonians burned the palace and homes and tore down Jerusalem’s walls. (The temple’s burning is detailed in 52:13.)

f.w: brake down the walls of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Nebuzaradan, commander of the imperial guard, deported the remaining population to Babylon—including those who had already defected.

f.g: Babylonian Nabû-zēr-iddin; his title appears in Babylonian records.

f.w: those that fell away, that fell to him
f.g: Deserters who had already surrendered.

chapters.n: He left the poorest people, who owned nothing, in Judah and gave them vineyards and fields. A reversal: the poor inherited the land of those who had oppressed them.

f.w: the poor of the people, which had nothing

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar himself gave orders concerning Jeremiah. The Babylonians likely knew he had urged surrender.
“Take him, look after him, don’t harm him, and do whatever he asks.” The enemy king treats God’s prophet better than Judah’s own king did.
Nebuzaradan and the leading Babylonian officials sent for him.

f.g: Nabû-šūzibanni, chief official.

chapters.n: They took Jeremiah out of the guard courtyard and entrusted him to Gedaliah, grandson of Shaphan, to take him home. Shaphan’s family had protected Jeremiah for years. (Chapter 40 gives a fuller account of his release.)
Now a flashback: while Jeremiah was still confined, God gave him a message for Ebed-melech.
Tell Ebed-melech the Ethiopian: the disaster I promised will happen to this city, and you will see it.
But I will rescue you that day; you won’t fall into the hands of those you fear.
You will not die by the sword but will escape with your life, because you trusted in me. His rescue of Jeremiah was an act of faith, and God remembered it.

f.w: because thou hast put thy trust in me

chapters.n: After Jerusalem fell, Jeremiah had apparently been swept up with the captives and taken in chains to Ramah, a holding camp north of Jerusalem for deportees. There Nebuzaradan set him free.

f.g: About 5 miles north of Jerusalem; the staging point for the march to Babylon.

chapters.n: The Babylonian commander takes Jeremiah aside and says, “The Lord your God announced this disaster on this place.”
“And now he has done what he said, because you people sinned and didn’t obey him.” Strikingly, a pagan officer understands Judah’s fall better than Judah’s leaders did.
“I’m freeing you from your chains today. Come to Babylon if you wish, and I’ll look after you—or stay. The whole land is open to you; go wherever you think best.”

f.g: Don’t (come)—stay behind.
Fitting, right.

chapters.n: Before Jeremiah could reply, he added: “Go back to Gedaliah, whom Babylon has made governor of Judah, and live with him among the people—or go wherever you like.” He gave him food and a gift and let him go.

f.g: Food, provisions.
A seal impression reading “belonging to Gedaliah, who is over the house” found at Lachish may refer to him.

chapters.n: Jeremiah chose to stay with the poor remnant in the land, going to Gedaliah at Mizpah. He could have had comfort in Babylon but stayed with his people.

f.g: A town in Benjamin, about 8 miles north of Jerusalem, now the administrative center.

chapters.n: Army officers and their men still hiding in the countryside heard that Gedaliah had been appointed governor over the remaining poor people—men, women, and children not taken to Babylon.

f.w: the captains of the forces which were in the fields
f.g: Commanders of Judean troops who had escaped the city and were scattered in the countryside.

chapters.n: They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael, Johanan and Jonathan sons of Kareah, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai, and Jezaniah, with their men.

f.g: From Netophah, a village near Bethlehem.
From Maacah, a region northeast of Galilee.

chapters.n: Gedaliah swore to them: “Don’t be afraid to serve the Babylonians. Settle in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well.” This was Jeremiah’s own counsel.

f.w: Fear not to serve the Chaldeans

chapters.n: Gedaliah would represent them before the Babylonians at Mizpah; meanwhile they should harvest wine, summer fruit, and oil, store it, and live in the towns they had occupied.

f.g: Figs and similar fruits harvested in late summer.

chapters.n: Jews who had fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom, and other lands heard that a remnant had been left in Judah under Gedaliah.
They came home to Judah, to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gathered an abundant harvest. A brief, hopeful season of renewal after catastrophe.

f.w: gathered wine and summer fruits very much

chapters.n: Johanan and the other commanders came to Gedaliah at Mizpah with a warning.

“Do you know that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, has sent Ishmael to assassinate you?” But Gedaliah didn’t believe them. Ammon was resisting Babylon and wanted the pro-Babylonian government in Judah gone.

f.w: Baalis the king of the Ammonites
f.g: An Ammonite seal impression mentioning a king named Ba‘alyasha‘ has been found, possibly the same man.

chapters.n: Johanan offered secretly to kill Ishmael first: “Why let him kill you, scatter everyone gathered to you, and destroy the remnant of Judah?”
Gedaliah forbade it: “Don’t do this—what you say about Ishmael isn’t true.” His trusting, honorable nature would cost him his life.

In the seventh month, Ishmael—a member of the royal family—arrived at Mizpah with ten men and ate a meal with Gedaliah. Sharing a meal implied friendship and safety, making what followed even more treacherous.

f.g: Tishri (September–October). The year is debated—possibly just months after Jerusalem fell, or a few years later.
A descendant of David’s line, who may have resented Gedaliah, a non-royal ruling for Babylon.

chapters.n: Then Ishmael and his men rose up and killed Gedaliah with the sword. Jews still observe a fast, the Fast of Gedaliah, remembering this murder and the loss of the last Jewish self-rule in the land.

f.g: Commemorated by the Fast of Gedaliah, just after the New Year.

chapters.n: Ishmael also killed the Jews with Gedaliah, the Babylonian soldiers stationed there, and the fighting men.
The next day, before anyone outside knew of the murder…

…eighty men arrived from northern towns—Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria—in mourning, with shaved beards, torn clothes, and gashes on their bodies, carrying grain offerings and incense for the ruined temple site. They were pilgrims grieving Jerusalem’s fall.

f.w: having their beards shaven, and their clothes rent
f.g: Signs of mourning.
A mourning custom the law forbade.
Worship apparently continued at the ruined temple site.

chapters.n: Ishmael went out to meet them, pretending to weep, and invited them in to see Gedaliah.
Once they were inside the town, Ishmael and his men killed them and threw their bodies into a cistern.
Ten of them saved their lives by saying they had hidden stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey in the fields. Ishmael spared them—greed outweighing even his violence.

f.g: Underground storage pits for grain and supplies, common in the region.
Held back, refrained.

chapters.n: The cistern he filled with bodies had been built some 300 years earlier by King Asa of Judah, when he fortified Mizpah against King Baasha of Israel.
Ishmael took all the remaining people at Mizpah captive—including the king’s daughters entrusted to Gedaliah by Nebuzaradan—and set off to cross over to Ammon.

f.g: Princesses of the royal house, probably Zedekiah’s daughters.

chapters.n: Johanan and the other commanders heard about all the evil Ishmael had done.
They gathered their men to fight Ishmael and caught up with him at the great pool of Gibeon.

f.w: the great waters that are in Gibeon
f.g: A large pool at Gibeon; archaeologists have uncovered a huge rock-cut water shaft there.

chapters.n: When Ishmael’s captives saw Johanan and his forces, they were overjoyed.
All the captives turned around and went over to Johanan.

f.g: Turned around.

chapters.n: Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites. (He had started with ten; two may have been killed.)
Johanan and his commanders took charge of all the rescued survivors—soldiers, women, children, and court officials—whom they had brought back from Gibeon.
They traveled to Geruth Chimham near Bethlehem, intending to go on to Egypt.

f.g: Hebrew Geruth Kimham, “Chimham’s lodging”—perhaps a caravan stop. Chimham was a friend of King David.

chapters.n: They feared Babylon would take revenge for the murder of its appointed governor—even though they had nothing to do with it. Fear, not faith, is starting to drive their decisions.
All the military leaders, including Johanan and Jezaniah, and all the people, from least to greatest, approached Jeremiah.

f.g: Probably the same as “Azariah son of Hoshaiah” in 43:2.

chapters.n: They humbly ask him to pray to “the Lord your God” for them, since only a small remnant is left. Notice: “your God”—not yet “our God.”

f.w: we are left but a few of many

chapters.n: They ask God to show them which way to go and what to do. It sounds sincere—but their minds were already largely made up (41:17).
Jeremiah agrees to pray to “the Lord your God,” gently reminding them that God is theirs too, and promises to tell them everything God says, holding nothing back.

f.w: I will keep nothing back from you

chapters.n: They swear an oath: may the Lord be a true witness against us if we don’t do everything he tells us.
“Whether we like the answer or not, we will obey the Lord, so that it may go well with us.” A beautiful promise—if only they kept it.

f.w: Whether it be good, or whether it be evil
f.g: Whether pleasant or unpleasant to us.

chapters.n: God answered after ten days. Even a great prophet had to wait on the Lord’s timing rather than give a quick answer of his own.
Jeremiah gathered Johanan, the commanders, and all the people.
He delivered the answer from the God to whom they had sent him.
If you stay in this land, God will build and plant you—the words of Jeremiah’s call again—because he grieves over the disaster he brought on them.

f.w: will I build you, and not pull you down
I repent me of the evil
f.g: I am grieved over, or relent concerning, the calamity.

chapters.n: Don’t fear the king of Babylon—God is with you to save and rescue you from him.

f.w: I am with you to save you

chapters.n: God will show you mercy and move Babylon’s king to treat you mercifully and let you stay in your land.

f.w: that he may have mercy upon you

chapters.n: But if you say, “We won’t stay here,” disobeying the Lord…
…and insist, “No! We’ll go to Egypt, where there’s no war, no battle trumpet, and no hunger”—Egypt seemed like a safe haven…

f.g: The shofar, sounded as a war alarm.

chapters.n: …then hear the Lord: if you are determined to go and settle in Egypt…

f.g: Firmly determine.

chapters.n: …the very sword and famine you fear will catch up with you in Egypt, and you’ll die there. Running from God’s counsel doesn’t outrun trouble.
Everyone determined to go will die by sword, famine, or disease; none will escape.
As God’s anger fell on Jerusalem, it will fall on you in Egypt. You will become a curse and disgrace, and never see this land again.

f.g: An object of cursing.

chapters.n: The Lord’s clear word to the remnant: Do not go to Egypt. Know for certain I have warned you today.

f.g: Warned, testified to.

chapters.n: Jeremiah sees through them: you were deceiving yourselves when you asked me to pray and promised to obey whatever God said.

f.g: You were insincere; or, you have put your own lives at risk.

chapters.n: I have told you his answer today, but you haven’t obeyed any of it. Asking for revelation while intending to ignore it is a dangerous kind of prayer.

f.w: ye have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God

chapters.n: So know for certain: you will die by sword, famine, and disease in the place where you want to go.
As soon as Jeremiah finished delivering every word God had sent…
…Azariah, Johanan, and other “proud men” accused him: “You’re lying! The Lord didn’t send you to tell us not to go to Egypt.” When the answer didn’t match their wishes, they rejected the messenger.

f.g: Arrogant, insolent men—pride lay at the root of their rejection.

chapters.n: They blamed Baruch for turning Jeremiah against them, claiming he wanted them handed to the Babylonians to be killed or exiled.

f.g: Incites you, puts you up to it.

chapters.n: So Johanan, the commanders, and all the people disobeyed the Lord’s command to stay in Judah.
Johanan and the commanders took the entire remnant—including those who had returned from neighboring lands to live in Judah.

f.w: that were returned from all nations

chapters.n: Men, women, children, the king’s daughters, everyone left with Gedaliah—and Jeremiah and Baruch too, apparently against their will.
They went to Egypt in disobedience and arrived at Tahpanhes, an Egyptian border fortress in the eastern Nile Delta. Judah’s history had come full circle—back to Egypt.

f.g: A frontier city in the northeastern Nile Delta, known to the Greeks as Daphnae.

chapters.n: Even in Egypt, God continued to speak through Jeremiah.
God told Jeremiah to bury large stones in the clay pavement at the entrance to Pharaoh’s government building in Tahpanhes, while the men of Judah watched—another acted-out prophecy.

f.g: Perhaps a brick pavement or terrace in front of the building.
A royal residence or government building, not the main palace.

chapters.n: Then announce: God will bring Nebuchadnezzar, “my servant,” who will set his throne on these very stones and spread his royal canopy over them. Egypt is no refuge from Babylon.

f.g: A royal canopy or carpet.

chapters.n: He will strike Egypt, sending each person to the fate appointed—death, captivity, or the sword. A fragmentary Babylonian text records a Nebuchadnezzar campaign against Egypt around 568/567 BC.

f.w: such as are for death to death

chapters.n: God will set fire to Egypt’s temples. Nebuchadnezzar will burn them and carry off their gods, and wrap himself in Egypt’s wealth as easily as a shepherd wraps himself in his cloak, then leave unharmed.

f.w: array himself with the land of Egypt
f.g: Perhaps “pick Egypt clean as a shepherd picks lice from his cloak”—either way, an image of easy conquest.

chapters.n: He will smash the sacred obelisks of Beth-shemesh and burn Egypt’s temples. Even Egypt’s gods can’t protect the refugees.

f.w: Beth-shemesh, that is in the land of Egypt
f.g: “House of the sun”—Heliopolis (biblical On), the center of sun worship, famous for its obelisks.
Sacred pillars—here the obelisks.

chapters.n: Jeremiah’s last recorded message is to Jews now scattered across Egypt—from border towns in the northeast delta down to Upper Egypt in the south.

f.g: A fortress on Egypt’s northeastern frontier.
Memphis, the old capital near modern Cairo.
Upper (southern) Egypt. A Jewish colony later flourished at Elephantine there.

chapters.n: You have seen the disaster God brought on Jerusalem and Judah’s towns—they lie empty today.
It happened because they angered God by burning incense and serving other gods—gods they had no real knowledge of or relationship with.
Yet God kept sending prophets, earnestly pleading, “Please don’t do this detestable thing I hate!” A glimpse of God’s grief and patience.

f.w: Oh, do not this abominable thing that I hate

chapters.n: But they didn’t listen or turn away from offering incense to other gods.
So God’s anger blazed against Judah and Jerusalem, leaving them ruined as they are today.
Why are you now doing such great harm to yourselves, cutting off men, women, children, and babies until no one of Judah remains?

f.g: Against yourselves, your own lives.
A nursing baby.

chapters.n: By worshipping idols in Egypt you are destroying yourselves and becoming a curse among the nations.
Have you forgotten all the sins of your ancestors, your kings and their wives, and your own and your wives’—committed in Judah and Jerusalem?
Even now they haven’t humbled themselves, shown reverence, or followed God’s law. Catastrophe alone hasn’t changed their hearts.

f.g: Literally “not crushed”—not contrite.

chapters.n: So God has set his face against them for disaster, to cut off all Judah in Egypt.
The remnant that insisted on going to Egypt will all perish there by sword and famine, from least to greatest, becoming a curse and disgrace.

f.w: that have set their faces to go into the land of Egypt

chapters.n: God will punish those in Egypt as he punished Jerusalem.
None of those who went to Egypt will return to Judah as they hope—only a few fugitives.

f.w: none shall return but such as shall escape

chapters.n: A huge crowd—men who knew their wives offered incense to other gods, the women themselves, and all the Jews in Pathros—answered Jeremiah.
Their answer is blunt: “We will not listen to what you say in the Lord’s name.”
“We’ll do exactly what we vowed—burn incense and pour drink offerings to the Queen of Heaven, as we and our ancestors and kings did. Back then we had plenty of food and no trouble.”

f.g: A popular goddess, probably Ishtar/Astarte, linked to the planet Venus and to fertility.

chapters.n: “Since we stopped (probably during Josiah’s reforms), we’ve lacked everything and been destroyed by sword and famine.” They read history backwards: they blamed their disasters on abandoning idols, not on abandoning God.

f.g: Lacked.

chapters.n: The women add: “Did we make cakes in her image and pour offerings without our husbands’ approval?” Under the law a husband could cancel his wife’s vow; they say their husbands approved.

f.g: Cakes perhaps shaped in the goddess’s image or stamped with a star.

chapters.n: Jeremiah responds to everyone who gave that answer.
Didn’t the Lord remember and take note of all the incense you and your ancestors burned in Judah?
The Lord could no longer endure your evil deeds and abominations—that’s why your land is a desolate ruin today. Jeremiah corrects their reading of history.

f.w: the LORD could no longer bear

chapters.n: This disaster came because you sinned, burned incense, and didn’t obey his law, statutes, or testimonies.

f.g: God’s covenant stipulations, his solemn witnesses.

chapters.n: Jeremiah addresses the people again, especially the women: hear the Lord’s word, all Judah in Egypt.
With biting irony: you and your wives said you would keep your vows to the Queen of Heaven, and you did. Go ahead then—keep your vows!

f.w: ye will surely accomplish your vows

chapters.n: But God swears by his great name: no one of Judah in Egypt will invoke his name in an oath again. They will have lost the right to call on him.

f.w: I have sworn by my great name

f.g: A common oath formula.

chapters.n: God will watch over them for harm, not good, until they are consumed—a dark reversal of his promise to watch over Israel “to build and to plant.”

f.w: I will watch over them for evil, and not for good

chapters.n: Only a small number will escape and return to Judah. Then everyone will know whose word stands—God’s or theirs.
God gives them a sign so they’ll know his words against them will surely come true.
Pharaoh Hophra, the king they trusted, will be handed over to enemies who seek his life, just as Zedekiah was. Hophra was in fact overthrown by his general Amasis and later killed (about 570 BC).

f.g: Wahibre, Greek Apries; reigned about 589–570 BC.

chapters.n: This short, personal message to Baruch goes back to Jehoiakim’s fourth year (605 BC), when Baruch first wrote Jeremiah’s prophecies on a scroll. It may be placed here as a kind of signature to the story of Jeremiah’s life.

f.w: when he had written these words in a book

chapters.n: God has a word specifically for Baruch. The Lord notices the faithful helpers behind the scenes.
Baruch had cried, “Woe is me! The Lord has added grief to my pain; I’m exhausted with groaning and find no rest.” Writing and reading those warnings had cost him dearly.

f.g: I am worn out with groaning.

chapters.n: God’s answer: I am tearing down what I built and uprooting what I planted—the whole land. God himself feels the loss too.

f.w: that which I have built will I break down

chapters.n: “Are you seeking great things for yourself? Don’t.” Baruch, from a notable family, may have had ambitions for prominence. In a time of collapse, the greatest gift is life itself—and God promises he will keep Baruch alive wherever he goes.

f.w: seekest thou great things for thyself?
thy life will I give unto thee for a prey

chapters.n: Chapters 46–51 gather Jeremiah’s prophecies against foreign nations, fulfilling his call as “a prophet unto the nations.” The God of Israel is Lord over all peoples.

f.g: The nations, non-Israelite peoples.

chapters.n: First, Egypt. This oracle concerns Pharaoh Necho’s army, defeated by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish on the Euphrates in 605 BC—one of the turning-point battles of ancient history, which ended Egypt’s power in the region.

f.g: Necho II (about 610–595 BC), who had killed King Josiah at Megiddo.
A city on the upper Euphrates, on today’s Turkey–Syria border.

chapters.n: The poem opens with officers barking orders: prepare your shields—small and large—and advance into battle!

f.g: A small round shield; the “shield” was a larger body shield.

chapters.n: Harness the chariot horses, mount up, take your positions with helmets on, polish your spears, and put on armor!

f.g: Polish, sharpen.
Coats of armor—scale mail.

chapters.n: Suddenly the scene flips: why are they terrified and retreating? Their warriors are beaten and fleeing without looking back—terror on every side.

f.g: Hebrew magor missabib, Jeremiah’s signature phrase.
Quickly.

chapters.n: Not even the fastest or strongest can escape; they stumble and fall in the north, by the Euphrates.

f.w: Let not the swift flee away

chapters.n: Who is this rising like the Nile in flood, with surging waters?

f.g: The Nile’s annual flood was Egypt’s defining image of power.

chapters.n: It’s Egypt, boasting: “I will rise and cover the earth, destroying cities and their people.”
Charge, horses! Race, chariots! March out, warriors—Egypt’s mercenaries from Cush, Put, and Lud, skilled with shields and bows.

f.g: Hebrew Cush and Put—peoples south and west of Egypt who served as mercenaries.
Hebrew Ludim; Lydian (in western Asia Minor) or African archers.

chapters.n: But this is the Lord’s day of vengeance. The battle at the Euphrates is pictured as his “sacrifice”—a grim image of a vast slaughter that settles accounts with his enemies, including the Pharaoh who killed Josiah.

f.w: the day of the Lord GOD of hosts

f.g: Satisfied, glutted.

chapters.n: Go up to Gilead for healing balm, Egypt—but no medicine will cure you. Egypt was famous for its physicians, yet this wound is beyond them.

f.g: A healing resin from Gilead, famous in the ancient world.

chapters.n: Nations hear of Egypt’s humiliation; warriors trip over one another and fall together in panic.
A second oracle: Nebuchadnezzar will come and attack Egypt itself, not just its army abroad.

f.w: should come and smite the land of Egypt

chapters.n: Sound the alarm in Egypt’s cities—Migdol, Memphis, Tahpanhes: get ready, for the sword is devouring all around you. These are the very towns where Judean refugees later settled.

f.g: Memphis.

chapters.n: Why are your mighty ones swept away? They couldn’t stand, because the Lord drove them down. Some ancient versions read, “Why has Apis fled?”—Apis being Egypt’s sacred bull god.

f.g: The Greek Septuagint reads “Apis, your chosen calf,” as though Egypt’s bull-god himself had fled.

chapters.n: Soldiers stumble and fall over each other. Foreign mercenaries say, “Let’s go home to our own people, away from the oppressor’s sword.”
They mock Pharaoh: “He’s just a lot of noise—he missed his chance.”

f.w: Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise
f.g: Perhaps a pun on Pharaoh’s title: “Loudmouth who let the moment pass.”

chapters.n: The true King, the Lord of hosts, swears: as surely as Mount Tabor towers over the plain and Mount Carmel over the sea, the conqueror will come. His arrival is as certain and conspicuous as those mountains.

f.g: A prominent rounded mountain in Galilee.
A mountain ridge jutting out to the Mediterranean.

chapters.n: Pack your bags for exile, people of Egypt; Memphis will become a ruin without inhabitants.

f.g: Prepare your baggage.

chapters.n: Egypt is like a beautiful young cow, but a stinging horsefly is coming from the north. (Egypt worshipped sacred bulls, which makes the image pointed.)

f.g: Hebrew qerets—probably a gadfly or biting insect.

chapters.n: Her hired mercenaries, fat like stall-fed calves, also turn and run—their day of disaster has come.

f.g: Mercenary soldiers.

chapters.n: Egypt slithers away hissing like a snake as the enemy marches in with axes like woodcutters.

f.w: The voice thereof shall go like a serpent
f.g: Egypt’s royal crown bore a cobra (uraeus); now the snake can only hiss in retreat.

chapters.n: They will cut down her “forest”—her people and defenses—though it seems endless, because the invaders outnumber locusts.

f.g: Locusts—an image of an innumerable, devouring army.

chapters.n: Daughter Egypt will be put to shame, handed over to the people of the north.
God will punish Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh, Egypt, its gods and kings, and all who trust in Pharaoh—including Judeans who ran to Egypt for safety.

f.g: Amon of No—the chief god of No (Thebes), Egypt’s great southern religious capital.

f.w: all them that trust in him

chapters.n: Egypt will fall to Nebuchadnezzar and his officers—but afterward, God says, it will be inhabited as before. Judgment isn’t God’s final word, even for Egypt.

Then a sudden word of comfort to Israel: don’t fear, my servant Jacob. God will rescue you and your children from far-off lands; you will return and live in peace. (Repeated almost word for word from 30:10.)

f.w: fear not thou, O my servant Jacob

chapters.n: God will destroy the nations where Israel was scattered, but never completely destroy Israel. He will discipline them justly, but not abandon them.
A message against the Philistines, Israel’s ancient coastal rivals, given before a Pharaoh attacked Gaza. Which Pharaoh and when is uncertain—possibly Necho around 609 BC.

f.g: A people who settled on the southern coast of Canaan around 1200 BC; the name “Palestine” comes from them.
The southernmost of the five main Philistine cities.

chapters.n: Waters are rising from the north—an image of Babylon’s army sweeping in like a river in flood, drowning towns and people. Everyone cries and wails.

f.w: waters rise up out of the north

chapters.n: At the thunder of galloping horses and rumbling chariot wheels, fathers are so paralyzed with fear they don’t even turn back to help their children.

f.g: Limp, helpless hands—paralyzing fear.

chapters.n: The day has come to destroy the Philistines and cut off Tyre and Sidon’s last allies. The Philistines are the “remnant of Caphtor,” their ancestral island home.

f.g: Usually identified with Crete or the Aegean region, from which the Philistines came.
Phoenician cities that may have been allied with the Philistines.

chapters.n: Gaza shaves its head in mourning; Ashkelon is silenced. How long will you gash yourselves in grief?

f.g: Shaving the head was a sign of mourning.
Cutting the body was a pagan mourning rite.
Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BC; archaeologists have found its destruction layer.

chapters.n: Someone cries out: “Sword of the Lord, how long until you rest? Go back into your sheath and be still!”

f.w: O thou sword of the LORD

chapters.n: The answer: how can it rest when the Lord has given it orders against Ashkelon and the coast? Babylon’s sword moves only under God’s command.
Now a long lament over Moab, Israel’s neighbor east of the Dead Sea. It borrows heavily from Isaiah 15–16. It opens by naming Moabite towns already falling: Nebo, Kiriathaim, and the stronghold.

f.g: A kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea. Ruth, ancestor of David and of Jesus, was a Moabite.
A Moabite town named for the mountain where Moses died.
Hebrew “the high fortress”—perhaps a place name, or Moab’s strongholds in general.

chapters.n: Moab’s glory is gone. In Heshbon enemies plot to wipe it out as a nation; the town of Madmen will be silenced. The Hebrew is full of puns on the place names.

f.w: in Heshbon they have devised evil
f.g: Wordplay: “in Heshbon they have planned (hashbu).”
A Moabite town; its name sounds like the Hebrew for “be silenced” (tiddommi).

chapters.n: Cries rise from Horonaim: devastation and great destruction.
Moab is shattered; her little ones cry out.
Refugees weep as they climb the ascent of Luhith and descend toward Horonaim, hearing cries of disaster.
Run for your lives! Be like a scrubby desert bush—alone, stripped, in the wilderness.

f.g: A juniper or desert shrub—possibly a play on the Moabite town Aroer.

chapters.n: Because Moab trusted its own achievements and wealth, it too will be captured. Even its god Chemosh will be carried into exile with his priests and officials—powerless to save.

f.g: Moab’s national god. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription from about 840 BC, names Chemosh repeatedly.

chapters.n: The destroyer will come against every town; valley and plateau alike will be ruined, as the Lord said.

f.g: The Mishor, Moab’s high tableland north of the Arnon River.

chapters.n: Give Moab wings so it can fly away—its towns will be emptied. (The Hebrew may also mean “put salt on Moab,” sowing it to make it barren.)

f.g: The rare word tsits may mean “wings” or “salt.”

chapters.n: A grim warning to the instruments of judgment: cursed is anyone who does the Lord’s assigned work half-heartedly or holds back the sword. When God appoints a task, it must be done fully.

f.g: Negligently, slackly.

f.w: Cursed be he that doeth the work of the LORD deceitfully

chapters.n: Moab has always been comfortable, never invaded or exiled—like wine left sitting on its dregs, never poured from jar to jar. So it kept its original harsh “flavor”: its character was never refined.

f.g: Lees = sediment in wine. Winemakers poured wine from one vessel to another to clarify it; wine left on its lees grew thick and harsh.

chapters.n: So God will send “pourers” who will tip Moab over, empty its jars, and smash them.

f.w: wanderers, that shall cause him to wander
f.g: Better “tilters/pourers who will pour him out”—continuing the wine image.

chapters.n: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as northern Israel was ashamed of trusting the shrine at Bethel, with its golden calf.
How can you say, “We’re heroes, mighty warriors”?
Moab is destroyed; its finest young men go down to slaughter—declares the King, the Lord of hosts.

f.w: the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts

chapters.n: Moab’s disaster is near, and its ruin approaches quickly.
All neighbors, mourn for Moab: “How the mighty scepter is broken, the glorious staff!”

f.g: A ruler’s scepter—symbol of Moab’s power.

chapters.n: Come down from your glory, people of Dibon, and sit in the parched dust; the destroyer is coming against your strongholds.

f.g: A major Moabite city, where the Mesha Stele was discovered in 1868.

chapters.n: People of Aroer, stand by the road and watch; ask the refugees, “What happened?”

f.g: A town on the north rim of the Arnon gorge.
Watch, look out.

chapters.n: “Moab is shamed and broken! Wail and cry; announce by the Arnon River that Moab is destroyed.”

f.g: The deep gorge and river flowing into the Dead Sea, Moab’s traditional northern border.

chapters.n: Judgment has come on the plateau towns: Holon, Jahazah, and Mephaath…

f.g: Jahaz, where Israel defeated King Sihon.

chapters.n: …Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim…
…Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon…

f.g: Also called Baal-meon; mentioned in the Mesha Stele.

chapters.n: …Kerioth, Bozrah, and all Moab’s towns, near and far. The long list conveys how total the devastation is.

f.g: A Moabite town, different from Bozrah in Edom.
Possibly a sanctuary town of Chemosh, named in the Mesha Stele.

chapters.n: Moab’s “horn” (strength) is cut off and its “arm” (power) is broken.

f.g: A symbol of strength and power, like an animal’s horn.

chapters.n: Make Moab drunk on the cup of God’s wrath, because it exalted itself against the Lord. Let it wallow in its own vomit and become a joke.
Didn’t you mock Israel as if it were caught among thieves, shaking your head with glee every time you mentioned it? Now the mocker becomes the mocked.

f.g: Or “you shook your head” in scorn.

chapters.n: Abandon your towns, Moabites; live among the rocks like doves nesting in the cliffs at the edge of a gorge.
We have heard of Moab’s pride—exceedingly proud: loftiness, arrogance, pride, and a haughty heart. The pile of words underscores its main sin.
God knows Moab’s insolent rage, but its boasting is empty and will accomplish nothing.
Surprisingly, God (through the prophet) wails for Moab and mourns for the people of Kir-heres. Even in judgment, God grieves for a foreign people.

f.g: Kir-hareseth, a major Moabite fortress, probably modern Kerak.

chapters.n: “Vine of Sibmah, I weep for you more than Jazer weeps.” Moab’s famous vineyards spread far and wide, but the destroyer has fallen on its summer fruit and grape harvest.

f.g: A town famous for its vineyards.
Possibly a scribal error; Isaiah 16:8 has simply “Jazer.”

chapters.n: Joy and celebration are gone from Moab’s fertile fields. No more wine from the presses, no more joyful harvest shouts—only battle cries.

f.g: Grape treaders shouted rhythmically as they worked.

chapters.n: Cries echo from town to town, from Heshbon to Jahaz and from Zoar to Horonaim; even the springs of Nimrim are dried up.

f.w: an heifer of three years old
f.g: Perhaps a place name, Eglath-shelishiyah.

chapters.n: God will stop those who offer sacrifices and incense to false gods at Moab’s high places.

f.w: him that offereth in the high places

chapters.n: God’s heart moans for Moab like the mournful flutes played at funerals, because all its hard-won wealth is lost.

f.g: Flutes played by professional mourners at funerals.

chapters.n: Every head shaved, every beard cut, hands gashed, sackcloth on every waist—all the signs of deep mourning.

f.g: Coarse goat-hair cloth worn in grief.

chapters.n: Lament fills every rooftop and street, because God has broken Moab like an unwanted pot.

f.w: a vessel wherein is no pleasure

chapters.n: “How shattered it is! How Moab has turned its back in shame!” Moab becomes a joke and a terror to its neighbors.
The enemy swoops down like an eagle, spreading its wings over Moab—Babylon’s army as a bird of prey.

f.w: he shall fly as an eagle

chapters.n: Kerioth and the strongholds are seized; Moab’s warriors panic like a woman in labor.
Moab will be destroyed as a nation because it exalted itself against the Lord. Historically, Moab disappears as an independent people after this era.
Terror, pit, and trap await you, people of Moab.

f.w: Fear, and the pit, and the snare
f.g: In Hebrew a sound-play: pachad, pachat, pach.

chapters.n: Whoever flees the terror falls into the pit; whoever climbs out of the pit is caught in the trap. There’s no escape when the time of reckoning comes.

Refugees stand exhausted in Heshbon’s shadow, but fire bursts from Heshbon—the old city of King Sihon—and consumes Moab’s brow and the heads of the boasters. This echoes an ancient victory song in Numbers.

f.w: a fire shall come forth out of Heshbon

f.g: The Amorite king whose capital was Heshbon; Israel defeated him under Moses.

chapters.n: Woe to you, Moab! The people of Chemosh are finished; your sons and daughters are taken captive.

Yet a final surprise: in the latter days, God will restore Moab’s fortunes. Even for a proud enemy nation, God’s last word is mercy. Latter-day Saints see in such promises God’s concern for all his children.

f.w: Yet will I bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days

chapters.n: Next, Ammon, a kingdom northeast of Moab. When the Assyrians deported Israel’s eastern tribes in the 700s BC, Ammon moved into Gad’s territory. God asks: doesn’t Israel have heirs? Why has Ammon’s king taken their land?

f.g: Descendants of Lot, like the Moabites; their capital was Rabbah (modern Amman, Jordan).
Hebrew malkam—probably “Milcom,” Ammon’s god (also in verse 3).

chapters.n: Battle alarms will sound in Rabbah, the Ammonite capital; it will become a ruin mound and its villages burned. Then Israel will reclaim its inheritance from those who took it.

f.g: Her surrounding villages.

chapters.n: Wail, Heshbon, for Ai is ruined; cry, women of Rabbah, put on sackcloth and run about inside the walls, for Milcom will go into exile with his priests and officials.

f.g: Not the Ai near Bethel, but an otherwise unknown Ammonite town; the name means “ruin.”
Walls or enclosures, perhaps sheepfold walls.

chapters.n: Why boast in your fertile valleys, faithless daughter, trusting your wealth and saying, “Who could ever attack me?”

f.g: Your valley flowing with abundance—or with blood.

chapters.n: God will bring terror on you from every side; you’ll be driven out headlong, with no one to gather the scattered refugees.
Yet afterward God will restore Ammon’s fortunes—another note of mercy for a hostile neighbor.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon

chapters.n: Now Edom, south of the Dead Sea, descended from Jacob’s brother Esau. Edom was famous for its wise men—has wisdom vanished from Teman? This section closely parallels the book of Obadiah.

f.g: A leading region or city of Edom; Job’s friend Eliphaz was a Temanite.

chapters.n: Flee, hide deep in caves, people of Dedan (Arabian traders in Edom), for God will bring Esau’s disaster on him.

f.g: Hide in deep places, caves.
An Arabian trading people whose caravans passed through Edom.

chapters.n: Grape pickers leave a few grapes behind; thieves take only what they want. But Edom’s destruction will be total.
God will strip Esau bare, exposing every hiding place; his children, relatives, and neighbors will be destroyed.

f.w: I have uncovered his secret places

chapters.n: Yet a tender note: “Leave your orphans with me—I will keep them alive; let your widows trust in me.” Even in judgment on a nation, God cares for its most vulnerable.

f.w: Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive

chapters.n: If even those who didn’t deserve to drink the cup of wrath (Judah, God’s own people) must drink, how could Edom go unpunished? It will surely drink.
God swears by himself: Bozrah, Edom’s fortress capital, will become a perpetual ruin and byword.

f.g: Edom’s capital, modern Buseirah in southern Jordan.

chapters.n: Jeremiah has heard a report from the Lord: a messenger has been sent among the nations calling them to rally and attack Edom.

f.w: I have heard a rumour from the LORD

f.g: Report, message.

chapters.n: God will make Edom small and despised among the nations.

f.w: I will make thee small among the heathen

chapters.n: Edom’s fearsome reputation and pride deceived it. Living in rocky cliffs (like the later city of Petra), it felt untouchable. But even if it nests as high as an eagle, God will bring it down.

f.g: Edom’s mountain strongholds; Hebrew sela‘, “rock,” was also an Edomite place name.
The terror you inspired in others.

chapters.n: Edom will be a ruin; passersby will be shocked and hiss at its wounds.
Like Sodom and Gomorrah, it will be overthrown and empty of people.

f.w: the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah

chapters.n: The invader will come like a lion from the Jordan’s thick jungle against a secure pasture, driving Edom’s people away in an instant. Who can stand against God? Who can summon him to court? What shepherd can resist him?

f.g: The dense thickets along the Jordan River, where lions lived.

f.w: who will appoint me the time?
f.g: Who can summon me to trial?

chapters.n: Hear God’s plan for Edom and Teman: even the smallest of the flock will be dragged away, and their pastures left desolate.

f.w: the least of the flock shall draw them out

chapters.n: The earth shakes at the crash of their fall; the cry is heard as far as the Red Sea.

f.g: Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds”; here probably the Gulf of Aqaba, on Edom’s southern edge.

chapters.n: The enemy will swoop like an eagle over Bozrah, and Edom’s warriors will be terrified like a woman in labor.
Next, Damascus and the Syrian cities of Hamath and Arpad. They are shamed by bad news and melt with fear, restless like a troubled sea.

f.g: The capital of Aram (Syria), north of Israel.
A city on the Orontes River in Syria.
A city in northern Syria.

chapters.n: Damascus grows weak and turns to flee; panic and anguish grip her like a woman in labor.

f.g: Grown weak.

chapters.n: “How can the famous city, the city of joy, be abandoned!” Damascus’s own people lament its fall.
Her young men will fall in the streets, and all her soldiers will be silenced that day.

f.w: her young men shall fall in her streets

chapters.n: God will set fire to Damascus’s walls and burn the palaces of Ben-hadad—a royal name used by several Syrian kings.

f.g: “Son of Hadad” (the storm god)—a title of several Aramean kings.

chapters.n: Next, the Arabian desert tribes of Kedar and the “kingdoms of Hazor.” Nebuchadnezzar attacked Arab tribes around 599/598 BC, as Babylonian chronicles record.

f.g: Nomadic Arab tribes descended from Ishmael, known for flocks and tents.
Not the Galilee city, but probably settled Arab villages (Hebrew hatserim).
Desert peoples east of Israel.

chapters.n: Their tents, flocks, tent curtains, goods, and camels will be taken, and people will shout, “Terror on every side!”

f.g: Tent cloths.

chapters.n: Flee far away and hide deep, people of Hazor, for Nebuchadnezzar has made plans against you.
Rise up and attack the carefree, prosperous nation that lives alone, without gates or bars—secure only because it seemed too remote to bother.
Their camels and herds will be plundered. God will scatter to every wind those who clip the corners of their hair, bringing disaster from every side.

f.w: them that are in the utmost corners
f.g: Those who trim the hair at their temples—a desert custom.

chapters.n: Hazor will become a lair for jackals, desolate forever, with no one living there.

f.g: Jackals.

chapters.n: Finally, Elam, a distant kingdom east of Babylon (in today’s southwest Iran). This message came early in Zedekiah’s reign (about 597 BC).

f.g: An ancient kingdom with its capital at Susa; later part of the Persian Empire.

chapters.n: God will break Elam’s bow—its famous archers were its greatest strength.
God will bring winds from all four directions and scatter Elam everywhere; its exiles will reach every nation.
Elam will be shattered before its enemies; God’s fierce anger and the sword will pursue them until they’re consumed.
God will set up his throne in Elam and remove its king and officials. He is sovereign even over the most distant lands.

f.w: I will set my throne in Elam

chapters.n: But in the latter days God will restore Elam’s fortunes. Fittingly, Elamites were among those who heard the gospel on the day of Pentecost.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity of Elam

chapters.n: Chapters 50–51 are a long prophecy against Babylon itself—the empire God had used to punish Judah. In scripture Babylon also becomes a symbol of the wicked world; the Lord in our day says, “Go ye out from Babylon.”

f.g: The great capital on the Euphrates, in today’s Iraq; also a scriptural symbol of worldliness.

chapters.n: Proclaim it to the nations—raise a banner and hold nothing back: Babylon is captured! Her chief gods Bel and Marduk are humiliated, her idols smashed.

f.g: “Lord”—a title of Marduk, Babylon’s chief god.
Marduk, patron god of Babylon.
Raise a signal flag on a hill to announce news.

chapters.n: A nation from the north will come against Babylon and make its land desolate; people and animals will flee. Historically, the Medes and Persians, from the north and east, conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

f.w: out of the north there cometh up a nation

chapters.n: At that time Israel and Judah will come together, weeping as they go, seeking the Lord their God. Babylon’s fall opens the way for repentance and return.
They will ask the way to Zion, facing toward it, and say, “Come, let’s bind ourselves to the Lord in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.”

f.g: Toward that place.

chapters.n: God’s people have been lost sheep; their own shepherds led them astray to wander from mountain to hill—places of idol worship—and they forgot their true resting place, the Lord.

f.w: My people hath been lost sheep

chapters.n: Whoever found them devoured them, saying, “We’re not guilty—they sinned against the Lord, their true pasture and their ancestors’ hope.” Even enemies recognized Israel had abandoned its God.

f.g: Righteous pasture—the Lord as Israel’s true home.

chapters.n: Flee from Babylon! Leave the land of the Chaldeans, and be like the male goats that lead the flock out first. Be among the first to leave.

f.w: Remove out of the midst of Babylon

f.g: Lead goats that go out ahead of the flock.

chapters.n: God will raise up a coalition of great nations from the north against Babylon. Their archers are expert—no arrow comes back empty.

f.g: Like a skilled warrior whose arrows always hit.

chapters.n: Babylonia will be plundered, and its plunderers will have their fill.
Because you rejoiced as you plundered God’s inheritance, frisking like a heifer in the grass and snorting like stallions…

f.g: Israel, God’s own inheritance.
Or “neigh like stallions.”

chapters.n: …your “mother” (Babylon) will be humiliated. She will become the last of the nations—a wilderness, dry land, and desert.

f.g: The least or last of the nations.

chapters.n: Because of God’s wrath, Babylon will be uninhabited; passersby will be shocked and hiss at its wounds. Babylon did decline over centuries and was eventually abandoned.

f.w: every one that goeth by Babylon shall be astonished

chapters.n: Archers, take your positions around Babylon and shoot—spare no arrows—because she sinned against the Lord.
Raise the battle cry! She surrenders; her towers fall and walls are torn down. This is the Lord’s vengeance—do to her as she did to others.

f.g: She has surrendered (literally “given the hand” in submission).

f.w: as she hath done, do unto her

chapters.n: Cut off the farmers who sow and harvest in Babylon. Foreigners living there will flee home from the oppressor’s sword.

f.w: they shall turn every one to his people

chapters.n: Israel is a scattered sheep chased by lions: first Assyria devoured the northern kingdom (722 BC), and finally Nebuchadnezzar gnawed its bones (586 BC).

f.w: first the king of Assyria hath devoured him

chapters.n: So God will punish Babylon’s king and land as he punished Assyria’s king. Assyria’s capital Nineveh fell in 612 BC.

f.w: as I have punished the king of Assyria

chapters.n: God will bring Israel home to graze on rich pastures—Carmel, Bashan, the hills of Ephraim, and Gilead.

f.g: Lush pastures west and east of the Jordan.

chapters.n: In that day, if anyone searches for Israel’s sin, none will be found, because God will forgive the remnant he preserves. Complete forgiveness through the Atonement is the heart of restoration.

f.w: the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none

f.g: The remnant God spares.

chapters.n: Attack the land of Merathaim and the people of Pekod—destroy them completely, as God commands. Both names are wordplays on real Babylonian places.

f.g: “Double rebellion”—a pun on a region in southern Babylonia (mat marratim, “land of the bitter waters”).
“Punishment”—a pun on the Puqudu, an Aramean tribe in eastern Babylonia.

chapters.n: The noise of battle and great destruction fills the land.
How the “hammer of the whole earth” is shattered! Babylon, which smashed other nations, is itself broken.

f.w: the hammer of the whole earth

chapters.n: God set a trap and Babylon was caught unaware, because she fought against the Lord. According to ancient historians, Babylon fell in 539 BC with surprisingly little resistance.
The Lord opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath—the armies he uses for his purposes.
Come from the farthest borders, break open her granaries, pile her up like heaps of grain, and destroy her completely.
Kill all her young bulls—her warriors—let them go down to slaughter. Their day of reckoning has come.

f.g: Young bulls—a picture of her strong young soldiers.

chapters.n: Listen: refugees escaping Babylon arrive in Zion announcing that the Lord has avenged his temple, which Babylon destroyed.
Summon archers to surround Babylon so none escape. Repay her for her deeds, because she defied the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

f.g: A favorite title of God in Isaiah; Latter-day Saints understand it as a name of Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: Her young men will fall in the streets and her soldiers be silenced.

f.w: her young men fall in the streets

chapters.n: “I am against you, O Pride,” says God—Babylon is so proud that “Pride” becomes her name. Her day of reckoning has come.

f.g: Hebrew zadon, “Arrogance”—used as a name for Babylon.

chapters.n: Pride will stumble and fall with no one to lift it up; God will set fire to its cities.

f.w: the most proud shall stumble and fall

chapters.n: Israel and Judah have both been oppressed; their captors hold them tightly and refuse to let them go—like Pharaoh in Egypt.

f.w: they refused to let them go

chapters.n: But their Redeemer is strong—the Lord of hosts is his name. He will plead their case, bringing rest to his people and unrest to Babylon. Latter-day Saints see in “Redeemer” a title of Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew go’el—the kinsman who buys back and defends a family member.
Thoroughly.

chapters.n: A sword on the Chaldeans, on Babylon’s people, its officials, and its wise men! (A poem of repeated “sword” lines, each one falling on a different pillar of Babylon’s pride.)

f.g: Babylon was famed for its astrologers and scholars.

chapters.n: A sword on her false prophets, who will be exposed as fools; a sword on her warriors, who will be terrified.

f.g: Diviners or omen-readers who made false predictions.
Become foolish.

chapters.n: A sword on her horses, chariots, and foreign mercenaries, who will lose their courage; a sword on her treasures, which will be plundered.

f.g: Foreign troops and residents.
An ancient idiom for losing courage in battle.

chapters.n: A drought on her waters to dry them up. Babylon depended on the Euphrates and its canals; the Greek historian Herodotus says Cyrus diverted the river to enter the city. God says it is because Babylon is a land of idols—people obsessed with them.

f.w: A drought is upon her waters
they are mad upon their idols
f.g: They are infatuated with frightful images.

chapters.n: Desert creatures, hyenas, and ostriches will live there; it will never again be inhabited.

f.w: the wild beasts of the islands
f.g: Probably hyenas or jackals.
Probably ostriches.

chapters.n: Like Sodom and Gomorrah, Babylon will be overthrown and no one will live there.

f.w: As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah

chapters.n: A people from the north, a great nation, and many kings are rising from the far ends of the earth.

f.w: Behold, a people shall come from the north

chapters.n: Armed with bows and spears, cruel and merciless, roaring like the sea and riding horses in battle formation—against you, daughter Babylon. These same words once described Babylon’s attack on Jerusalem (6:22-23); now the tables are turned.

f.w: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy

chapters.n: Babylon’s king hears the news and goes limp; anguish seizes him like a woman in labor—just as Jerusalem once felt when Babylon came.
Like a lion from the Jordan thickets attacking a secure pasture, God will chase Babylon away in an instant. Who is like God? Who can challenge him? (Repeating what was said of Edom in 49:19.)

f.w: he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan

chapters.n: Hear God’s plan against Babylon: even the smallest of her flock will be dragged away, and her pastures made desolate.

f.w: the least of the flock shall draw them out

chapters.n: At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth trembles, and the cry is heard among the nations. The empire that seemed eternal falls, as God declared.
The prophecy against Babylon continues. God will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon and against “Leb-kamai”—a coded name for Chaldea.

f.w: them that rise up against me
f.g: Hebrew Leb-qamai, “heart of my adversaries”—an atbash cipher for Kasdim, Chaldea (compare “Sheshach,” verse 41).

chapters.n: God will send “winnowers” to scatter Babylon like chaff and empty her land, attacking from every side in her day of trouble.

f.g: Winnowers—workers who toss grain in the wind to blow away the chaff.

chapters.n: Don’t let her archers draw their bows or her soldiers put on armor; spare none of her young men—destroy her whole army.

f.g: Scale armor.
Army.

chapters.n: The slain will fall throughout Babylonia, pierced through in her streets.
Israel and Judah have not been abandoned by their God, even though their land was full of guilt before the Holy One of Israel. God’s covenant outlasts their failures.
Flee from Babylon! Save your lives; don’t be destroyed in her punishment. This is the time of the Lord’s vengeance. Modern revelation echoes this call to flee spiritual Babylon.

f.w: Flee out of the midst of Babylon

chapters.n: Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord’s hand, making the whole earth drunk; the nations drank her wine and went mad. God used her to deliver his judgment, but she is accountable for her cruelty.
Suddenly Babylon has fallen and shattered! Wail for her; bring balm for her wounds—maybe she can be healed.
“We tried to heal Babylon, but she can’t be healed. Let’s leave her and go home—her guilt reaches the heavens.”
The exiles respond: the Lord has vindicated us; let’s go tell in Zion what our God has done.

f.g: Our vindication—God has shown we were in the right.

chapters.n: Sharpen the arrows! Fill the quivers! God has stirred up the kings of the Medes to destroy Babylon—his vengeance for his temple.

f.g: The Medes, later united with Persia under Cyrus, helped conquer Babylon.
Polish or sharpen them.
