chapters.n: Raise the signal against Babylon’s walls, strengthen the guard, post watchmen, set ambushes—the Lord has planned it and will do it.
You who live by many waters, rich in treasure—your end has come, the thread of your life is cut. Babylon lay on the Euphrates, surrounded by canals.

f.w: O thou that dwellest upon many waters

f.g: Possibly “the thread of your life is cut off,” like a weaver cutting finished cloth.

chapters.n: The Lord swears by himself: he will fill Babylon with enemies as many as locusts, and they will shout in triumph over her.

f.g: Locusts.

chapters.n: Verses 15–19 repeat a hymn from chapter 10: the true God made the earth by his power, founded the world by his wisdom, and stretched out the heavens by his understanding—unlike Babylon’s idols.

f.w: He hath made the earth by his power

chapters.n: When he speaks, the heavens roar with water; he lifts clouds from the ends of the earth, makes lightning for the rain, and brings wind from his storehouses.
Every idol-maker is shown to be foolish; their metal images are frauds with no breath of life.

f.g: Stupid, senseless.
A metalworker who casts idols.

f.w: there is no breath in them

chapters.n: Idols are worthless, objects of mockery; when judgment comes, they will perish.

f.g: Emptiness, a breath.

chapters.n: But the “Portion of Jacob”—Israel’s God—is nothing like them. He made everything, and Israel is the tribe of his inheritance; the Lord of hosts is his name.

f.g: A title for God, who is Israel’s inheritance and treasure.

chapters.n: God addresses his “war club,” the instrument he uses to smash nations and kingdoms. In context this was Babylon herself; now her own ruin is near (some read it as Cyrus or Israel).

f.g: A war club or mace.

chapters.n: With it God shatters horses, riders, chariots, and charioteers…
…men and women, old and young, young men and young women…

f.g: A young woman.

chapters.n: …shepherds and flocks, farmers and oxen, governors and officials. The ninefold “break in pieces” hammers home the totality of the destruction.

f.g: Farmer.

chapters.n: God will repay Babylon and its people, before your eyes, for all the evil they did in Zion.

f.w: all their evil that they have done in Zion

chapters.n: “I am against you, destroying mountain,” says God. He will roll Babylon down from its heights like a burned-out volcano. Babylon was flat, so “mountain” pictures its towering power and perhaps its great temple-tower.
No one will take even a cornerstone or foundation stone from her ruins; she will be desolate forever.

Raise a banner, blow the trumpet, summon nations against her: Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz—peoples of the northern mountains (around modern Armenia) under Median control. Appoint a commander; bring horses like swarming locusts.

f.g: Urartu, the region around Lake Van in eastern Turkey and Armenia.
The Manneans, south of Lake Urmia in northwest Iran.
Probably the Scythians.

chapters.n: Prepare the nations—the kings of the Medes, their governors, officials, and all their subject lands.
The land trembles and writhes, for the Lord’s purpose against Babylon stands: to make it a desolate land.
Babylon’s warriors have stopped fighting and huddle in their fortresses; their strength is gone. Her homes are burning and the bars of her gates are broken.

f.g: Strongholds, fortresses.
Ceased, held back.

chapters.n: Runner after runner, messenger after messenger, races to tell the king that his city has been taken from end to end.

f.g: A courier, running messenger.

f.w: his city is taken at one end

chapters.n: The river crossings are seized, the reed marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.

f.g: Fords or river crossings.
Reed marshes, perhaps used as defenses.

chapters.n: Babylon is like a threshing floor being stamped down before harvest; soon her “harvest” of judgment will come.

f.g: A hard-packed area where harvested grain was trampled to separate it from the stalks.

chapters.n: Jerusalem speaks: “Nebuchadnezzar devoured me, crushed me, emptied me like a jar, swallowed me like a sea monster, stuffed himself with my delicacies, and spit me out.”

f.g: A sea monster or serpent.
Delicacies, choice things.

chapters.n: “May the violence done to me be on Babylon,” Zion says; “May my blood be on the Chaldeans,” Jerusalem says—a cry for justice.

f.w: my blood upon the inhabitants of Chaldea

chapters.n: God answers: I will plead your case and avenge you. I will dry up Babylon’s “sea” and springs—the Euphrates and its canals that were her lifeblood.

f.w: I will dry up her sea

chapters.n: Babylon will become rubble heaps, a haunt of jackals, a horror and a byword, empty of people.

f.g: Jackals.

chapters.n: Babylon’s nobles roar together like lions and growl like lion cubs—ravenous and proud at their feasts.

While they are heated with appetite, God will set a feast for them and make them drunk, so they fall into a sleep they never wake from. Daniel 5 describes Belshazzar’s feast on the night Babylon fell.
God will lead them down like lambs, rams, and goats to the slaughter.
How Sheshach (Babylon) has been captured! The pride of the whole earth seized! What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!

f.g: A cipher for Babylon.
Captured, seized.

chapters.n: The sea has risen over Babylon; she is covered by its roaring waves—the flood of invading armies.

f.w: The sea is come up upon Babylon

chapters.n: Her towns become a dry, desolate wasteland where no one lives or even travels.
God will punish Bel (Marduk) in Babylon and make him vomit up what he swallowed—the nations, people, and temple treasures. Nations will no longer stream to him, and Babylon’s wall will fall.

f.w: that which he hath swallowed up

chapters.n: “My people, get out of her! Save yourselves from the Lord’s fierce anger.” The call to leave Babylon is a theme carried into the New Testament and modern revelation.

f.w: My people, go ye out of the midst of her

chapters.n: Don’t lose heart or panic at the rumors that will come year after year—violence in the land, ruler against ruler. Upheaval will precede the end.

f.g: Report, news.

f.w: a rumour shall both come one year

chapters.n: The days are coming when God will judge Babylon’s idols; the whole land will be shamed, and its slain will fall within it.
Heaven and earth and all in them will sing for joy over Babylon’s fall, when destroyers come from the north.
Babylon must fall for Israel’s slain, just as the slain of all the earth fell because of Babylon.
You who escaped the sword, go—don’t linger! Remember the Lord from far away, and keep Jerusalem in your heart.

f.w: let Jerusalem come into your mind

chapters.n: The exiles reply: “We are ashamed and disgraced, because foreigners have entered the holy places of the Lord’s house.”

f.w: strangers are come into the sanctuaries

chapters.n: God answers: the days are coming when I will judge her idols, and her wounded will groan throughout the land.

Even if Babylon climbed to heaven and fortified her lofty heights, destroyers would still come from God. Babylon’s towering temple-tower recalls the original tower of Babel, built to “reach unto heaven.”

f.w: Though Babylon should mount up to heaven

chapters.n: Listen! A cry from Babylon—the sound of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans.
The Lord is destroying Babylon and silencing her noisy din, though the enemy’s waves roar like great waters.

f.g: Babylon’s loud bustle, the noise of a great city.

chapters.n: The destroyer has come; her warriors are captured and their bows broken, for the Lord is a God of recompense who will surely repay.

f.g: Repay.

chapters.n: God will make Babylon’s officials, wise men, governors, officers, and warriors drunk, and they will sleep forever—declares the King, the Lord of hosts.
Babylon’s massive walls will be leveled and her high gates burned. The nations’ labor to build her ends only in fire—they wear themselves out for nothing.

f.g: Ancient writers described Babylon’s walls as wide enough for chariots to drive on top.

f.w: the people shall labour in vain

chapters.n: A narrative postscript: Jeremiah gave instructions to Seraiah, Baruch’s brother, who traveled with (or for) King Zedekiah to Babylon in his fourth year (about 594/593 BC). Seraiah was the quartermaster in charge of the king’s lodging.

f.g: Brother of Baruch the scribe.
Hebrew sar menuchah—“quartermaster,” the officer in charge of rest-stops.

chapters.n: Jeremiah wrote on a scroll all the disaster that would come on Babylon—the words recorded here.
He told Seraiah: when you reach Babylon, look around and read all these words aloud.
Then pray: “Lord, you have declared that you will cut off this place so that nothing lives here, and it will be desolate forever.”
When you finish reading, tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates.
And say, “So Babylon will sink and never rise again because of the disaster God brings.” The book adds: “Thus far are the words of Jeremiah”—chapter 52 is a historical appendix.

f.w: Thus far are the words of Jeremiah
f.g: An editorial note marking the end of Jeremiah’s own prophecies.

chapters.n: This final chapter is a historical appendix, nearly identical to 2 Kings 24:18–25:30. It confirms that Jeremiah’s prophecies came true. Zedekiah became king at 21 and reigned eleven years (597–586 BC). His mother was also the mother of King Jehoahaz.

f.w: Zedekiah was one and twenty years old

f.g: Not the prophet, who was from Anathoth.

chapters.n: Zedekiah did evil in the Lord’s eyes, just as his brother Jehoiakim had.

f.w: according to all that Jehoiakim had done

chapters.n: Because of the Lord’s anger, things in Judah reached the point where he cast them out of his presence—and Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, breaking his oath of loyalty. This was the trigger for the final siege.

f.w: Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon

chapters.n: On the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah’s ninth year, Nebuchadnezzar arrived with his whole army, camped around Jerusalem, and built siege works.

f.w: in the tenth day of the month

f.g: Siege walls or towers built around the city.

chapters.n: The siege lasted until Zedekiah’s eleventh year—about a year and a half.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, famine was so severe there was no food left for the people. Lamentations describes the horror of these days.

f.w: the famine was sore in the city

f.g: Severe.

chapters.n: The wall was breached. The soldiers fled by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, slipping past the encircling Babylonians toward the Jordan Valley.

f.w: the gate between the two walls

chapters.n: The Babylonians chased and caught Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; his army scattered.

f.w: all his army was scattered from him

chapters.n: They took him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in Syria, who passed sentence on him.

f.w: Riblah in the land of Hamath

chapters.n: Nebuchadnezzar killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and all Judah’s officials at Riblah. The Book of Mormon tells that one son, Mulek, escaped and was brought to the promised land.
Then he blinded Zedekiah, bound him in bronze chains, took him to Babylon, and imprisoned him until he died. Had he followed Jeremiah’s counsel to surrender, it could have been different.

f.w: put out the eyes of Zedekiah

chapters.n: On the tenth day of the fifth month in Nebuchadnezzar’s nineteenth year (586 BC), Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, came to Jerusalem. (2 Kings gives the seventh day.) Jews mourn the temple’s destruction on the ninth of this month, Tisha B’Av.

f.w: in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month

chapters.n: He burned the Lord’s temple, the royal palace, and all Jerusalem’s houses, including the homes of the leading families. Solomon’s temple, about four centuries old, was gone—as Jeremiah had warned in his temple sermon.

f.w: burned the house of the LORD

chapters.n: The Babylonian army tore down all the walls around Jerusalem, leaving it defenseless. Nehemiah would rebuild them about 140 years later.

f.w: brake down all the walls of Jerusalem

chapters.n: Nebuzaradan deported some of the poor, the rest of the people still in the city, the deserters who had gone over to Babylon, and the remaining craftsmen.

f.g: Deserters who had already surrendered.
Or “the rest of the craftsmen.”

chapters.n: But he left some of the poorest people to tend vineyards and farm the land.

f.g: Vineyard workers and farmers.

chapters.n: The Babylonians broke up the huge bronze pillars, the stands, and the great bronze “sea” from the temple and carried the metal to Babylon. Jeremiah had predicted exactly this.

f.g: Bronze (copper alloy).

chapters.n: They also took the bronze pots, shovels, wick-trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and all the bronze utensils used in temple service.

f.g: Tools for trimming lamp wicks.
Small dishes for incense.

chapters.n: The commander took the basins, fire pans, bowls, pots, lampstands, dishes, and cups—anything of gold or silver.

f.w: that which was of gold in gold
f.g: Whatever was gold, as gold; whatever was silver, as silver—taken for their metal value.

chapters.n: The bronze from the two pillars, the sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it, and the stands Solomon made was beyond weighing—too much to measure.

f.g: Too much to be weighed.

chapters.n: Each pillar was 18 cubits tall (about 27 feet / 8 meters), 12 cubits around (about 18 feet), hollow, with bronze four fingers thick.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), the length of a forearm.
A measuring cord—here, the circumference.

chapters.n: Each pillar had a bronze capital five cubits high, decorated with bronze latticework and pomegranates all around. These details remind readers of the glory that was lost.

f.g: Capital—the decorative top of a pillar.
A temple symbol of fruitfulness, also on the high priest’s robe.

chapters.n: There were 96 pomegranates on the sides and 100 in all around the latticework.
Nebuzaradan also arrested the top temple leaders: Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three chief doorkeepers. Seraiah was an ancestor of Ezra the scribe.
From the city he also took an officer over the soldiers, seven royal advisers, the army’s chief scribe who drafted men for service, and sixty prominent citizens.

f.g: Literally “who saw the king’s face”—close advisers. 2 Kings 25:19 says five.
Enlisted, drafted.
Sixty.

chapters.n: Nebuzaradan brought them to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.
Nebuchadnezzar executed them at Riblah. So Judah went into exile from its own land—the covenant curse of exile fulfilled.

f.w: Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land

chapters.n: Here is a count of the people Nebuchadnezzar deported: in his seventh year, 3,023 Jews—likely the 597 BC deportation (counted differently in 2 Kings, which lists about 10,000, probably including families or using a different count).
In his eighteenth year (586 BC), 832 people from Jerusalem.
In his twenty-third year (about 582 BC), Nebuzaradan deported 745 more—perhaps a reprisal after Gedaliah’s murder. Total: 4,600 people, probably counting only adult men.

f.w: In the three and twentieth year

chapters.n: The book ends with a glimmer of hope. In the 37th year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity (about 561/560 BC), the new Babylonian king Evil-merodach released him from prison and treated him with honor.

f.g: Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk,” Nebuchadnezzar’s son (reigned about 562–560 BC). “Evil” is not an English word here.
An idiom for showing favor, releasing from prison.

chapters.n: He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above other captive kings in Babylon.

Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life. Babylonian ration tablets found by archaeologists actually list oil allotments for “Yaukin, king of Judah” and his sons.

He received a daily allowance from the king until he died. Jeremiah’s book thus closes not in total darkness: David’s line survives in exile, a quiet sign that God’s promises of restoration and of a righteous Branch were still alive.

f.g: A regular daily allowance of food.

f.w: all the days of his life
